comments.body:
Six additional adversarial `review diff --staged` rounds run against this PR's final content (on top of the author's own 14 rounds before opening it), fixing what surfaced as real and documenting the rest here per this issue's acceptance criteria.

**Fixed in the PR** (each confirmed by a fresh reviewer round, not self-assessed):
- Unsanitized label containing `/` broke the state-file write silently, falling back to the shared `default` session with no error.
- `tr` sanitization alone is many-to-one (`review/quorum` and `review_quorum` collapsed to one file) — fixed by appending a checksum of the un-sanitized label.
- Check-then-write race on first-time session creation between two parallel Bash calls for the same task — fixed with `set -C` (noclobber) for exclusive creation.
- A reader could land in the instant between file creation and the write landing, reading an empty name — fixed with a bounded 5x50ms retry-read loop, only exporting on non-empty.
- The close snippet regenerated and closed a fresh, never-opened session when its state file was already gone, reporting success while the real daemon leaked — fixed to warn instead of fabricating.
- `tr` without `LC_ALL=C` aborts with "Illegal byte sequence" on this exact platform (macOS/BSD tr, UTF-8 locale) for any non-ASCII label.
- TMPDIR fallback directory and state file were world-readable (default `mkdir`/umask) — fixed to `0700`/`umask 077`.
- A permanently-empty state file (writer terminated between create and write) never self-healed under any code path — fixed with a one-shot reclaim (remove + recreate) when the retry loop exhausts against an existing-but-empty file.

**Documented as accepted, not fixed — real gaps, out of proportion to fix as prose in this pass:**
1. **Open and close snippets are cwd-dependent and can silently resolve different state directories** if the agent's working directory changes between them (e.g. a tool harness that doesn't guarantee a stable cwd across calls). The close snippet then reports "nothing to close" while the real daemon leaks up to Rule 2's 1-hour idle timeout, and the wording actively misattributes the cause. No one-line fix exists short of pinning the resolved directory at setup time and threading it through, which is real state-passing, not a doc fix.
2. **Concurrent same-label siblings silently share one session**, including inheriting each other's cookies/storage, and one's `close` can end the other's live session mid-task. The label-uniqueness contract is advisory and unenforceable from inside the snippet.
3. **Stale-file reuse**: a state file from a genuinely unrelated earlier task (same label, different day) is indistinguishable from this task's own crashed attempt by content alone — the skill documents the ambiguity but doesn't resolve it (an mtime-vs-idle-timeout heuristic was proposed but not implemented).
4. **TMPDIR fallback plant/ownership**: `mkdir -m 700 -p` is a no-op on a directory that already exists with different ownership, so a pre-planted fallback directory from another local user isn't detected. Real fix is an ownership check before trusting the directory's contents.
5. **~50 lines of this race-sensitive shell are duplicated verbatim across two skill files** (`agent-browser-concurrency` and `web-page-reading-agent-browser`), with zero test coverage in either location, in a repo that otherwise pytest-tests every shipped hook/lib script. A future edit to one copy silently un-fixes the other. The credible fix is extracting a real `setup`/`close` script (with a small pytest exercising the parallel-create, terminated-writer, and overlong-label scenarios argued about in prose here) rather than continuing to hand-sync markdown.
6. **The reclaim branch (fix for the empty-state-file item above) is itself a single-shot read with no retry**, so under 3+ concurrent actors all hitting the reclaim path simultaneously, the same empty-window race it exists to fix can reopen one level up. Probability assessed as very low (requires a terminated writer plus genuine 3-way concurrency on one label) — not fixed in this pass.

None of items 1-6 are believed to be reachable by this repo's actual current usage pattern (single-operator machine, tasks not deliberately colliding on labels) — they're recorded here so the real-tooling follow-up (extracting a tested script per item 5) has a concrete spec instead of starting from a blank page, and so nobody re-discovers the same six things from scratch.
The reviewed diff (agent-browser session isolation for concurrent tasks) merged as PR #458 (2026-08-28). Closing — already shipped.

## Why (motivation)
Incident: [HYP-1295](https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-1295/release-cut-and-publish-extension-v0174) in [hyperide/hyper-saas](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas), 2026-08-19. PR [#735](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/pull/735)'s body said the magic-close keyword followed by the ticket id; Linear's own GitHub integration auto-closed the ticket the instant the PR merged, while the ticket's second acceptance criterion (tag pushed and both registries live) had not happened yet. This is the exact case Alex flagged as a process bug: gh ship should not let something merge until acceptance has passed. [task-cli PR 103](https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/pull/103) adds POST-merge detection only -- the merge has already happened by the time it fires. This ticket is the actual prevention: a PRE-merge gate in ship.sh itself.

## User impact
Without this, any PR that references a ticket with a magic-close keyword can trigger the tracker's native auto-close on merge even when that ticket's acceptance criteria describe work that only completes after the merge (a follow-up publish step, a tag push, extra verification) -- the tracker silently shows Done work that is not actually finished, and nobody notices unless they happen to re-check the criteria by hand.

## Cost of inaction
The HYP-1295 class of incident recurs on any future release-style PR that references a ticket with post-merge acceptance steps and a magic-close PR-body keyword -- the exact pattern that triggered Alex's incorrect-order-of-operations complaint keeps happening, only now silently, since the post-merge warning is easy to miss if nobody reads mark-shipped's output.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] ship.sh scans the PR body for a GitHub-Linear magic-close keyword (case-insensitive) followed by a ticket-like token before merging -- proof: a unit test in the ship test suite exercises the scanner against real magic-close phrasings
- [ ] when a magic-closed ticket is resolvable via task-cli and has any unchecked or unproven acceptance criterion, ship.sh refuses the merge with a clear error naming the ticket and the unmet criteria (or requires an explicit override flag), rather than merging and letting the tracker auto-close prematurely -- proof: a ship.sh test with a fake task-cli backend reporting unmet criteria asserts a non-zero exit and no merge call
- [ ] when the ticket has no unmet criteria, or the code cannot resolve the ticket at all (task-cli absent, foreign repo, etc), ship.sh proceeds exactly as it does today -- proof: existing ship.sh tests continue to pass unmodified

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links

## Skipped gates

title: EnterWorktree into a foreign agent's worktree reports success then bricks Bash for the rest of the session
body:
## What's broken

When an agent (orchestrator or a dispatched Claude Code subagent) calls the `EnterWorktree`
tool with `path=<a worktree a DIFFERENT agent created>`, the call reports **SUCCESS**, but
every subsequent Bash tool call for the rest of that agent's session is then refused, even
`pwd`. `ExitWorktree` does not recover it. There is no error message pointing at the actual
cause.

## Where it was hit

Confirmed at least four times in the `hyperide/hyper-saas` project's Claude Code session
history (2026-08), always the same shape: a later agent needing to resume or ship a PR/branch
that a different, earlier agent built in its own worktree tried to `EnterWorktree(path=...)`
directly into that other agent's `.claude/worktrees/agent-<id>` directory instead of pulling
the branch into its own worktree.

## Fix shipped here

Since `EnterWorktree` itself is Claude Code's own built-in tool (not something this repo
controls), the fix is a `pre-worktree-enter` `agents-hooks/v1` guard —
`agent-hooks/enterworktree-foreign-guard/` — wired through `cc_hook_bridge` (see
`lib/cc_hook_bridge/dispatch.py`'s new `EnterWorktree` -> `pre-worktree-enter` mapping) that
intercepts the call BEFORE the tool runs and blocks it outright when the target worktree's
`agent-<id>` directory name doesn't match the calling agent's own `agent_id`, pointing at the
safe alternative (`gh pr checkout <N>`) instead. See that hook's README for the full rule.

Companion rig-cli PR registers the `EnterWorktree` PreToolUse matcher so the mapping actually
fires (the same two-repo split `pre-agent`/`pre-skill` went through).

This is a hyperide-project-reported incident; there is no reproduction harness in THIS repo
(EnterWorktree is a Claude Code built-in, not testable in isolation here) — the fix is
verified via the hook's own unit tests plus a clean-room `cc_hook_bridge` subprocess test that
drives the real dispatcher + the real guard script.

title: feat(block-devserver-primary): unwrap command wrappers (nohup/env/sudo/bash -c) before classification
body:
## What's broken

block-devserver-primary (agent-hooks/block-devserver-primary/, added in #454) recognizes a
dev-server launch by inspecting the FIRST token of a Bash chain segment. A command wrapped in
nohup, env, sudo, time, nice, setsid, exec, command, or bash -c/sh -c has a head token that is
the wrapper, not the package-manager or dev-server binary, so the launch is invisible to the
hook and is allowed even when the underlying checkout is the protected shared one on its
default branch.

## Why this matters

nohup npm run dev & (start a dev server and detach so it survives the current shell/session) is
arguably the most realistic way an agent actually launches a long-running dev server for a
quick live-verification pass, which is exactly the incident class block-devserver-primary
exists to prevent. Right now that exact realistic shape bypasses the hook entirely.

## Prior art in this repo

The sibling no-shell-file-edit hook (agent-hooks/no-shell-file-edit/) already unwraps
bash -c/sh -c and peels leading no-op wrappers (timeout 5 sed -i, env X=1 perl -i,
nice -n10 gawk -i inplace) before its own pattern match. See its README's "Leading no-op
wrappers are peeled before scanning" section for the recursion-depth-capped approach already
working for a structurally similar problem.

## Why this is a separate issue, not folded into #454

Unwrapping needs its own care: a recursion-depth cap (mirroring no-shell-file-edit's),
bash -c re-tokenizing and re-scanning the inner script string (not just skipping the wrapper),
and env's own VAR=val arguments vs. its target command needing to be told apart. Enough
independent complexity to deserve its own focused review.

## Acceptance criteria

- nohup npm run dev &, env npm run dev, sudo -u dev npm run dev, bash -c "npm run dev" (and
  sh -c) are all recognized and blocked when the effective cwd sits on an enrolled repo's
  default branch, matching the bare npm run dev behavior already shipped.
- A recursion/depth cap prevents pathological wrapper nesting from hanging or looping the hook.
- Regression tests for each wrapper, plus a wrapped-and-backgrounded combination.
- README known-scope-limits section in block-devserver-primary is updated once closed.

comments.body:
Update: PR #454 (still open) now peels the BARE form of these wrappers (nohup, env, sudo,
time, nice, setsid, command, exec — no flags), including env's own VAR=val arguments, closing
the single most realistic shape (nohup npm run dev &). Verified:

  nohup npm run dev / env npm run dev / sudo npm run dev / time npm run dev /
  nice npm run dev / setsid npm run dev / command npm run dev / exec npm run dev /
  env NODE_ENV=development npm run dev

all now correctly block. What's left, still open here:

- A wrapper followed by its OWN flag is still unpeeled (sudo -u dev npm run dev,
  nice -n10 npm run dev) — deliberately conservative for now, matches the sibling
  no-shell-file-edit hook's flag-aware peel that this issue should eventually adopt.
- bash -c "npm run dev" / sh -c "npm run dev" — re-parsing the inner script string — still
  fully unhandled.
- A recursion/depth cap for nested wrapping, mirroring no-shell-file-edit's cap.

Scope narrowed accordingly; acceptance criteria below updated.

title: visual-proof-gate: RIG_HATCH_REQUEST approval succeeds with no overrides.log entry
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Reproduced twice in one session working on [hyperide/hyper-saas PR 767](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/pull/767), 2026-08-28 ~13:02 and ~13:29 CEST: committed [client/App.tsx](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/blob/main/client/App.tsx) with RIG_HATCH_REQUEST_VISUAL_PROOF_GATE=<justification> set inline, no fresh legacy marker in ~/.cache/agent-tools/visual-proof (newest was over 2 hours old, outside the 3600-second window), the commit succeeded both times, but ~/.config/agent-tools/overrides.log gained zero new lines either time (checked immediately, file mtime unchanged both times). The [hatch escalation helper module](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/main/lib/agenttools_hatch_escalation/__init__.py)'s own docstring says every attempt where the env var carries a value is logged best-effort, unconditionally.

## User impact
An agent, or a human reviewing the audit trail later, cannot tell whether a visual-proof bypass went through a real live Telegram approval or some other undocumented path. This defeats the audit sink's stated purpose (retrospective gap G-8) and makes it impossible to honestly state in a PR body whether a human actually approved a screenshot-less UI commit.

## Cost of inaction
The escape-hatch audit trail stays silently incomplete; incidents like the [hyperide/hyper-saas PR 764](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/pull/764) zero-review ship (which PR 767 exists to retroactively review) become harder to detect because the audit log itself cannot be trusted as complete.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Reproduce a git commit blocked by visual-proof-gate with RIG_HATCH_REQUEST_VISUAL_PROOF_GATE set to a real justification, confirm the commit is allowed through, and confirm whether ~/.config/agent-tools/overrides.log gains a corresponding line.
- [ ] If the log gains no line, find why request_hatch_approval's unconditional _append_overrides_log call did not fire (or fired to a different path) and fix it so every hatch attempt is auditable as the module's own docstring promises.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

comments.body:
Investigated this directly against the live hook. **The premise here is false — there is no internal error and no `on_error: "open"` fail-open on this path.** The real mechanism is a detection bug, fixed in #474 (ticket #472).

Two separate things were conflated:

**1. The commit named in this report is correct behaviour, not a bug.** `bc04eb11` (`client/App.tsx`, 2026-08-28 10:43:48 +02:00) was allowed by `_proof_fresh()`: the attestation marker `attest-1787906592-f436f6c8c814.json` was written at 10:43:12, **36 seconds earlier**. The gate was already satisfied, so it returned `allow` at that branch and never reached `_decide_block` — which is the only place `request_hatch_approval` (and therefore the audit write) is called. `RIG_HATCH_REQUEST_VISUAL_PROOF_GATE` was set as a precaution and was simply never needed. Zero log entries is the *correct* outcome there: nothing ever asked for an override, so there was no override to log.

Reproduced in isolation — staged `.tsx`, fresh marker, hatch env var set:
```
{"hook_api": "agents-hooks/v1", "decision": "allow"}  exit=0     # overrides.log: 0 new lines
```

**2. The symptom described — an allow with no audit line — is real, but it comes from a different bug.** `_strip_shell_comment` flattened the command with `" ".join(shlex.split(...))`, erasing every newline, while `GIT_COMMIT` anchors to a command head (string start, or after `|`/`&`/`;`). So any **multi-line** command whose first line was not itself the `git` invocation was never recognised as a commit at all:

| command | exit |
|---|---|
| `git commit -m x` | 10 (blocked) |
| `cd <repo>`⏎`git add -A`⏎`git commit -m x` | **0 (allowed)** |
| `echo hi`⏎`git commit -m x` | **0 (allowed)** |

That produces exactly this ticket's signature — commit succeeds, no proof, no hatch prompt, no `overrides.log` line — on the most common shape an agent writes a commit in. Details and fix: #472 / #474.

**Why this matters for the proposed fix here:** the audit log was never the broken component, so hardening the logging would have left the actual hole open while making the gate look better instrumented. Worth noting the guarantee that a draft fix asserted ("whenever the hatch env var carried a value, `overrides.log` gains a line either way") cannot hold as stated anyway — the fresh-marker path above has the hatch set and legitimately logs nothing.

Closing as misdiagnosed; the real defect is tracked in #472 and fixed in #474.

title: Add memory-pressure admission gate + periodic VS Code orphan reaper (2026-08-27/28 hang incident)
body:
## What happened

A long-running orchestrator session in hyperide ran ~10-15 background agents
concurrently, several doing heavy local work at once (extension rebuilds,
multi-model `review` passes -- each spawning multiple provider subprocess
trees, full test suites). Free memory on a 24GB dev machine dropped to
~65MB. Several real VS Code windows hung on native "reload required"/"app
not responding" modals and required manual Force Quit + process cleanup.

## Root cause (two contributing factors, both addressed)

1. Nothing on the machine checked "is there room for one more heavy
   operation" before starting one -- no admission control on memory
   pressure at all.
2. The hyperide e2e test harness (`ext-test-projects/e2e/setup/
   electron-app.ts`) launches isolated VS Code Electron windows for
   capture/debug scripts. When a launching script dies before reaching its
   teardown function, the window is orphaned -- nothing else was watching
   for that class of leak. (340 leaked `hvsc-*` userDataDir fossils found
   on the dev machine, proving this is routine, not rare.)

## What this PR adds

- `agent-hooks/heavy-op-memory-gate/` -- a stateless pre-bash hook that
  reads the machine's real jetsam memory-pressure level
  (`sysctl kern.memorystatus_vm_pressure_level`, the same signal Activity
  Monitor and the OS's own OOM killer use) and blocks STARTING a heavy
  operation (extension rebuild, multi-model `review diff`/`quorum`/
  `brainstorm`/`just-ask`, build/test suite) while pressure is at
  WARN-or-worse. Deliberately NOT a concurrency counter/semaphore/lock --
  see the hook's own module docstring for why that shape was considered and
  rejected (leak/deadlock risk on agent churn). Fails open on any platform
  without the signal.
- `ops/vscode-orphan-reaper/` -- a periodic (15 min) launchd sweep that
  kills leaked isolated VS Code Electron windows the primary fix (a
  pre-launch sweep, landed separately in `hyper-ext-e2e`) doesn't cover:
  when no new harness launch happens for a while. Manually installed for
  now (`install.sh`) -- NOT yet wired into `rig apply`, see the directory's
  README for the follow-up needed (StartInterval support in
  `agenttools_service`).

## Acceptance criteria

- [x] `heavy-op-memory-gate` hook + manifest, unit-tested (48 tests),
      ruff-clean
- [x] `vscode-orphan-reaper` script + plist template + install/uninstall,

      machine

comments.body:
Two more findings from the final review round (Codex), on the STABLE_DIR copy mechanism added to install.sh earlier in this PR's review cycle. Filed rather than fixed here to stop review-round churn on an already-large diff:

- **P1 — non-atomic replacement can permanently break an already-installed reaper.** `install.sh` overwrites the live script at `$STABLE_DIR/reap_vscode_orphans.py` before the plist is validated or the update completes. If disk fills or I/O is interrupted mid-`cp`, the destination could be left truncated while the already-loaded launchd plist keeps invoking that now-corrupt path every 15 minutes. Fix: copy to a temp file in `STABLE_DIR`, validate it (including a Python compile check), then atomically `mv` into place only after the whole update (including the plist swap) is ready.
- **P2 — uninstall leaves the machine-level executable copy behind.** `install.sh --uninstall` only unloads/removes the plist; the script copied to `$STABLE_DIR` is never removed, since that path is computed after the `--uninstall` early-exit branch. Violates the README's documented "unload + remove" contract and accumulates stale code after uninstall. Fix: compute the stable path before option handling, and remove the script (and empty owned directories) during `--uninstall` too.

Both are about the stable-path copy mechanism itself (added to fix a separate, real bug: a worktree-relative plist path going stale after normal post-merge cleanup), not about the reverted marker-configurability feature.

title: Wire vscode-orphan-reaper (and future periodic jobs) into rig apply's machine-wide provisioning

title: ci/ship: extract shared hatch-helper + audit-log logic (3rd/4th copy drift, found by review-cli across GH-459)
body:
## Context

While building `ci/ship/external_review_hatch.py` and its shell-side gate in `ci/ship/ship.sh` (PR #460, closes #459), three independent review-cli passes (GLM in the light preset, GLM again in the default-preset pass, and GLM a third time after the gate was relocated) all flagged the same underlying issue: this is now the THIRD near-verbatim copy of the "hatch CLI helper" pattern (`skip_ci_hatch.py`, `review_quorum_hatch.py`, `external_review_hatch.py`), and the FOURTH copy of the shell-side JSONL audit-log pipeline (`_skip_ci_audit_log`, `_review_quorum_audit_log`, `_external_review_audit_log`, plus the known-flake audit).

Concrete drift already visible after only one more copy:
- `external_review_hatch.py` dropped several of `skip_ci_hatch.py`'s explanatory comments (why the module is registered in `sys.modules` before `exec_module`; why blank/bare is denied locally) while keeping the code.
- The escaping pipeline (`tr '\n\r\t' '   ' | tr -d '\000-\010\013\014\016-\037' | sed 's/\\/\\\\/g; s/"/\\"/g'`) — the one place a bug would be a real vulnerability (JSONL injection into the audit sink) — is now copy-pasted 4 times. A fix would need to land 4x.
- The hatch verdict-parsing stanza (`hrc=0; hout=$(...) || hrc=$?; hverdict=...; case "$hverdict" in DENIED) ...`) is now triplicated across the quorum/skip-ci/external-review gates, with a structural inconsistency: the external-review copy is top-level (leaks variables globally, can't use `local`) while the other two are wrapped in functions.
- `external_review_hatch.py`'s `# pragma: no cover` comment claims the import-failure path is "exercised via the detached-copy integration test" — that test exists for the OTHER two helpers, not this one, so the claim is currently false for this file.
- The `$HOME`-vs-real-home divergence between the Python helper's `_audit()` (uses `resolve_home()`, the real OS home) and each shell-side `_*_audit_log()` fallback (`${SHIP_AUDIT_FILE:-$HOME/...}`) is pre-existing (same in `_skip_ci_audit_log`), not new — but now exists identically in a 3rd/4th place too, so a fix should cover all of them at once.

## Suggested fix

- Extract the Python hatch-CLI skeleton into a shared runner, e.g. `ci/ship/_hatch_cli.py` exposing something like `run(hook_id: str, gate_label: str, decision_prefix: str, extra_ctx: dict) -> int`, loaded via the same `spec_from_file_location` fixed-path mechanism each thin entrypoint already uses (preserves the `-I` isolation / fixed-path-import security invariant). Each of `skip_ci_hatch.py`, `review_quorum_hatch.py`, `external_review_hatch.py` shrinks to ~20 lines of constants + a call into the shared runner.
- Extract the shell-side JSONL escaping + audit-append into one `_gate_audit_log <gate> <decision> [reason]` helper (fixing the $HOME-vs-real-home divergence for all callers in one place while at it).
- Extract the hatch verdict-parsing stanza into a shared `_hatch_refuse_unless_approved <hatch-check-fn> <gate-prefix>` shell function.
- Along the way: restore the dropped explanatory comments, fix the `# pragma: no cover` claim (either add the missing detached-copy test for `external_review_hatch.py`, or drop the claim), and expose a public `is_bare_flag_value()` on `agenttools_hatch_escalation` instead of every caller reaching into the private `_BARE_FLAG_VALUES`.

## Why deferred rather than fixed in #460

#460's job is closing the "ship.sh has zero check for an actual GitHub review" gap (issue #459) — a real, independently-verified incident (hyperide/hyper-saas PR #764 merged with zero reviews). The duplication above is a pre-existing pattern (2 copies already existed before #460 added a 3rd) that #460 replicated faithfully rather than introduced. A shared-extraction refactor touching 3 Python files + ~4 shell functions used by every `gh ship` invocation across every repo that consumes this shared script is a genuine architecture change with its own blast radius — doing it inside #460 would have mixed a security-gate PR with an unrelated structural refactor, and delayed closing #459 further. Tracked here instead per the repo's own deferred-findings-tracking discipline.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] One shared Python hatch-CLI runner backs all three (`skip_ci_hatch.py`, `review_quorum_hatch.py`, `external_review_hatch.py`), each reduced to its gate-specific constants.
- [ ] One shared shell `_gate_audit_log` helper backs all four current audit call sites (skip-ci, review-quorum, external-review, known-flake), with a single, consistent real-home-vs-`$HOME` default.
- [ ] One shared shell hatch-verdict-parsing helper backs the quorum/skip-ci/external-review hatch call sites.
- [ ] Full `tests/test_ship.py` + `tests/test_ship_notify_task_cli.py` suite still green after the refactor (currently 255 tests).
- [ ] `external_review_hatch.py`'s `# pragma: no cover` comment is either backed by a real detached-copy test or removed.

comments.body:
## Additional finding (Codex, PR #460 review thread): hatch approval context shows `os.getcwd()`, not the actual target repo

Flagged as a P2 on PR #460's GitHub review: `external_review_hatch.py`'s Telegram approval context sets `"repo": os.getcwd()`. When `ship.sh` is invoked with `--repo owner/target` (or `GH_SHIP_REPO`/an ambient `GH_REPO`), the actual PR being merged lives in a DIFFERENT repo than the local checkout — so the live Telegram approval prompt shown to Alex can display the wrong repo, while the merge proceeds against the real `--repo` target. Confirmed this is a pre-existing pattern: `skip_ci_hatch.py:158` and `review_quorum_hatch.py:137` both have the identical `"repo": os.getcwd()`, predating PR #460.

Suggested fix (once the shared extraction from this ticket lands, or standalone): thread `ship.sh`'s already-resolved `_EFFECTIVE_TARGET` (see `ship.sh:496`, which already folds `--repo`/`GH_SHIP_REPO`/ambient `GH_REPO` together) into the hatch subprocess as an env var (e.g. `SHIP_HATCH_REPO`), and have each hatch helper prefer that over `os.getcwd()` when set. Applies to all three hatch helpers identically — fix once, apply to all three (naturally falls out of the shared-runner extraction this ticket already tracks).

Deferred from #460 for the same reason as the rest of this ticket: pre-existing pattern across 2 other files, not introduced by that PR, and a proper fix touches shared plumbing (ship.sh's env exports + all 3 helpers) rather than being a local, isolated change.

title: visual-proof-gate & skills-read-gate: a multi-line command silently bypasses both gates (newline is not treated as a command separator)
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Both hooks call _strip_shell_comment, which does a space-join over shlex.split(command, comments=True). That erases every newline. Their detection regexes GIT_COMMIT and BUILD_OR_TEST anchor a match to a COMMAND HEAD (string start, or just after a pipe/ampersand/semicolon) and a newline is in neither class. So once newlines were flattened to spaces, the only commit still detectable was one whose FIRST line was itself the git invocation.

## User impact
Multi-line is the ordinary shape an agent writes a shell command in, so in practice the visual-proof gate was open for most real commits: UI files committed with no screenshot, no Telegram approval prompt, and no audit line in the overrides log. Externally indistinguishable from a gate that simply never fired. Reproduced directly against the live hook: a three-line cd/add/commit with a staged .tsx file and no proof marker returns exit 0 (allow), while the identical command on one line returns exit 10 (block).

## Cost of inaction
The repo's two commit-time security gates keep failing open on the most common command shape while continuing to look healthy: no error, no log line, nothing to notice. Every audit of whether an agent looked at a screenshot before committing UI silently under-reports, and the recurring symptom keeps being re-diagnosed as an audit-logging bug instead of a detection bug.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A git commit staging user-visible files is BLOCKED when written multi-line (a cd / set -e / echo on line 1, the commit below it), not only when git is the first word of the whole command.
- [ ] skills-read-gate likewise fires on a multi-line commit or build or test invocation.
- [ ] Multi-line PROSE stays unmatched: the words git and commit on two lines of one quoted echoed string must NOT be read as an invocation.
- [ ] A backslash-newline continuation is treated as ONE command, and a hash comment is stripped per LINE so it cannot swallow the command below it.
- [ ] Regression tests cover all of the above in both hooks, and the full pytest suite is green.

title: block-devserver-primary: shell-parser fidelity gaps (escaped whitespace before #, escaped & adjacent to real &, over-cap cd base)
body:
Follow-up from PR #469 round-4 Codex review (all P2, deliberately deferred per the PR's own termination rule — see PR body). Not folded into #463, which is scoped to command-wrapper peeling specifically.

Three deliberate-evasion-only gaps in `block_devserver_primary.py`'s hand-rolled shell scanner (`_split_chain`, `_apply_cd_to_candidates`). Each requires a crafted, unusual shell construct to trigger — none regress the common-path shapes (`npm run dev # comment`, `npm run dev &`, `cmd 2>&1`) already covered by tests.

## 1. Escaped whitespace before `#` is not recognized as mid-word

`echo \ #literal; cd /protected-main; npm run dev` — bash treats `#literal` as part of the word containing the escaped space (the space itself is a literal character, not a real word boundary), so the whole thing including the following `;`-separated commands executes for real. The current word-start check (`agent-hooks/block-devserver-primary/block_devserver_primary.py:357`) only looks at the raw last character of `buf`, not whether it was itself an escaped/literal space — so it misreads `#literal` as opening a real comment and discards the real, executing `cd`/`npm run dev` as comment text, wrongly allowing the launch.

Codex's exact finding: "Fresh evidence adjacent to the comment fix is that raw trailing whitespace does not necessarily mean shell word-start... word-start tracking must account for whether whitespace was escaped."

## 2. A bare `&` immediately following an escaped `&` is not recognized as a real operator

`echo \&& npm run dev` — bash treats the first `&` as a literal argument character (escaped) and the SECOND `&` as a real background operator, so `npm run dev` really launches as its own backgrounded command. The current escape check (`agent-hooks/block-devserver-primary/block_devserver_primary.py:365`) looks at the raw previous character in the command string when deciding whether an ampersand is part of `&&`/background syntax — since that raw previous character is also `&`, the guard treats the SECOND ampersand as escaped/non-operator too, leaving one `echo`-headed segment and missing the real `npm run dev` launch entirely.

Codex's exact finding: "Bash treats the first ampersand as a literal argument and the second as a real background operator, so npm launches... this guard suppresses that operator and leaves one `echo`-headed segment."

## 3. A candidate dropped for being "safe and over the cap" can't be the base of a later relative `cd`

After the round-3 fix (`_apply_cd_to_candidates`, `agent-hooks/block-devserver-primary/block_devserver_primary.py:984`), a candidate is only dropped once confirmed NOT gated (`_resolve_gate` returns `None`) — but "not gated as an absolute base" doesn't mean "safe to drop as a base for a LATER relative `cd`". With 7 harmless conditional branches already filling the candidate cap, `true && cd /base; cd repo; npm run dev` can resolve to an enrolled `/base/repo` on `main` — but `/base` itself isn't gated (only `/base/repo` is), so `/base` gets dropped for being over the cap, and the later relative `cd repo` transition from it is never evaluated at all.

Codex's exact finding: "a target being safe now does not make it safe as the base of a later relative cd... over-cap states need a conservative representation that remains usable by later directory changes."

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `echo \ #literal; cd /protected-main; npm run dev` from a protected default-branch checkout is BLOCKED (currently allowed)
- [ ] `echo \&& npm run dev` from a protected default-branch checkout is BLOCKED (currently allowed)
- [ ] A chain with 7+ harmless conditional `cd` branches followed by a conditional `cd` to a safe-but-still-relevant base, then a relative `cd` from that base into a gated directory, then a launch, is BLOCKED (currently allowed)
- [ ] Regression tests for all three, following the existing test file's pattern (`tests/test_block_devserver_primary.py`)
- [ ] No regression on the existing 125+ tests

## Context

Part of the worktree-mutation-guard effort (#454) — a `pre-bash` hook that blocks a dev-server launch (`npm run dev`, `vite`, etc.) against a repo's shared/default-branch checkout. Went through 3 full review rounds on PR #469 (4, 5, 5 findings respectively, all fixed) before this 4th round surfaced these 3 remaining, deliberately-crafted-evasion-only gaps. Deferred per the PR's own stated termination rule (only P0/P1 get fixed inline; P2s here go to a follow-up) to avoid an unbounded review-fix loop on a hand-rolled shell parser that will never fully equal a real shell.

title: visual-proof-gate: the proof marker is machine-global and content-blind, so any agent's screenshot satisfies every other agent's gate
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
_proof_fresh() accepts ANY file in ~/.cache/agent-tools/visual-proof whose mtime is within the freshness window. It never reads the file, never checks which repo or which diff it relates to, and the directory is one shared machine-global path. Verified directly: writing a file containing the text 'totally unrelated garbage' into that directory makes the gate return allow for a staged .tsx in an unrelated scratch repo.

## User impact
With many agents working concurrently on one machine, one agent capturing a single screenshot opens the gate for every other agent, in every repo, for the whole freshness window (default one hour). The gate then reports success while proving nothing about the change actually being committed, which is worse than a gate that is visibly off because it produces false confidence in the audit trail.

## Cost of inaction
The visual-proof gate keeps looking enforced while being satisfiable by an unrelated or empty marker, so UI changes continue to ship without anyone having looked at them, and the freshness window silently converts one screenshot into a machine-wide hour-long exemption.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A proof marker records what it attests to (at minimum the repo and the changed files it was captured for), and the gate only accepts a marker that matches the commit it is gating.
- [ ] A marker written while working on repo A does not satisfy a commit in unrelated repo B.
- [ ] A file with arbitrary unrelated content dropped into the proof directory does not satisfy the gate.
- [ ] Concurrent agents each need their own proof for their own change; one agent's capture does not open the gate for the others.

title: visual-proof-gate & skills-read-gate: residual shell-parser divergences from bash in the heredoc path
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The heredoc support in these two hooks exists to avoid false blocks on commands that write a script via a heredoc. It is a hand-written shell parser built from a regex plus shlex, and six review rounds each found a further construction where it diverges from bash: escaped operators before a hash, arithmetic nesting at successive depths, delimiter words assembled from adjacent quoted fragments, and shlex's own comment handling firing mid-word. Every one was found and fixed, but the supply is clearly not exhausted, because regex plus shlex has unbounded divergence from a real shell grammar.

## User impact
None of these are reachable by an agent writing an ordinary commit; they are adversarial constructions, and this hook's declared contract is process discipline with an explicit fail-open on error rather than a security boundary. The residual risk is therefore narrow. It is still worth deciding deliberately whether these hooks should own a shell parser at all, instead of discovering the answer one review round at a time.

## Cost of inaction
The parser keeps growing inside a hook that runs before every shell command on the machine, and each new construction is discovered by review rather than by design. The alternative - dropping heredoc handling and accepting a rare fail-closed false block - never gets evaluated on its merits.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Each adversarial construction listed in the ticket body is either handled to match bash, or explicitly documented as an accepted divergence with its fail direction stated.
- [ ] The decision recorded in the ticket says whether these hooks keep a hand-written shell parser at all, or drop heredoc handling and accept fail-closed false blocks instead.
- [ ] If the parser is kept, a property test fuzzes it against a real bash parse for the constructions in scope, rather than relying on hand-written cases only.

title: vscode-orphan-reaper's hvsc- naming convention is hardcoded, not safely configurable yet
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
A first attempt at this (review round on [GH-467](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/467)) accepted an arbitrary env-var string validated only by minimum length, and was reverted before merge: a real, live VS Code session's argv legitimately contains --user-data-dir=/Users/.../Application Support/Code (verified live on a real machine), so a plausible marker like the literal word 'Code' would match ANY session's userDataDir value -- including an actively-debugged extension-development window (which also legitimately carries --extensionDevelopmentPath, the reaper's OTHER required marker) older than 90 minutes, and get it SIGKILLed

## User impact
Today this ops script only works for hyperide's own hvsc-<n>-<uuid> convention, hardcoded -- a different project that wants this same orphan-reaping capability for its own isolated E2E harness cannot adopt it without forking the file and re-auditing the same safety trap, since the review round already showed the obvious 'just take an env var' approach is a real hazard

## Cost of inaction
This ops script stays hyperide-specific forever despite living in a shared, multi-project catalog repo -- either it never gets reused by another project, or someone re-implements naive substring configurability again and reintroduces the exact SIGKILL-a-real-session hazard this ticket documents

title: ship.sh task-cli notify: wrong-ticket derivation can mark an unrelated open ticket as shipped
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
During a ship of [hyperide/hyper-saas](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas) pull request [#768](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/pull/768) (gh ship 768), the [ci/ship/ship.sh](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/main/ci/ship/ship.sh) task-cli notify step associated the merge with [HYP-1367](https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-1367) instead of [HYP-1399](https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-1399), the ticket the PR actually closed. The unrelated ticket was a related but already-completed one, so this occurrence was harmless. Likely mechanism: the notify step derives the ticket code by trying, in order, a reused Guard-B TASK_CODE (itself derived from branch then PR body only, never the title), then branch, then PR title, then PR body, via a first-match regex. If the real closing ticket is named only in the PR title, but a related or superseded ticket appears earlier in the branch name or PR body and gets adopted as Guard-B's own TASK_CODE, the notify step's title fallback never runs, because a non-empty reused TASK_CODE short-circuits the search before the title is ever consulted. This looks structurally similar to a previously fixed bug in the same file (checked PR body before title, picking up a wrong-ticket mention), fixed in [agent-tools#451](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/451) -- this may be a recurrence of the same class of bug through a different code path, or a genuinely separate cause; needs investigation to confirm which.

## User impact
A wrong ticket notified by the shipping tool produces a false signal a teammate can trust incorrectly: task-cli's mark-shipped updates the ticket's tracked state to show it was shipped via this PR, even though it never closes the ticket outright. If the wrongly-notified ticket is a distinct, still-in-progress ticket, a reader could mistake that shipped marker for real completion and stop tracking genuinely outstanding work on it.

## Cost of inaction
The next time two genuinely distinct open tickets are both referenced near a shipped PR, the ship tool will silently mark the wrong one as shipped. Nothing currently catches this: the notify step is deliberately best-effort and never fails the ship, so no error surfaces anywhere; the mismatch is only ever found by a human noticing an unexpected shipped marker on the wrong ticket.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Reproduce with a PR that references two distinct, genuinely OPEN tickets (one real closer, one merely related/mentioned): confirm whether _ship_derive_task_code_for_notify / _ship_notify_task_cli in [ci/ship/ship.sh](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/main/ci/ship/ship.sh) picks the PR's actual closing ticket, or the first HYP-<n> match found by source-priority order.
- [ ] Audit the derivation order (reused TASK_CODE, then branch, then PR title, then PR body, via _review_quorum_extract_ticket's first-regex-match logic): confirm/deny whether the Guard-B review-quorum gate's own TASK_CODE (derived from branch then body only, never title) gets reused as-is by the notify step without ever falling through to the title, even when the title carries the real ticket code.
- [ ] If confirmed, fix so the notify step either independently verifies title/body agreement with a reused TASK_CODE, or checks the title before accepting a branch- or body-derived code, so the notified ticket always matches the PR's real closing ticket.
- [ ] Add a test fixture to the ship.sh test suite covering a PR with two distinct open ticket codes (one in the title as the real closer, one earlier in the branch name or body) to lock in the fix.

title: refresh-agent-tools-checkout.sh: recheck ship-running immediately before merge, not just before fetch
body:
## Background

Follow-up from a Codex GitHub-side review comment on #470 (agent-tools checkout staleness
gate + refresh-agent-tools-checkout.sh self-heal script), P2, deliberately deferred rather
than fixed in that PR so its diff stays tight.

## The gap

`refresh-agent-tools-checkout.sh`'s guard 5 (`_ship_running`) checks — once, via `pgrep` —
whether a `ci/ship/ship.sh` invocation from the checkout being refreshed looks to be
running, BEFORE the `git fetch` (which can take up to the script's own 30s timeout, or be
unbounded when no `timeout`/`gtimeout` binary is on PATH). If a `gh ship` invocation starts
during that fetch window, the refresh script has already passed its one running-process
check and proceeds straight to `git merge --ff-only`, potentially rewriting `ci/ship/ship.sh`
out from under a `gh ship` process that is mid-way through interpreting the file.

Reviewer's suggested fix: recheck `_ship_running` again immediately before the merge step
(after the fetch), not only before it.

## Why deferred, not fixed inline

This narrows an existing best-effort race window; it does not create a new one, and the
script is not yet installed anywhere (no launchd/cron job references it yet — see its own
header's install recipe), so this is a latent hardening item, not a live bug. Fixing #470's
confirmed data-loss P1 (ignored-path collision, ancestor/descendant directions) needed
priority and its own dedicated regression tests; bundling this race-window fix in risked
diluting review attention on the more severe finding.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `_ship_running "$ROOT"` (or equivalent) is rechecked after the `git fetch` and
      immediately before `git merge --ff-only`, not only before the fetch.
- [ ] A regression test simulates (or directly asserts) that a `ci/ship/ship.sh` process
      appearing between the pre-fetch check and the merge step causes the refresh to skip,
      mirroring the existing `test_skips_when_ship_running_from_this_checkout` test's style.
- [ ] No behavior change for the common case (no ship running throughout) — existing tests
      in `tests/test_refresh_agent_tools_checkout.py` still pass unmodified.

## User impact if not fixed

Low likelihood, but real if it fires: an unattended `refresh-agent-tools-checkout.sh` run
(once actually installed via launchd/cron) could rewrite `ci/ship/ship.sh` mid-interpretation
by a concurrently-running `gh ship`, causing an unpredictable failure or partial execution of
that ship invocation. Bounded to the fetch-duration window (up to ~30s, or the network
timeout when no `timeout` binary is resolvable).

comments.body:
Two more, related hardening findings from the same class of "the script's guards are checked once, before a fetch that can take time, and something can change underneath them" — adding here rather than opening two more tickets, since this one already covers the ship-running race.

1. Guards 1-3 (on main, clean, not-ahead) aren't rechecked after the fetch. If the checkout switches from main to a feature branch WHILE the fetch is running, the stale _guards_ok result (checked before the fetch) still applies, and the merge fast-forwards that feature branch — violating the script's own promise to never touch a feature checkout mid-development. Fix: rerun _guards_ok immediately before the git merge --ff-only, not only once up front.

2. Canonicalizing ROOT breaks live-ship detection through a symlinked checkout alias. _ship_running searches pgrep -f for the canonicalized (pwd -P) path, but a gh ship process invoked as "bash /path/alias/ci/ship/ship.sh" keeps the alias in its own command line, not the canonical path — so a live ship through a symlinked checkout is missed. Fix: preserve the originally-supplied path alongside the canonical one and check both, or use a detection method that doesn't depend on matching the exact command-line path string.

## Acceptance criteria (additional, on top of the existing one)

- [ ] _guards_ok (or equivalent) is rechecked immediately before the merge, not only before the fetch — a regression test simulates the checkout branch changing between the two.
- [ ] _ship_running recognizes a live process invoked via a symlinked/aliased path, not only the canonicalized one — a regression test covers a symlinked checkout.

Source: Codex GitHub-side review on #470's second round (commit 04222314), findings on refresh-agent-tools-checkout.sh lines 218 and 81.

title: vscode-orphan-reaper is coupled to hyperide's e2e-harness convention but lives in the shared agent-tools catalog
body:
## What

`ops/vscode-orphan-reaper/` (added in #477, tracking parent #467) hardcodes hyperide's `hvsc-<n>-<uuid>` userDataDir naming convention and `--extensionDevelopmentPath` argv marker (see `_ISOLATED_MARKERS` in `reap_vscode_orphans.py` and the matching predicate in hyperide's own `ext-test-projects/e2e/setup/electron-app.ts`). This is documented and deliberate (see the ops directory's README 'Documented coupling' section, and #481 for why the marker isn't safely configurable yet), but a real GitHub-side Codex review on #477 flagged it P1: this operational artifact is not portable catalog content and will drift independently from the hyperide project that owns its matching contract, since agent-tools is a shared, multi-project repo.

## Why (motivation)

agent-tools is meant to be a shared catalog consumed by multiple projects. An ops script whose entire safety-critical matching logic is hardcoded to one consumer's private naming convention doesn't belong there long-term -- it should either move into the owning repo (hyperide, next to `ext-test-projects/e2e/setup/electron-app.ts`, the file it already says it mirrors by hand) or be redesigned to accept its markers from a config file the owning repo ships, once #481's safety concerns about arbitrary configurability are resolved.

## User-facing impact if not done

No immediate breakage -- the reaper keeps working correctly for hyperide today. The risk is silent drift: if hyperide's e2e harness ever changes its `hvsc-*` convention or the `--extensionDevelopmentPath` marker, this script's copy won't be updated in the same PR (different repo, different reviewers), and the periodic launchd sweep either stops catching real orphans (naming changed, script's markers didn't) or -- lower probability given the two-marker conjunction and age gates, but the actual failure mode #481 exists to prevent -- starts missing/mismatching a live session's markers.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Decide and document (in this issue or a linked design note) whether the fix is (a) moving `ops/vscode-orphan-reaper/` into the hyperide repo, or (b) parameterizing agent-tools' copy via a config file hyperide ships, with the safety analysis from #481 folded in for option (b).
- [ ] Whichever direction is chosen, implement it, and remove or update the 'Documented coupling' caveat in the ops directory's README (or delete the directory here, if moved).

## Where this came from

Codex GitHub-side review on alex-mextner/agent-tools#477 (P1, on `ops/vscode-orphan-reaper/README.md`), 2026-08-28. Ticket filed 2026-08-29 while landing #477 (part of a systemic fix for a real macOS out-of-memory crash from leaked VS Code test-instance processes) -- deferred here per this repo's merge-discipline rule that a finding requiring cross-repo restructuring can't be fixed inside a single-repo PR.

title: heavy_op_memory_gate: shell operators (;, &&, etc.) can hide a heavy command from classification
body:
## What

`classify_heavy_operation()` in `agent-hooks/heavy-op-memory-gate/heavy_op_memory_gate.py` uses `shlex.split` to tokenize a command before checking for heavy-operation runner/subcommand names. A shell separator attached directly to a token (`pytest; echo done`, `npm test;`, `(pytest)`) is preserved as PART of that token by `shlex.split`, so these real workloads are classified as non-heavy and bypass the gate during WARN-or-higher memory pressure.

Found by real GitHub-side Codex review on PR #477, 2026-08-29.

## Why (motivation)

This function is a hard-block memory-safety gate added after a real 2026-08-27/28 near-total memory-exhaustion incident (agent-tools#467) -- silently ALLOWING a genuinely heavy operation under memory pressure is the dangerous failure direction (the exact thing this gate exists to prevent), not a cosmetic classification miss.

## User-facing impact if not done

A heavy test/build/review command with a shell operator directly attached (no space before `;`/`&&`) can run unthrottled during a WARN-or-higher memory-pressure window, contributing to the same class of incident this gate was built to stop -- on a machine already under strain from concurrent agent work.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Split on shell operators (`;`, `&&`, `||`, `|`, subshell parens) before applying the existing basename/subcommand classification, so each resulting segment is classified independently.
- [ ] Verify live (not just unit-tested) that this doesn't reintroduce the false-negative regression a previous, stricter classifier attempt caused (`cd /repo && pnpm test`, `sudo pytest`, `env CI=1 npm test`, `npm --prefix x test` all stopped matching in that attempt -- see the docstring above `classify_heavy_operation` and commit 335944a for the full history). This function has already had one review round revert a fix that traded one failure class for a worse one; this follow-up needs the same live-verification discipline before landing, not just passing unit tests.
- [ ] Add regression tests for the specific attached-operator cases from the review finding: `pytest; echo done`, `npm test;`, `(pytest)`.

## Where this came from

GitHub-side Codex review on alex-mextner/agent-tools#477 (P2, on `agent-hooks/heavy-op-memory-gate/heavy_op_memory_gate.py:163`), 2026-08-29.

title: vscode-orphan-reaper: ps args= is a space-flattened display string, not real argv -- fundamental limit on marker-boundary anchoring
body:
## What

`reap_vscode_orphans.py` (and its TypeScript sibling in the hyperide repo, `ext-test-projects/e2e/setup/electron-app.ts`) read process command lines via `ps -o args=`, which returns a SPACE-FLATTENED display string, not the process's actual argv array -- argv boundary information (which spaces are real separators between arguments vs. spaces that were INSIDE one argument's own value) is destroyed before this reaper ever sees it.

A real GitHub-side Codex review on PR #477 (round 6) demonstrated the consequence: a process with a real, hvsc-shaped `--user-data-dir=` and one unrelated argument whose OWN value contains an internal space immediately followed by text spelling out the `--extensionDevelopmentPath` marker (e.g. `--note="diagnostic --extensionDevelopmentPath"`) would satisfy both markers via the current token-boundary-anchored regexes, even though there's no real `--extensionDevelopmentPath` flag. No regex-level anchor over `ps`'s flattened string can close this -- the ambiguity is structural, not a diff-level bug. Codex's own suggested remedy is to preserve real argv boundaries (i.e. stop using `ps -o args=` and read via `sysctl(KERN_PROCARGS2)` through ctypes, or an equivalent mechanism that gives NUL-separated argv), which is a different implementation, not a fix to the current one.

## Why NOT fixed inside #477

This is genuinely different in kind from the earlier findings fixed in #477 (rounds 1-6): those were all plausible ACCIDENTS a real developer could trigger unintentionally (a fixture folder literally named `hvsc-test-fixture`, a flag value that happens to embed another flag's literal text). This one requires an argv token whose value contains an internal space followed by text that spells out a marker flag, co-occurring with a real hvsc-shaped `--user-data-dir=` on the SAME process -- adversarial construction, not something that occurs by accident in normal usage. Given the fix requires a genuinely different mechanism (real argv, not `ps` text), it does not belong inside an already-large, already-rounds-deep PR.

## User-facing impact if not done

Extremely low in practice (requires deliberately constructed argv, not accidental), but real: a live, unrelated VS Code window could theoretically be misidentified as an orphan and SIGKILLed if its argv happened to have this exact shape.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Investigate replacing `ps -o args=` with a mechanism that preserves real argv boundaries on macOS (`sysctl(KERN_PROCARGS2)` via `ctypes`, or an equivalent). This affects BOTH the Python reaper (`ops/vscode-orphan-reaper/reap_vscode_orphans.py`) and its TypeScript sibling in the hyperide repo (`ext-test-projects/e2e/setup/electron-app.ts`) -- the marker predicates there have the identical `ps`-flattening exposure.
- [ ] If that's too heavy an investment relative to the (very low) real-world risk, at minimum document this as an accepted, structural limitation in both files' module docstrings (not just this ticket), so a future reviewer doesn't re-discover it as a surprise.

## Where this came from

GitHub-side Codex review on alex-mextner/agent-tools#477 (P1, round 6, on `ops/vscode-orphan-reaper/reap_vscode_orphans.py`), 2026-08-29. A local GLM review pass on the same round independently confirmed the same structural gap (narrower anchor char class doesn't close it).

comments.body: Additional instance of the same root cause, found in a later review round on #477: `_list_electron_processes`'s anchor-selection check (`_ELECTRON_PATTERN in p.args`) has the identical exposure -- a wrapper/diagnostic process whose argv embeds the full Electron invocation as TEXT (e.g. `/bin/sh -c '/Applications/.../MacOS/Electron --user-data-dir=/tmp/hvsc-2-id ...'`) gets treated as a real Electron anchor, since `ps`'s flattened args= can't distinguish 'this process's own binary path' from 'this process's argv happens to quote that path as a string'. Same fix direction as the rest of this ticket (real argv via sysctl KERN_PROCARGS2, not text matching over ps -o args=).

title: heavy_op_memory_gate: doesn't recognize namespaced npm scripts (test:unit) or Gradle/Maven wrappers
body:
## What

Two related gaps in `classify_heavy_operation()` (`agent-hooks/heavy-op-memory-gate/heavy_op_memory_gate.py`), found by real GitHub-side Codex review on PR #477:

1. Namespaced package-manager scripts (`npm run test:unit`, `pnpm test:e2e`, `yarn build:prod`) never match the exact-token `test`/`build` check, so the gate allows these heavy operations through even at critical memory pressure.
2. `./gradlew` and `./mvnw` (the standard checked-in wrapper scripts most Java/Kotlin/Android projects invoke build tools through) aren't in the runner set alongside `gradle`/`mvn`, so `./gradlew build` / `./mvnw test` bypass the gate entirely.

## Why NOT fixed inside #477

Both are real gaps but out of scope for a PR whose purpose is the VS Code orphan-reaping / memory-pressure-gate incident fix -- neither namespaced-script matching nor Gradle/Maven support is needed for the hyperide VS Code extension workflow this gate was built to protect, and this PR has already gone through many review rounds on the narrower reaper-safety issues. Real fixes here deserve their own scoped verification (this function's own history shows stricter-matching attempts have previously traded one false-positive/negative class for a worse one -- see the docstring above `classify_heavy_operation`).

## User-facing impact if not done

A genuinely heavy `npm run test:unit` or `./gradlew build` can run unthrottled during a WARN-or-higher memory-pressure window, missing the gate's protection for those specific invocation shapes.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Match task-prefix namespacing (`test:*`, `build:*`) the way the sibling long-process classifier already does, not just exact script names.
- [ ] Add `gradlew`/`mvnw` wrapper basenames alongside `gradle`/`mvn` in the runner set.
- [ ] Live-verify (not just unit tests) that neither change reintroduces the false-negative regression a previous stricter-classifier attempt caused (see the docstring's documented history) before landing.

## Where this came from

GitHub-side Codex review on alex-mextner/agent-tools#477 (2x P2, on `agent-hooks/heavy-op-memory-gate/heavy_op_memory_gate.py`), 2026-08-29.

comments.body: Additional instance of the same basename-matching gap class, found in a later review round on #477: version-qualified npm package specs (`npx @vscode/vsce@latest package`, `npx playwright@1.55.0 test`, `npx vitest@latest run`) also bypass the gate since `_basename()` retains the `@version` suffix and never matches the bare runner name. Same fix direction as the other findings here -- normalize/strip version qualifiers before basename comparison, with the same live-verification discipline before landing.

title: vscode-orphan-reaper install.sh: plist replacement is not atomic -- a failed activation can leave the reaper unloaded with no rollback
body:
## What

`install.sh` unloads the existing launchd unit and replaces its only plist BEFORE confirming the new one activates successfully. If both `launchctl bootstrap` and the legacy `load` fallback fail (e.g. launchd rejects a semantically invalid but XML-valid plist), the script exits under `set -e` with the periodic reaper UNLOADED and no old plist available to restore -- silently disabling the whole safety mechanism this repo's memory-exhaustion incident fix depends on, with no visible signal beyond the install script's own exit code.

Found by real GitHub-side Codex review on PR #477, 2026-08-29.

## Why NOT fixed inside #477

Deployment-atomicity/rollback safety is a different KIND of concern than the kill-safety and marker-matching bugs already fixed across this PR's many review rounds -- it needs its own careful design (backup-then-restore-on-failure, or install-new-before-removing-old) rather than a quick patch under continued review-round pressure on an already large diff.

## User-facing impact if not done

A rare but real failure mode: re-running install.sh (e.g. after updating the reaper script) on a machine whose new plist happens to be rejected by launchd leaves the periodic orphan sweep silently disabled, with no automated recovery -- exactly the protection this whole effort exists to keep running.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Retain the previous plist/unit until the replacement has activated successfully (e.g. write the new plist to a temp path, activate it, only then remove/replace the old one), or explicitly roll back to the old plist on activation failure.
- [ ] Add a repro/test for the activation-failure path.

## Where this came from

GitHub-side Codex review on alex-mextner/agent-tools#477 (P2, on `ops/vscode-orphan-reaper/install.sh`), 2026-08-29.

title: agent-hooks deadlock opencode orchestrator: background-subagent-gate demands CC-only fields (fork/background), orchestrator-stays-thin blocks every fallback
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The hooks were written against the Claude Code Agent tool contract but rig wires them into opencode, whose Task tool has no background field (schema additionalProperties:false rejects it) and no fork/remote agent types. The gate then blocks EVERY dispatch, and orchestrator-stays-thin blocks the inline Edit/Write/bash fallback, so the orchestrator can only do trivial single-command reads. Reproduced live 2026-08-30 while urgently stopping a partner kimi token burn: 5 Task dispatches blocked (gate says "set native background: true flag" — impossible in this client), fork -> "Unknown agent type", Edit blocked repeatedly >15min apart (TTL never visibly expired), sleep 90/300 blocked as long-inline-process, jq pipelines blocked while single rg/wc/date commands passed. Hooks live in ~/.config/opencode/hooks/ and execute scripts from ~/xp/agent-tools/agent-hooks/.

## User impact
Any urgent inline action in an opencode session (config hotfix, incident stop, token-burn stop) deadlocks until a human intervenes; delegation discipline becomes a liveness bug instead of a guard.

## Cost of inaction
Next urgent incident in an opencode session (CI fix, security stop, token-burn stop) deadlocks the same way; agents keep asking humans permission for 2-line config edits.

## Acceptance criteria

title: gh ship <N> without --repo can misresolve the target repo when run from a linked git worktree
body:
## What
ADDENDUM (mundane 4th lead, added after initial filing): the most likely and boring explanation for the observed incident is that the invoking cwd was simply a linked worktree of the WRONG repo -- i.e. the operator ran gh ship from a directory that git (correctly) resolves to a different repository than the one they believed they were in, not a bug in gh resolution logic at all. This machine own worktree layout supports this: worktrees for different repos are parked under shared parent directories (e.g. a top-level .worktrees folder holding branch-named subdirectories for multiple unrelated repos), so a directory name alone does not reliably signal which repo it belongs to, and cd-ing into a remembered path can land in the wrong repo worktree while looking superficially correct. Since git config (and therefore remote get-url origin, and gh resolution built on it) is genuinely and correctly shared per-repo across that repo own worktrees, this explanation requires zero defect in gh or in ship.sh git-remote handling -- the fix in that case is purely UX: ship.sh should print the resolved target repo (e.g. Shipping into: owner/repo) before doing anything, so a wrong-repo cwd is caught immediately by inspection instead of silently proceeding. This should be the FIRST hypothesis the investigation rules out or confirms, before the more exotic gh-defect / per-worktree-config-override / env-var-leak leads already on this ticket.

## Why (motivation)
Surfaced today during unrelated task-cli investigation work while using gh ship from a linked worktree; caught by chance because the reported PR title/state did not match expectations. ship.sh's own header comment documents this exact no-repo-flag code path as intentionally delegating repo resolution entirely to gh with zero verification.

## User impact
gh ship <N> run without --repo from a linked worktree (the normal, encouraged way to work across this whole ecosystem per the repos' own worktree_only guidance) can report success against the WRONG repository, while the user believes their intended PR shipped. This is silent: no error, no repo-mismatch warning, just a plausible-looking result for the wrong target. It is a correctness/safety bug in exactly the worktree-based multi-repo agent workflow this tool exists to support.

## Cost of inaction
The next agent or human running gh ship from a linked worktree without explicitly passing --repo risks the same silent wrong-repo report again — and unlike this incident, may not notice the mismatch, potentially leaving an intended PR unshipped while a confusing/incorrect merged status is reported, or worse, coincidentally hitting a valid PR number in the wrong repo and actually triggering a real merge there.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A root cause is identified and documented: either (a) a specific gh CLI worktree-resolution defect with a reproduction recipe and the gh version it affects, (b) a per-worktree git config override that legitimately changes the origin URL per worktree, or (c) an environment-variable leak from the invoking session that overrides gh's repo targeting.
- [ ] Once root-caused, ship.sh either (a) explicitly re-derives and asserts the target repo from the worktree's own git remote before every gh call in the no-flag path (removing the 'trust gh completely, unverified' assumption), or (b) if the cause is an external environment leak, ship.sh sanitizes the offending variables before invoking gh — whichever the investigation shows is the correct fix.
- [ ] A regression test exists that runs ship.sh (dry-run or with a stubbed gh) from a linked-worktree scenario matching the reproduction and asserts the correct repo is targeted.

- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: identifiers named (ci/ship/ship.sh, env var names, owner/repo strings, '#109') are code/config references inside prose explaining the bug mechanism, not links to other tickets/repos — no external ticket is being referenced

title: require-ticket-before-commit fails to find ticket refs in heredoc-sourced commit messages
body:
## What
The commit-gate hook's shell tokenizer ([require_ticket_before_commit.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/main/agent-hooks/require-ticket-before-commit/require_ticket_before_commit.py)) has no handling at all for command substitution or heredocs (confirmed: zero matches for '$(' or '<<' in the file). When a commit message is passed as `git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF' ... EOF)"` — the exact pattern this repo's own CLAUDE.md tells every agent to use for multi-line messages — the tokenizer cannot correctly extract the message value, so a real ticket reference inside the heredoc body (e.g. 'Closes' [#502](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/502)) is not recognized. Only a single-line -m "..." message is parsed correctly today.

## Why (motivation)
Discovered while implementing [#502](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/502) (Stop-hook self-check improvement); this repo's CLAUDE.md instructs agents to author every commit message via this exact heredoc pattern, so the parser gap directly misfires against the project's own documented workflow

## User impact
A developer who writes a normal multi-line commit message (the documented way, via a heredoc) and correctly references the ticket they're fixing gets told 'no ticket reference found' and is blocked from committing, even though they did everything right

## Cost of inaction
Every heredoc-authored commit with a ticket reference keeps getting incorrectly rejected by this gate, forcing developers to either abandon the documented multi-line commit-message convention or fight the hook

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A commit made via 'git commit -m "$(cat <<'"EOF"' ... EOF)"' with a valid ticket reference inside the heredoc body is recognized by the hook exactly like an equivalent single-line -m message is today
- [ ] A new automated test case covering a heredoc-sourced multi-line commit message with an embedded ticket reference passes

(none)

- PR: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/599
- Merge commit: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/commit/eef1a1172952e170cbfa0a87d559d69b88ea85d9

Also folds in two duplicate reports (#406, #430 — same root cause, now closed pointing here) and partially covers #570's `-F <path>`-written-by-a-same-command-heredoc variant (left open — see the PR body for exactly what is and isn't covered).

title: block-no-verify fails to detect heredocs opened inside an unclosed outer quote, so its whole-blob quote-balance fallback blocks legitimate prose
body:
## What
block-no-verify's heredoc-body-stripping ([_heredoc_terminators/_tokenize_line](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/main/agent-hooks/block-no-verify/block_no_verify.py)) only recognizes a here-document opener when that OPENING LINE tokenizes as balanced on its own. The project's own mandated commit convention, git commit -m "$(cat <<'EOF' ... EOF)", has an unclosed outer double-quote on its opening line by construction, so the opener is never recognized and the heredoc body is never stripped. The code then falls through to _tokenize's whole-multi-line-blob quote balancing, which fails closed on any single unmatched quote CHARACTER anywhere in the (unstripped) heredoc body prose - reproduced live with a commit body containing one lone double-quote character used as a scare-quote in ordinary English prose.

## Why (motivation)
Found live while committing the fix for [https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/503](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/503) (require-ticket-before-commit's own heredoc-parsing bug) in this same session: the commit message described that bug's shell-quoting nature in English prose and got fail-closed blocked by block-no-verify, requiring a rewording workaround. Root cause confirmed by reading [block_no_verify.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/main/agent-hooks/block-no-verify/block_no_verify.py) and reproducing empirically: feeding the script a synthetic pre-bash event for a heredoc commit whose body contains one lone double-quote character returns exit 10 / decision:block with the unbalanced-quotes message, while the identical structure without that stray quote returns decision:allow.

## User impact
Agents and developers following this repo's own documented commit-message convention intermittently and unpredictably hit a fail-closed block on legitimate, safe commits whenever their prose happens to contain an odd count of a quote character - forcing a rewording workaround instead of a straightforward commit, with no indication that the true cause is the heredoc-opener-detection gap rather than a real ambiguous-quoting hazard

## Cost of inaction
Agents will keep intermittently hitting spurious fail-closed blocks on legitimate heredoc-sourced commits any time their message prose contains a lone quote character, and will keep working around it by guessing at rewording rather than understanding the real cause

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A git commit using the project's own -m "$(cat <<'EOF' ... EOF)" heredoc convention is correctly recognized as a heredoc by block-no-verify (its body is stripped before quote-balance checking), the same way it already would be for a -F - <<'EOF' ... EOF form
- [ ] A heredoc-sourced commit message body containing an odd/unmatched count of a quote character in ordinary prose (e.g. one lone double-quote used as a scare-quote) is no longer fail-closed blocked, reproducible via the existing test harness for this hook
- [ ] Existing block-no-verify bypass-detection tests (--no-verify, -n, core.hooksPath, wrapper peeling, etc.) still pass with no regression

title: require-review-before-commit: bind the gate to the reviewed diff, not just marker mtime
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)

## User impact
Someone can review part of their change, commit all of it, and honestly believe the whole commit was reviewed because the gate let it through. The unreviewed half lands with a green light, which is worse than no gate at all — it manufactures false confidence.

## Cost of inaction
The gate keeps certifying commits nobody reviewed whenever staging and committing disagree, which is the normal shape of a git commit -a.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The hook accepts a commit only when the staged diff it is about to commit matches a diff that was actually reviewed (review-cli already records this as a diff-scoped review-stamp under the repo's git dir), instead of accepting any commit made within an hour of any review.
- [ ] The mtime marker stays as the fallback for repos or tools that produce no stamp, so nothing that works today starts failing.
- [ ] A test covers the concrete hole: stage file X, review the staged diff, then commit with -a so file Y rides along unreviewed — that commit must not pass.

agent-browser has --idle-timeout / AGENT_BROWSER_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS, whose help text says the default is one hour, and the mechanism demonstrably works: a session started with a 20-second timeout self-terminated within 30 seconds. Twice today this machine ran out of memory and the operating system killed running work: swap was 13.6 GB used of 14.3 GB, and abandoned browser sessions were a large part of it — two cleanups found four and then five stale sessions, together roughly 2.4 GB and 82 processes at peak. The periodic sweep just installed (issue for it separately) stays the primary defence instead of a backstop, and it works from a coarser signal: it estimates age from process start time and file timestamps, so a session driven for hours without navigating looks its full lifetime old and can be closed while in use.

## What

The better the change, the more likely it is blocked: a pull request with defects gets a review record and ships, a spotless one does not. Every clean pull request needs an escalation that asks Alex in person, and the escalation path itself is unreliable: the request for these two returned 'daemon declined or unreachable' and never reached him. So the practical outcome is that clean work waits on a person who was never asked.

- [ ] A pull request that the Codex connector reviewed and found nothing wrong with passes the external-review gate without an override.
