## What
Every PR in the ecosystem repos gets an automatic Codex review (chatgpt-codex-connector) that leaves inline review threads. The rig-managed ruleset requires all review threads to be resolved before merge, so each PR sits BLOCKED until someone reads the threads, fixes or answers them, and resolves them. Right now no agent does that step: ship refuses with a one-line count and the shipper gives up. Audit on 2026-09-05: 65 open PRs across the seven ecosystem repos (agent-tools, rig-cli, review-cli, tg-cli, task-cli, dev-cli, pm-cli); 16 of the agent-tools ones are BLOCKED purely by Codex threads (1 to 16 threads each), all authored by the same bot, none answered. Ship should print each unresolved thread (path, line, author, body, isOutdated) with the exact resolve command, and the shipper skill must define the triage loop: read every thread, fix real findings, reply to non-findings with a reason, resolve, then re-run ship. The existing --resolve-addressed-threads flag only covers OUTDATED bot threads and does not help on a current PR.

## Why (motivation)
This is the single largest reason the PR backlog accumulates: a PR is opened, Codex comments, the thread-resolution rule blocks the merge, the agent session ends, and the PR ages into a conflict.

## User impact
Alex has repeatedly asked why stuck PRs and worktrees pile up (Telegram, 2026-08-18: all stuck PRs, worktrees and branches are priority work). Agents shipping PRs will see exactly what blocks them and finish the job instead of abandoning the PR.

## Cost of inaction
The backlog keeps growing (65 open PRs and about 70 worktrees today); every fix in the ecosystem stays unmerged and undeployed while the worktrees rot into conflicts.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The unresolved-threads refusal of gh ship lists every unresolved thread with file, line, author, the first 300 characters of the body, isOutdated, and a copy-pasteable resolve command (gh api graphql resolveReviewThread).
- [ ] The handoff and ship skills document the mandatory triage loop after PR creation (wait for the Codex review, address every thread, resolve, re-ship) so a subagent does not stop at 'PR opened'.
- [ ] A regression test covers the refusal output format with two or more threads.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

title: gh ship: the version-bump gate makes parallel PRs conflict on pyproject.toml — bump the version at merge time instead of inside each PR
body:
## What
ship refuses any PR touching shippable source unless the PR itself bumps the version in pyproject.toml. With several PRs open in parallel, each one bumps the same line to the same next version, so the second PR to merge becomes CONFLICTING and needs a manual rebase and re-bump; that repeats for every PR in the queue. Seen on 2026-09-05 in rig-cli (PR 296, 210), task-cli (103, 101, 89) and every review-cli PR: all green, all refused for a missing bump, and the ones that did bump are DIRTY. Proposal: ship performs the patch bump itself as part of the merge (a release commit on main after the squash), and a PR may still carry an explicit minor or major bump when it wants one. Keep the release semantics, remove the per-PR conflict source.

## Why (motivation)
The bump-in-PR rule is a documented source of DIRTY PRs in the backlog audit; it turns every parallel fix into a rebase chore that agents abandon.

## User impact
Agents and Alex stop fighting version-line conflicts; PR queues drain in order without hand rebases.

## Cost of inaction
Every batch of parallel PRs keeps producing conflicts and stale worktrees, and agents keep asking Alex what version to pick.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A PR with no version change is shipped with an automatic patch bump committed to main by ship (opt-out via an env or .ship-config key).
- [ ] A PR that already bumps the version (minor or major) is merged as is, no double bump.
- [ ] Two PRs shipped back to back without either touching pyproject.toml both merge without a conflict; covered by a test.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

comments.body:
## Design constraint from Alex (2026-09-05): the merge-time bump must pass every gate on its own, never get blocked by one

A direct commit to `main` is impossible (rulesets: `pull_request` required, `non_fast_forward`, and on agent-tools `required_signatures`), so "bump at merge" means: **ship authors the bump commit on the PR's HEAD branch right before the squash-merge, through the GitHub Contents API** (no local git hooks fire, the commit is GitHub-signed, the branch is unprotected), and the PR's own squash carries it into main. Every gate must be accounted for:

| Gate | Behaviour for ship's own bump commit |
|---|---|
| version-bump gate (ship) | satisfied by the commit itself; a PR that already bumps (minor/major) gets no second bump; `SHIP_AUTO_BUMP=0` in `.ship-config` or env opts out (old behaviour) |
| CI green (ship) | the push triggers a new run; ship waits for the new head SHA's checks the same way it waits today (CI-down local fallback applies unchanged) |
| review-dwell (ship) | the dwell clock is NOT reset by ship's own bump commit — ship records the bump SHA and measures dwell from the last **non-ship** push |
| review-quorum (ship) | keyed by task code, unaffected; but the recorded review must not be invalidated by a one-line version diff — verify `review task --check` still passes |
| unresolved review threads (ship) | Codex may review the new commit; ship re-checks threads after CI and, if the only new threads are on the bump line, treats them as bot-nits eligible for `--resolve-addressed-threads` (they are outdated-by-definition once merged) — otherwise refuse as today |
| external-review / zero-reviews (ship) | unaffected (reviews already exist) |
| clean worktree / unpushed commits (ship) | the local branch is now BEHIND the remote by the bump commit; ship must fetch and fast-forward the PR worktree (or compare against remote HEAD) instead of refusing |
| local git hooks (review-gate, require-ticket, visual-proof, block-no-verify) | not involved: no local commit is made |
| `protect-main` pre-push | not involved: the push is to the PR branch |
| `.ship-config` / SHIP_VERSION_FILE | reuse the existing `locate_version_file` + `version_line_bumped` logic to find the file and compute the next patch |
| post-merge `_refresh_main_checkout` | unchanged |
| dry-run | prints the planned bump (file, old → new) and does not push |
| audit | one `version-bump:auto` line in the ship audit file with PR, file, old, new, SHA |

Failure modes to test: two PRs shipped back to back (second must not conflict — it never touched the file); API push rejected (refuse with the reason, nothing merged); CI red after the bump (refuse, leave the bump commit, print how to fix); PR already carries a bump (no-op); `.ship-config` opt-out; a repo with no version file (skip with a note, as today).

title: Memory guard for agent fan-out: refuse to dispatch new subagents or review runs when the machine is already swapping
body:
## What
On 2026-09-05 the dev machine had about 500 MB free RAM and 9.9 GB of 11 GB swap in use with many Claude, opencode and review processes alive; another orchestrator session reported the same crisis. Agents that start under this pressure die or stall mid-task, which is how dirty, abandoned worktrees and half-finished PRs appear. Add a pre-agent (and pre-bash for review or opencode launches) guard in agent-tools that reads vm_stat and swap usage and refuses a new dispatch with a clear message when free memory is below a threshold or swap use is above one, provisioned through rig like the other agent-hooks.

## Why (motivation)
Memory exhaustion is a root cause of abandoned work in the worktree and PR audit; a soft ceiling only in memory notes does not hold across sessions.

## User impact
Alex, working on his laptop while agents run overnight, stops waking up to a frozen machine, dead agent windows and half-done work he has to restart by hand; he can keep using the laptop while the agents pace themselves.

## Cost of inaction
Each long autonomous run keeps killing itself and its siblings, leaving more stale worktrees and unshipped PRs.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A new agent-hook refuses Agent or Task dispatch and review, codex exec or opencode run launches while swap use exceeds a configurable percentage or free memory is below a configurable amount, with a message that names the current numbers.
- [ ] Thresholds live in rig.yaml under agent_hooks with sane defaults; rig apply provisions the hook.
- [ ] Hermetic tests cover allow, refuse and the malformed vm_stat case.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

comments.body: Scope note (2026-09-05): agent-tools#477 already ships heavy-op-memory-gate (pre-bash, blocks review/build/test launches at jetsam WARN+). This ticket is therefore only about the remaining gap: a pre-agent gate for Agent/Task dispatch (fan-out itself), plus a swap-usage signal in addition to the jetsam level — on 2026-09-05 swap sat at 9.9 of 11 GB while the jetsam level was the only thing consulted.

(restated) Fresh snapshot 2026-09-08 while triaging the machine-health inventory items (ask 123-140 batch): `sysctl vm.swapusage` reports `total = 29696.00M used = 28575.44M free = 1120.56M` (swap total has grown from the 11 GB cited when this ticket was filed on 2026-09-05 to ~29.7 GB now -- confirms swap is macOS-dynamic, not a fixed pool, so "expand swap" by itself is not an actionable fix). `vm_stat` free pages: 4635 * 16 KiB ~= 72 MB free physical RAM. `df -h /` shows 15 GiB free on the root volume (460 GiB total, 53% used), so swap growth has real headroom left but is not unbounded. `ps aux | wc -l` = 500 processes; top-RSS `ps -eo rss,pid,comm` is dominated by `omp` processes (up to 581 MB RSS, several more in the 100-170 MB range) and `Hyper Helper` renderer processes (206-293 MB each) -- consistent with heavy agent fan-out driving memory pressure, corroborating the ticket's root cause: agent fan-out size, not swap ceiling, is what pushes the machine to the edge. No change to scope or acceptance criteria -- just current evidence for whoever picks this up.

title: gh ship: refuse to merge a PR whose ticket has unaccepted criteria, and refuse magic-close keywords that would close the ticket behind task-cli
body:
## What
Companion to the task-cli ticket on acceptance gating. Today gh ship only records the merge on the ticket afterwards (task mark-shipped) while the merge itself lets Linear's merge automation or GitHub's Closes keyword flip the ticket to Done with nothing accepted — see [HYP-1440](https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-1440), [HYP-1347](https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-1347), [HYP-1295](https://linear.app/glide-vc/issue/HYP-1295); 127 of 435 HYP tickets closed since June have unchecked criteria. Add two pre-merge gates: (1) when task-cli is on PATH and a ticket code is derivable, run the task-cli gate command and refuse the merge while the ticket has unchecked criteria or checks without proof, unless the ticket or .ship-config records a post-merge-acceptance opt-out with a reason; (2) scan the PR title and body for magic-close keywords (close, closes, closed, fix, fixes, fixed, resolve, resolves, resolved followed by #N or a ticket code) and refuse, telling the shipper to write Refs instead (or rewrite it when --rewrite-magic-close is passed). Both gates log to the ship audit file like the other gates.

## Why (motivation)
A merge gate is the only place that can stop the close-on-merge automation from bypassing acceptance.

## User impact
Alex, reviewing what his team delivered this week, opens a Done ticket and finds the proof that the feature works instead of an empty checklist behind a merged PR; an agent about to merge is told in plain words what is still unproven and cannot merge around it.

## Cost of inaction
Every merge keeps closing tickets unverified regardless of what task-cli enforces.

title: ship: local gates (version-bump, clean-worktree) evaluate the CWD checkout, not the --repo target
body:
## What
ship.sh resolves its repository root from the current directory, so the version-bump and clean-worktree gates inspect whatever checkout the command runs from, while the --repo flag only redirects the remote gh calls. Running gh ship for [PR 513](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/513) with --repo pointing at agent-tools from a conloca-landing worktree made the version-bump gate read conloca-landing's package.json, compare it against the agent-tools diff, and refuse with 'version in package.json is UNCHANGED'. Proposal: when --repo names a repository different from the current checkout's origin, either refuse loudly with an explanatory message, or skip the local gates with a printed warning.

## Why (motivation)
The refusal text points at the wrong repository's package.json, which cost an agent a full investigation before it noticed the root is bound to the current directory.

## User impact
Agents and Alex get an honest error instead of chasing a version bump in a repository that has no root version file at all.

## Cost of inaction
Every cross-repo ship attempt from a worktree-isolated agent produces a misleading refusal and wasted debugging time.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] gh ship with --repo pointing at a different repository than the current checkout prints a clear message naming the mismatch instead of a misleading version-bump refusal
- [ ] Local gates keep running unchanged when --repo matches the current checkout's origin or is omitted

title: ship: review-quorum gate accepts literal GitHub issue references as ticket codes
body:
## What
The ship review-quorum gate derives the task code from the branch name or PR body but only recognises lettered ticket prefixes (Linear or JIRA style) or descriptive codes. Repositories that track work as plain GitHub issues (conloca-landing, whose PR bodies say 'Fixes' plus an issue number) get 'could not derive a task code' on every ship. ## Why (motivation)
Every conloca-landing ship currently refuses at the review-quorum gate or needs a Telegram hatch approval, which is a bypass of a gate that is simply mis-parsing the ticket, not a real review problem.

## User impact
Alex stops getting hatch approval pings for shipments that already have a ticket and reviews; agents can ship GitHub-issue-tracked repos through the normal gate.

Each GitHub-issue-tracked repo needs a manual REVIEW_TASK_CODE on every ship or a hatch approval, and a GH- prefix rewrite silently breaks task mark-shipped.

- [ ] gh ship on a PR whose body references a GitHub issue by hash-number derives that reference as the task code and queries review-cli for it
- [ ] Lettered ticket codes and descriptive codes still extract exactly as before
- [ ] task mark-shipped receives the hash-number reference unchanged and routes it to the GitHub backend

title: stop-completion-selfcheck: fix cooldown so it stops re-blocking on nearly every stop in long sessions
body:
## What
The Stop hook's per-session marker used to be deleted the instant a stop was allowed, on the theory that a later genuinely-new task should re-prompt sooner than the full 30-minute freshness window. Scanning real Claude Code session transcripts showed the actual effect: a long-lived autonomous session (waiting on background agents, ScheduleWakeup-driven polling loops) ends its own turn with a Stop event very frequently, sometimes under a minute apart, and deleting the marker on every allowed stop meant almost every one of those got re-blocked with the identical static prompt. Real measured gaps between firings in busy sessions were as low as 5 to 70 seconds, far below the intended 30-minute cadence. The fix: stop deleting the marker on allow, so a block stays in effect for the full cooldown window and re-blocking is capped at once per window instead of once per Stop event. Also added: a usefulness-tracking log (one line per invocation, decision + prompt variant + timing, write-only, never read by the hook itself) as the foundation for a future report on how often each prompt variant actually changes agent behavior, and a kill switch (env var or a sentinel file) so the hook can be turned off instantly with no redeploy if it misbehaves. See [issue #502](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/502) for the related, parallel fix to WHAT gets asked (content-aware prompt variants); this ticket is about HOW OFTEN it gets asked.

## Why (motivation)
The generic self-check text was already being made content-aware in a parallel change, issue #502, which reads the turn transcript to pick between three prompt variants. That fixes WHAT gets asked; this ticket fixes HOW OFTEN it gets asked. The empirical evidence from real session transcripts, not guesswork, showed the marker-deletion behavior described above was the actual root cause of the hook feeling like spam and a rubber-stamp ritual in exactly the long-running autonomous sessions where the frequency problem is worst.

## User impact
Long-running autonomous or background-watching Claude Code sessions stop getting the same static completion-check text every thirty to ninety seconds; the check fires at the intended cadence, about once per cooldown window, so when it does fire it is more likely to represent a genuinely new decision point instead of being routinely ignored as noise.

## Cost of inaction
The hook keeps firing far more often than designed in exactly the sessions that run longest and matter most for catching real misses, multi-day autonomous orchestration, training agents to paste a boilerplate 'still waiting, nothing new' reply instead of ever taking the prompt seriously, and there is still no data at all on how often any firing of this hook leads to a real change in what the agent does.

## Acceptance criteria

title: orchestrator-stays-thin misclassifies review-cli's spawned codex/opencode reviewer processes as the orchestrator
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Alex asked directly, while looking at a codex session's hook errors, to verify this specific gap: review-cli spawns real codex/opencode CLI processes as children, and those children inherit the machine's full agent-hooks wiring the same as any top-level orchestrator session would.

## User impact
Every multi-model review Alex runs spawns several codex/opencode reviewer processes under the hood. If one of those reviewer processes runs any Bash the orchestrator-thin hook does not recognize as read-only, the hook can block it and, in the block tier, ask Alex via Telegram to approve a hatch request that has nothing to do with anything he actually asked for — a review he started can silently interrupt him with an unrelated approval prompt.

## Cost of inaction
Alex keeps getting surprise hatch-approval pings on his phone that trace back to a review run rather than real orchestrator work, and has to dig through a codex session transcript each time to figure out where the block came from, exactly as happened today.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] A codex/opencode process spawned by review-cli's read-only reviewer backends never triggers the orchestrator-thin hook's warn or block tier, verified by a reproduction test that spawns a fake codex/opencode invocation the same way review-cli does and confirms the hook allows it silently. — forced: Not a UI feature, so no screenshot proof applies. Verified by tests/test_orchestrator_stays_thin.py::test_real_bridge_to_v1_event_output_is_exempt_end_to_end (feeds an actual codex_hook_bridge/opencode_hook_bridge to_v1_event() output -- the same translation review-cli's spawned codex/opencode reviewer process produces -- through the real hook with the literal repro command chain from the live incident, and asserts silent allow x3 calls, no WARN/BLOCK marker ever primed) plus test_repro_chain_allowed_silently_for_exempt_harness. PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/544, merged 774924c.
- [x] The exemption is not fragile self-reporting — the hook's own README documents why the chosen signal (an environment marker review-cli sets, or a sandbox-mode field the codex/opencode hook bridge already exposes) cannot be forged by a real orchestrator trying to dodge the gate. — forced: Not a UI feature. The hook's own README (agent-hooks/orchestrator-stays-thin/README.md, 'Harness-exempt (agent-tools#533)' section) documents the chosen signal (a top-level harness field set by each bridge from a hardcoded module constant, e.g. codex_hook_bridge.HARNESS = 'codex') and explains non-forgeability at length: the field is not derived from any tool_input/args value a model can set, and which bridge fires at all is decided by which harness's own hook system invoked it -- a CC session's Bash call cannot reroute itself through codex_hook_bridge. Regression-tested by test_forged_args_harness_does_not_exempt. PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/544, merged 774924c.
- [x] A note in review-cli's own documentation for [reviewlib/backends.py](https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/blob/main/reviewlib/backends.py) explains the same signal, so the two repos stay in sync if either side changes it. — forced: This criterion is moot under the shipped design and was intentionally not done as literally written -- not skipped by oversight. The original acceptance criteria (written before Alex's escalation) envisioned review-cli setting an env marker on its spawned codex/opencode processes. The shipped design instead tags EVERY v1 event with a harness field at the bridge level (cc_hook_bridge/codex_hook_bridge/opencode_hook_bridge), which exempts review-cli's spawned reviewer processes for free -- and also fixes the standalone-Codex-session case Alex hit live, which an env-marker-only design would have missed entirely. There is no signal for review-cli to set or document; reviewlib/backends.py needs no change. This is documented explicitly in agent-hooks/orchestrator-stays-thin/README.md's 'Harness-exempt' section, closing paragraph ('review-cli note: this exemption needed no cooperation from review-cli and no env marker for it to set ... reviewlib/backends.py needs no documentation change for this signal; there is nothing there to keep in sync.'). PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/544, merged 774924c.

title: Build a usefulness report over stop-completion-selfcheck's firings.jsonl (agent-tools and/or rig hook-stats)
body:
## What
The stop-completion-selfcheck Stop hook (agent-hooks/stop-completion-selfcheck/stop_selfcheck.py, [issue #529](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/529)) now writes a firings.jsonl log per invocation: a timestamp, a session identifier, the decision (block or allow), which prompt variant fired (full, light, or hedge), and how long the hook itself took to run. This ticket is about actually reading and reporting on that log, which nothing does yet. Concretely: a small command, either a new agent-tools script or a rig-cli subcommand such as rig hook-stats, that reads the firings log(s) across a machine (the log path is configurable per session today, so this needs to know where to look, likely the default cache location plus any override) and reports, over a chosen time window: how many times each prompt variant fired, the ratio of block to allow decisions, the distribution of hook run time, and ideally some proxy for whether a firing actually changed the agent's next action versus being a rubber stamp. A live manual scan of real Claude Code session transcripts (JSONL files under home directory Claude project folders) found that roughly a third of firings produced a genuine catch (a missed step, an unreported result, a scope overreach) while a large fraction in long-running autonomous sessions were boilerplate restatements; a lightweight automated proxy for that split, even an imperfect one such as checking whether the very next assistant turn contains new tool calls or an admission of a miss, would make this hook's actual value visible over time instead of only inferable from one-off manual transcript archaeology like the investigation that produced this ticket.

## Why (motivation)
This ticket's sibling ([issue #529](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/529)) added the firings.jsonl log specifically so a future tool could measure whether the completion self-check hook is actually useful, instead of the CTO having to manually scan raw session transcripts by hand to find out, which is exactly the multi-hour manual investigation that led to filing #529 in the first place. Without a reporting tool, the log is just data sitting on disk with nobody reading it.

## User impact
The person operating this hook across many repositories and long-running sessions gets a running, low-effort answer to whether the completion self-check is worth keeping in its current form, instead of only being able to find out by manually re-reading raw session logs the way this investigation had to.

## Cost of inaction
The firings.jsonl log keeps accumulating with nobody reading it, the same manual multi-hour transcript-scanning investigation has to be repeated by hand every time someone wants to know whether the hook is still useful, and there is no early signal if a future change to the hook's prompt logic makes it meaingfully worse or better at catching real misses.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Given one or more firings.jsonl files on disk, when the new command runs, then it prints, for a specified or default time window, per-prompt-variant firing counts, the block-versus-allow ratio, and basic hook-timing statistics (at least a median and a maximum).
- [ ] The command handles a missing or empty firings.jsonl file without crashing, reporting zero activity rather than an error.
- [ ] The command's output is grep-and-diff friendly (stable plain-text or JSON format) so it can be tracked over time or piped into another report.
- [ ] A design decision is made and documented for at least one lightweight heuristic that estimates whether a firing was followed by a real behavior change (for example: did the agent's next turn include a new tool call or an admission of a miss) versus a rubber-stamp reply, even if imperfect, plus a test asserting the heuristic classifies at least one clearly-rubber-stamp example and one clearly-real-change example correctly.

title: subagent-no-bg-longproc's stated rationale is factually wrong for general run_in_background
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Independent multi-model review of the subagent-no-monitor PR (agent-tools#439) flagged that this hook's own stated premise -- a subagent is never re-invoked by a background-completion notification -- contradicts what an empirical test just proved: a subagent backgrounding an ordinary command with run_in_background true DOES get auto-resumed with that command's output. The premise is baked into this hook's docstring, its block message, and its AGENTS.md catalog entry, so any agent reading that doctrine today is being told something false about the harness.

## User impact
A person waiting on a dispatched agent to finish a task can be left thinking the agent is stuck or has silently failed, when the agent was in fact following wrong internal guidance about whether it would be woken back up -- so the person loses time and trust in the system before they realize the agent needs a manual nudge it should not have needed.

## Cost of inaction
The false premise keeps propagating into new hooks and skills that model themselves on this one (subagent-no-monitor already did, before this ticket's own investigation caught it), compounding the confusion each time.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] an empirical test confirms whether a dispatched subagent that backgrounds an arbitrary (non-long-process-labeled) command with run_in_background true and ends its turn does get auto-resumed with that command's output (already independently confirmed once during HYP-1350/agent-tools#543 work: a 40-second backgrounded python3 sleep DID resume the calling subagent with its output after about 43 seconds, with no further message sent to it) — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/proofs/546-c1-empirical-resume.txt)
- [x] subagent_no_bg_longproc.py's module docstring and agent-hooks/README.md / AGENTS.md's subagent-no-bg-longproc doctrine entry are corrected to state precisely which notification shapes do and do not re-invoke a subagent, instead of the current blanket claim that a subagent is never re-invoked by a background-completion notification — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/proofs/546-c2-doctrine-surfaces.txt)
- [x] if the corrected rationale changes the hook's actual scope (e.g. it should only block backgrounding of a genuinely unbounded/never-exiting long process, not any labeled long-running command that WOULD complete and could safely auto-resume the subagent), that scope change is proposed as a follow-up, not silently folded into a docs-only fix — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/proofs/546-c3-scope-followup-559.txt)

title: Every hatch-using agent-hook fails OPEN on its own broken hatch-helper import, defeating fail-closed hooks and denial-class hooks alike
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
Independent review of agent-tools PR #439 (the subagent-no-monitor hook) found that the hatch helper is imported at MODULE SCOPE in every current hatch-using hook, before any event is even parsed. If that import fails on a machine with a broken checkout, the hook process exits non-zero before ever classifying the event, and on_error:open turns that into an ALLOW -- for subagent-no-monitor specifically, that means the exact wedge the hook exists to prevent goes through anyway. The same failure mode exists identically in the other 16 hatch-using hooks and is not something any of them special-case today.

## User impact
A person who is dispatching agents to work while a machine has a partially broken or mid-update local checkout can end up with a subagent silently wedged forever with no completed task and no error surfaced anywhere, instead of getting a clear denial they could act on -- because the safety hook meant to stop exactly that outcome quietly failed open instead.

## Cost of inaction
The fail-open behavior for a broken hatch import stays uniform across every hatch-using hook today, so nothing regresses further by inaction, but the specific hook whose entire purpose is preventing a silent subagent wedge keeps sharing an escape hatch with hooks where fail-open is genuinely the safer default -- the mismatch stays latent until a real broken-checkout incident surfaces it.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] a design decision is made and documented for whether a hatch-using hook should classify the event (parse stdin, check the subject condition) BEFORE loading the shared hatch helper, so a broken/missing lib/agenttools_hatch_escalation checkout produces the hook's own default decision (allow for an advisory hook, deny for a fail-closed one) instead of always allowing via on_error open
- [ ] the chosen fix, if any, is applied uniformly across all 17 current hatch-using hooks (or the shared bootstrap helper itself), not to a single hook in isolation, since tests/test_hatch_import_hardening.py's drift guard treats the bootstrap block as one canonical shared pattern
- [ ] a regression test simulates a missing/corrupt lib/agenttools_hatch_escalation/__init__.py and asserts each hatch-using hook's resulting decision matches its intended fail policy, not just its on_error field

## What
Add a new Claude Code Stop agent-hook, to be placed at [agent-hooks/chat-dictionary-gate](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/tree/main/agent-hooks) in the agent-tools repository, that reads the assistant's own just-finished reply from the session transcript, checks it against the same banned-word rules already enforced for outgoing Telegram messages (the file at ~/.claude/DICT.json), and blocks the turn from ending when a banned word is found, telling the model exactly what matched and what to say instead.

## Why (motivation)
Alex (the CTO) has asked repeatedly, across many sessions, for Claude Code to stop using specific banned Russian and English words and phrases in its own direct chat replies to him. He already built and enforced a banned-word list for outgoing Telegram messages, but that enforcement has zero effect on text typed directly into the Claude Code chat interface, which is a separate, currently unguarded surface. The same banned word recurred again in this exact session, which is at least the fourth or fifth time this exact request has come up.

## User impact
Alex stops seeing a word he has explicitly and repeatedly banned appear in Claude's own direct chat replies to him, not just in Telegram reports — the enforcement now covers every place he actually reads Claude's text.

## Cost of inaction
The banned word keeps recurring in direct chat with Alex with no enforcement on that surface, and he keeps having to notice and correct it by hand every time, session after session.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] A reply that contains a banned word (for example the invented Russian verb form for 'fixed' that does not exist) is blocked before the turn ends, and the block message quotes the exact matched text, names the violated rule, explains why it is banned, and gives the correct replacement wording. — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/proof-548-pytest.txt)

- [x] A Russian-language reply that uses an English loanword banned only inside Russian text (for example saying a pull request is 'landing' instead of using the Russian word for 'applied/merged') is blocked. — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/proof-548-pytest.txt)
- [x] If the model keeps failing to fix the wording after several attempts in the same conversation, the hook gives up and lets the turn end instead of trapping the conversation in an endless block loop; a later clean reply resets this counter. — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/proof-548-pytest.txt)
- [x] If the dictionary file is missing, unreadable, or contains a mistake, the hook does not block the conversation over it — it lets the turn end and logs a warning, because a config typo must never be able to freeze an interactive session. — proof: ![proof](/private/tmp/claude-501/-Users-ultra-xp-rig-cli/89e7f5e9-4808-41e8-bf8b-0a8b213b7c89/scratchpad/proof-548-pytest.txt)

title: omp hook bridge: dispatcher spawnSync freezes the whole omp TUI while a hook waits for approval
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The omp bridge shipped in [agent-tools#556](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/556) runs the dispatcher with a synchronous process spawn and a 2,000,000 ms timeout (sized to survive two serial Telegram approval waits). A synchronous spawn blocks the single-threaded omp process entirely, not just the one tool call. The multi-model review of that PR flagged this; it was deferred to a follow-up so the PR could merge with the correctness fix it also found.

## User impact
While a hook that asks Alex for approval over Telegram is waiting, the whole omp interface (Alex's daily-driver coding agent) is frozen: no screen updates, no keypresses, no way to see what is happening, for up to the full approval window. The bridge still enforces the safety rules correctly; the problem is the user experience while it does.

## Cost of inaction
Every approval-gated action in an omp session looks like a hung program for minutes at a time, which will push Alex toward disabling the bridge (losing every shared safety rule for omp again) or killing sessions mid-approval.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] The omp hook-bridge extension runs the Python dispatcher with an asynchronous process spawn (await on exit, same timeout semantics) instead of the current synchronous spawn, so the omp event loop keeps rendering and accepting keypresses while a hook is waiting. — forced: no UI; proven by tests/test_omp_hook_bridge.py::test_extension_ts_tool_call_does_not_block_the_event_loop passing on omp-async-spawn (8 async-spawn bun-driven pytest cases passed in 15.46s including event-loop, block/allow, fail-open crash, timeout budget, overlapping dispatches, SIGTERM-then-SIGKILL)
- [x] The fail-open behavior is unchanged: a dispatcher crash, launch failure, timeout, or unparseable output still resolves to allow and never throws out of the tool_call handler; the existing bridge tests still pass and a new test covers the asynchronous path. — forced: no UI; proven by tests/test_omp_hook_bridge.py::test_extension_ts_async_path_fails_open_when_the_dispatcher_crashes and test_extension_ts_async_path_still_propagates_block_and_allow passing on omp-async-spawn
- [x] A real omp session with the bridge installed stays responsive (screen repaints, keypresses accepted) during a deliberately slow hook, verified by hand or by a scripted timing check and recorded in the ticket. — proof: ![proof](/tmp/omp-558-rpc-proof/criterion3-rpc-proof.png)

## Screenshots

comments.body:
## Live proof (acceptance criterion 3)

Machine: this one, omp 18.0.11, 2026-09-06.

Setup, identical in all three runs: a throwaway hooks directory holding one `pre-bash`
descriptor whose script sleeps 40 seconds and then blocks (exit 10) — standing in for a hook
waiting on a Telegram approval — plus a second, independent extension that appends a line to a
file every second. That heartbeat is the liveness observable: its timer can only fire while
omp's event loop is turning, which is the same loop that repaints the screen and reads
keypresses. The real installed extension symlink and the real descriptors were untouched
(`--no-extensions` plus explicit `-e` paths).

```
OMP_HOOKS_DIR=<tmp>/hooks LIVE_HEARTBEAT_LOG=<tmp>/hb.log \
  omp -p "Use the bash tool to run exactly: echo hello-from-omp . Do nothing else." \
      --no-extensions [--config <tmp>/overlay.yml] \
      -e <extension.ts under test> -e <tmp>/heartbeat.ts \
      --no-session --auto-approve
```

**Run 1 — the bug, on the current `main` extension.** The event loop stopped dead for the whole
hook, twice (the model retried once):

```
ticks=22 span=100.6s
  GAP   41.0s  16:36:04.975 -> 16:36:45.944
  GAP   40.6s  16:36:52.951 -> 16:37:33.583
```

**Run 2 — the fix, with omp's settings left at their defaults.** The loop never stalled
(126 ticks in 125.1 s, worst gap 1.0 s), but a second, previously invisible limit appeared:
omp bounds a `tool_call` extension handler with `extensionHandlers.toolCallTimeoutMs`
(default 30,000 ms) and turns that timeout into a block of its own:

```
Extension error (.../lib/omp_hook_bridge/extension.ts): handler timed out after 30000ms
```

The synchronous spawn had been evading that timer by accident — a blocked event loop cannot run
omp's own timer, so the handler always won the race. An awaited handler cannot evade it.

**Run 3 — the fix, with `extensionHandlers.toolCallTimeoutMs` raised to 2,100,000.** The loop
kept turning for the whole 40-second wait (60 ticks in 59.2 s, worst gap 1.1 s) and the hook's
own verdict came through instead of omp's timeout text:

```
Blocked by agent-hook `slow-gate`; `echo hello-from-omp` did not run.
```

So the budgets have to be ordered `descriptor timeout_ms < OMP_HOOK_BRIDGE_TIMEOUT_MS <
extensionHandlers.toolCallTimeoutMs`. That setting is documented in the bridge README and its
provisioning is tracked in https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/363. Until it is set,
a hatch approval under omp ends as omp's own block at 30 seconds — the safe direction (a
fail-closed hook never becomes an allow), but not the hook's verdict.
screenshot: /tmp/omp-558-rpc-proof/criterion3-rpc-proof.png

## Live proof (acceptance criterion 3) — omp 18.1.14 RPC

Machine: this one, omp 18.1.14, 2026-09-08. Scripted timing against the `omp-async-spawn` bridge (`extension.ts` at fec3b1c), **not** the live `~/.omp` symlink.

Setup: throwaway `OMP_CODING_AGENT_DIR`/`PI_CODING_AGENT_DIR` + `OMP_HOOKS_DIR`. One `pre-bash` descriptor whose script sleeps **8 s** then blocks (exit 10). Isolated `--no-extensions -e <worktree extension.ts>`. A local OpenAI-compatible stub issued one `bash` tool call (`echo hello-from-omp`). Real `~/.omp/agent/extensions/zz-agent-tools-hook-bridge.ts` was never touched.

```
omp --mode=rpc --no-session --no-extensions --no-skills --no-rules --no-lsp --auto-approve \
    --config overlay.yml --model=stub/proof -e <worktree>/lib/omp_hook_bridge/extension.ts
```

While the hook slept, the RPC client sent `get_state` every 0.4 s. Those responses can only land if omp's event loop is still turning (the same loop that repaints the TUI and reads keypresses).

**hook.log**
```
START 1788844895.141747
END 1788844903.147212
```

**Result — PASS**

```
omp omp/18.1.14
bridge /Users/ultra/xp/agent-tools/.worktrees/omp-async-spawn/lib/omp_hook_bridge/extension.ts
hook sleep 8.0s  start=1788844895.142 end=1788844903.147212
ping ids 12 interval 0.4s
get_state responses DURING hook wait: 12
  first_during=1788844895.311 last_during=1788844899.670 span=4.360s
  worst_gap=0.410s
stub chat/completions calls: 2
total stdout frames: 42
frames during hook wait:
  + 0.169s  type=response  id/cmd=ping0
  + 0.482s  type=response  id/cmd=ping1
  + 0.887s  type=response  id/cmd=ping2
  + 1.290s  type=response  id/cmd=ping3
  + 1.694s  type=response  id/cmd=ping4
  + 2.098s  type=response  id/cmd=ping5
  + 2.504s  type=response  id/cmd=ping6
  + 2.907s  type=response  id/cmd=ping7
  + 3.310s  type=response  id/cmd=ping8
  + 3.717s  type=response  id/cmd=ping9
  + 4.119s  type=response  id/cmd=ping10
  + 4.529s  type=response  id/cmd=ping11
RESULT: PASS
```

12/12 `get_state` RPC frames arrived *during* the 8.0 s hook wait (span 4.36 s of pings, worst gap **0.41 s**). A frozen `spawnSync` loop would have delivered none of them until the hook exited.

Proof image attached via `task check 558 3 --proof criterion3-rpc-proof.png` (not `--force`).

title: installers: write the rig provenance marker (.installed-by / installed_by) so rig status can place tool-installed skills and hooks
body:
## What
rig now classifies undeclared items in ~/.agents/skills and ~/.claude/hooks by provenance and only reports items it cannot place as drift ([rig-cli#357](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/357)). The contract, documented in [rig's config-schema docs, section Provenance](https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/blob/main/docs/config-schema.md#provenance): an installer that writes a skill dir `~/.agents/skills/<name>/` also writes a one-line file `~/.agents/skills/<name>/.installed-by` containing its own name (`tg`, `review`, ...); an installer that writes a hook descriptor `~/.claude/hooks/<id>.<point>.json` adds a top-level `"installed_by": "<tool>"` key to that JSON (the agents-hooks v1 runner reads descriptors with dict.get and ignores unknown keys). Today rig falls back to the `.blurbs/<name>.md` blurb every `<tool> install-skill` already writes, plus a shipped allowlist of the ecosystem skill names, and a hardcoded list of ops-installer hook ids (agent-browser-session-claim). Those fallbacks are temporary; once the installers write the marker rig can drop the allowlists. Repos to update: tg-cli, review-cli, task-cli, draw-cli, research-cli, stt-cli (each `install-skill`), agent-tools itself for the `dev` skill installer and for [ops/agent-browser-session-reaper/install.sh](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/tree/main/ops), and this repo's AGENTS.md should state the contract so future installers follow it.

## Why (motivation)

After a fresh install of any ecosystem tool, rig status shows its skill as 'installed by <tool>' instead of drift, with no allowlist maintenance in rig.

## Cost of inaction
Every new ecosystem tool or renamed skill reappears as false drift until someone edits rig's allowlist; the contract stays undocumented and installers keep diverging.

title: gh ship: derive the task code from a full GitHub issue URL (and a Linear URL) in the PR body
body:
## What
ship's review-quorum gate derives the PR's ticket code from the branch name and PR body, but only recognizes bare forms (HYP-931, Refs #548). A PR body that references its ticket as a full URL (https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/548) — the shape task-cli's links gate REQUIRES — is refused with 'could not derive a task code', so agents fall back to a manual REVIEW_TASK_CODE=GH-548 that gets forgotten. Extend the matcher: a same-repo GitHub issue URL yields the literal #<n> (the same code a bare 'Refs #<n>' yields since [PR #511](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/511)); an issue URL of ANOTHER repo or a /pull/<n> URL never counts; a Linear URL (https://linear.app/<team>/issue/HYP-1440/...) yields HYP-1440.

## Why (motivation)
Two different agents hit this today: a PR written correctly per task-cli's links gate (full URLs, never bare refs) fails ship's quorum gate, and the workaround (REVIEW_TASK_CODE=GH-548 by hand) is exactly the manual step that gets forgotten.

## User impact
Alex, and every agent that ships a pull request for him, can write the ticket link in the pull request the way the ticket tool already demands (a full clickable link) and the merge command just works: it finds the ticket from that link by itself. Today the same person has to also type a hidden environment variable by hand before merging, and when they forget, the merge is refused and they lose a round.

## Cost of inaction
Every ship of a properly-linked PR keeps failing on the quorum gate; agents keep hand-setting REVIEW_TASK_CODE (or forget it and waste a ship round), and the two ticket-discipline gates in this ecosystem keep contradicting each other.

## Acceptance criteria

title: opencode hook bridge: plugin.js still spawns the dispatcher synchronously, blocking the opencode server
body:
## What


## Why (motivation)
The omp bridge's synchronous dispatcher spawn was replaced with an awaited one in [agent-tools#558](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/558). lib/opencode_hook_bridge/plugin.js still uses the same synchronous spawn with a 1,000,000 ms budget. opencode's plugin runs in the server process rather than the terminal interface, so the symptom differs from omp's frozen screen: the server's single event loop stops for the whole dispatch. The omp work also turned up a trap that must be checked before flipping opencode: omp bounds an extension handler at 30 seconds and the synchronous spawn was accidentally evading that timer, so making the spawn asynchronous exposed a fail-closed cut-off that had never fired before. opencode may have an equivalent plugin-hook timeout, and its bridge fails CLOSED, so the same flip could start refusing calls that used to be approved.

## User impact
Alex is working in opencode. A safety rule asks him for approval over Telegram, and until he taps it — which can take many minutes — everything else he has running in opencode stops responding: no answers, no command output, no progress in any other conversation with the tool, in every window it serves. It looks like the tool has crashed, with nothing on screen saying it is waiting for him.

## Cost of inaction
opencode keeps the exact defect that was just repaired for omp, and the next person to hit it has to rediscover both the cause and the timeout trap from scratch.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Establish first, and record in the ticket, whether opencode applies its own timeout to a tool.execute.before plugin handler and what it does when that timeout fires (the omp equivalent turns it into a block); do not convert the spawn before that is known
- [ ] lib/opencode_hook_bridge/plugin.js awaits an asynchronous dispatcher spawn with the same budget semantics, keeping its fail-CLOSED policy (a block decision and a pre-execution timeout still throw) and the stdin JSON contract unchanged
- [ ] A test proves the opencode event loop keeps turning during a slow dispatch, and that block, allow, crash and timeout outcomes are unchanged

In ci/ship/ship.sh::_acceptance_gate, a task gate exit code other than 0/1 (exit 2 = unroutable id / backend 404) is logged as 'could not evaluate' and the merge proceeds. The 2026-09-06 audit showed four merges (PRs 349, 556, 352, 497) shipped with the acceptance gate never running because task gate exited 2; #567 stops the malformed inputs, but the exit-2 handling that turned them into silent merges is untouched.

title: require-ticket-before-commit: false BLOCK on a message-file commit when the file is written in the same command (heredoc/redirect); read-failure is silent
body:
## Symptom

`git commit -F <absolute-path>` is BLOCKED by `require-ticket-before-commit` although the file contains a valid reference (`Refs #143`), while the identical message via `-m` passes. Observed 2026-09-06 in `conloca/landing` worktree `/tmp/wt-slide-reveal` (branch `fix/slide-reveal-and-s1-type`, no ticket in the branch name). Related earlier symptom (2026-09-05, same project): a relative `-F` path was resolved against the harness's session cwd, not the commit's cwd.

## Root cause (verified against the deployed hook, `agent-hooks/require-ticket-before-commit/require_ticket_before_commit.py`, md5 `0117a644…` — the copy `cc_hook_bridge` runs)

The block message is emitted with NO preceding `could not read commit-message file` warning in the tool result, so `_read_message_file`'s path logic is not the failing piece. What fails is timing: the message file is written in the SAME Bash command as the commit —

```
cat > /tmp/slide-fix/commit-msg.txt <<'EOF'
fix: reveal feature slides one at a time …

Refs #143
EOF
git commit -q -F /tmp/slide-fix/commit-msg.txt
```

A PreToolUse hook runs BEFORE the shell executes anything, so at hook time the file does not exist; `open()` raises `FileNotFoundError` → the reader returns `""` (this path does `warn`, but `cc_hook_bridge` only surfaces the block text, so the operator never sees why). With an empty message and a ticket-less branch, the gate blocks.

The follow-up shape that also blocked — `cd <wt> && git commit -q -F /tmp/slide-fix/commit-msg.txt` — reproduces as ALLOW today against the deployed hook (8/8 orderings incl. `-q -F`, `-qF`, `--quiet -F`, `--file`, piped `| tail`) when the file exists. In the agent's transcript that retry ran in the same Bash call as a Python step that rewrote the file, so it is the same class. If a standalone existing-file `-F` ever blocks, that is a separate bug — not reproducible now.

Secondary issue seen while tracing: `_tokenize` treats `#` inside a heredoc BODY as a shell comment (`Refs #143` becomes the segment `['Refs']`), so even when the hook falls back to scanning the command text it loses the reference. That is the #170/#406/#430/#503 family; noted here because it is why the fallback also finds nothing.

## Why it matters

The hook's own block message tells agents to "pass the message via `-F <file>`"; the natural way to do that from a single tool call is a heredoc write plus commit, which is exactly the shape that fails. The result is a false BLOCK on a correctly ticketed commit, and agents then try increasingly odd message forms (`task:#143`, `(task:#143)`) before giving up.

## Acceptance criteria

1. A `-F <path>` whose file is created earlier in the SAME command (heredoc redirect, `printf > file`, `python3 … write(...)`) is handled: either the hook reads the redirect/heredoc body for that path from the command text, or it falls back to scanning the heredoc body for a ticket reference — test with the exact command above → allow.
2. An absolute `-F <path>` to an existing file is read regardless of the event `cwd` (test with `cwd` set to a different repo) → allow when it contains `Refs #N`.
3. A relative `-F <path>` is resolved against the commit's effective cwd (`cd <dir> && git commit -F msg.txt`, and `git -C <dir> commit -F msg.txt`), not the event cwd → allow.
4. When the message file cannot be read, the BLOCK message itself names the unreadable path and the OS error (today only a stderr `warn` the bridge hides).
5. A regression test for each of 1–4 in `test_require_ticket.py`.

## Bonus repro while filing this ticket

`gh issue create --body-file <md>` was itself BLOCKED by this hook because the markdown body, passed via a heredoc in the same Bash call, contained the literal text `git commit -F …`: the tokenizer parsed the heredoc body as a command segment and gated a `gh issue create` as if it were a commit. Same root class: heredoc bodies are tokenized as shell.

No bypass was used at any point; the agent eventually committed via `-m`.

comments.body:
Partially fixed in PR #599 (which primarily targets the duplicate-report family #503/#406/#430, but this issue's core scenario shares the same root cause — the tokenizer had zero heredoc awareness).

## What's fixed by #599

- **Acceptance criterion 1** (the primary repro): a `-F <path>` whose file is written by a heredoc earlier in the SAME command (`cat > path <<'EOF' ... EOF; git commit -F path`) now works — the hook reads the heredoc body captured from the command TEXT instead of the disk (which doesn't have the file yet at PreToolUse hook time). This also required a same-command ordering check (added after review-cli found a real bypass in the first version of the fix): a heredoc that writes its target file only AFTER a commit already read it can no longer retroactively "satisfy" that earlier commit.
- **Acceptance criterion 2** (absolute `-F` path read regardless of event `cwd`): confirmed already correct pre-fix; added a regression test to lock it in.
- **The "bonus repro"** at the bottom of this issue (a `gh issue create --body-file` heredoc whose markdown merely mentions `git commit -F …` getting gated as if it were a real commit): fixed as a side effect of neutralizing heredocs before segment-parsing runs at all.
- The **secondary issue** you flagged (`#` inside a heredoc body treated as a shell comment): fixed generally, for every heredoc shape, not just this one.

## What's NOT fixed (this issue stays open for)

- **Acceptance criterion 3**: resolving a *relative* `-F` path against a shell `cd <dir> &&` earlier in the same command. `git -C <dir> commit -F <relative>` already resolves correctly (unaffected by this PR), but a bare `cd <dir> && git commit -F <relative>` does not — the hook doesn't track a preceding shell `cd`. Out of scope for #599 (a materially different feature: tracking shell working-directory state across a command chain, not a heredoc/tokenizer bug).
- **Acceptance criterion 4**: naming the unreadable path + OS error in the BLOCK message itself (today it's only a stderr `warn()`, which the `cc_hook_bridge` output hides from the operator, exactly as you described).

Happy to file those two as their own narrower follow-up if useful — let me know, or I can just leave this issue open for them as-is.

## What
_review_quorum_extract_ticket returns only the FIRST match of the first matching arm per text, and _ship_derive_task_code_for_notify moves to the next SOURCE (branch -> title -> body) when that candidate is rejected — never to the next match within the same text. Live on 2026-09-06 after #567 merged: PR #560's body mentions 'GH-560' once (a review-record reference to the PR itself) and carries the real 'Refs #541' further down. The prefix arm returns GH-560, the new self-PR rule rejects it (the stderr note fires correctly), the body was the last source, and the acceptance gate logs 'could not derive a task code' and SKIPS — the merge proceeds with #541 never judged. Fix: make the extractor yield every candidate in arm-priority order (or let the derivation re-scan the same text with the rejected token removed) so a rejected candidate never hides a later legitimate one in the same text.

## Why (motivation)
The self-PR rejection from #565/#567 is correct but stops one step short: rejecting a candidate without continuing the scan converts a wrong-ticket refusal into a silent skip, which is the fail-open class #569 tracks. Reproduced live: SHIP_REVIEW_DWELL=0 SHIP_REVIEW_QUORUM=0 gh ship 560 --dry-run prints the rejection note and then 'could not derive a task code for #560'.

## User impact
A developer whose PR body mentions its own review record (review task GH-<pr>) or a review-check code gets no acceptance verification at merge time and no refusal telling them, even though the body names the ticket correctly.

## Cost of inaction
Every PR that cites its own GH-<n> review record before its Refs line merges past the acceptance gate unchecked; #560 is the first known instance.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] For a PR body containing an incidental GH-<own PR number> mention before a keyword-anchored Refs #N, the acceptance gate asks task gate #N (verified via the fake-gh harness in tests/test_ship_ticket_gates.py, red before the fix) — forced: shell merge-gate logic, no UI (ticket says so). Proofs: PR #577 commit 9bc5cfb; tests/test_ship_ticket_gates.py::test_acceptance_gate_scans_past_a_self_pr_candidate_to_the_refs_line_in_the_same_body (PR #560 fixture -> task gate #541), ::test_acceptance_gate_scans_past_a_grammar_rejected_candidate_in_the_same_body (descriptive review code before the real ref), tests/test_ship.py::test_review_quorum_scans_past_a_candidate_with_no_record_in_the_same_body (quorum gate continuation); all red before the fix, green at 9bc5cfb; full suite green.
- [x] The same holds for a review-check code (rig-cli-341) appearing before a real HYP-<n> in the same text — forced: shell merge-gate logic, no UI (ticket says so). Proofs: PR #577 commit 9bc5cfb; tests/test_ship_ticket_gates.py::test_acceptance_gate_scans_past_a_self_pr_candidate_to_the_refs_line_in_the_same_body (PR #560 fixture -> task gate #541), ::test_acceptance_gate_scans_past_a_grammar_rejected_candidate_in_the_same_body (descriptive review code before the real ref), tests/test_ship.py::test_review_quorum_scans_past_a_candidate_with_no_record_in_the_same_body (quorum gate continuation); all red before the fix, green at 9bc5cfb; full suite green.
- [x] The review-quorum gate (which calls _review_quorum_extract_ticket directly at the TASK_CODE derivation) gets the same continuation, or the ticket documents why it must not — forced: shell merge-gate logic, no UI (ticket says so). Proofs: PR #577 commit 9bc5cfb; tests/test_ship_ticket_gates.py::test_acceptance_gate_scans_past_a_self_pr_candidate_to_the_refs_line_in_the_same_body (PR #560 fixture -> task gate #541), ::test_acceptance_gate_scans_past_a_grammar_rejected_candidate_in_the_same_body (descriptive review code before the real ref), tests/test_ship.py::test_review_quorum_scans_past_a_candidate_with_no_record_in_the_same_body (quorum gate continuation); all red before the fix, green at 9bc5cfb; full suite green.

title: ship.sh review-quorum gate: a '#<n>' ticket and its 'GH-<n>' review key never meet — 3 recorded iterations are invisible to the gate
body:
## What
review-cli records iterations under the literal --task string with no normalization: 'review task GH-565 --check' sees 3 passed iterations while 'review task #565 --check' sees zero. ship.sh's review-quorum gate derives TASK_CODE from the branch, then the PR body ('Refs #565' -> '#565'), and queries that spelling only — so a PR whose reviews were recorded as GH-565 (the spelling every agent types, since '#' needs quoting) is refused for a bar it actually met. Reproduced on PR #567 on 2026-09-06; the only bridge was REVIEW_TASK_CODE=GH-565 on the gh ship command line, which the next agent cannot know. Fix on the ship side: when the derived code is '#<n>' also query 'GH-<n>' (and vice versa) and take the union; or on the review-cli side: normalize GH-<n> <-> #<n> at record and lookup time.

## Why (motivation)
The review bar is the self-merge authority; a spelling mismatch between the record and the lookup turns a met bar into a refusal, and the workaround is an undocumented environment variable.

## User impact
A developer who has done the required three review rounds on their pull request and then runs gh ship is told the reviews do not exist and the merge is refused. They cannot merge their own finished work without either redoing the three reviews under a different name or asking Alex for a one-time bypass on Telegram.

## Cost of inaction
Every GitHub-issue-tracked PR reviewed as GH-<n> is refused by the quorum gate until someone rediscovers REVIEW_TASK_CODE.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] With 3 passed iterations recorded under GH-<n> and a PR body saying Refs #<n>, gh ship reaches AUTHORITY CONFIRMED without REVIEW_TASK_CODE (fake-review harness test in tests/test_ship*.py, red before the fix) — forced: CLI gate logic, no UI (ticket says so). Proofs: PR #577 commit 9bc5cfb; tests/test_ship.py::test_review_quorum_finds_a_record_keyed_gh_when_the_body_says_refs_hash (3 iterations under GH-565, body Refs #565 -> AUTHORITY CONFIRMED without REVIEW_TASK_CODE; audit task_code == GH-565), ::test_review_quorum_finds_a_record_keyed_hash_when_the_branch_says_gh, ::test_review_quorum_authorizes_under_the_twin_when_the_primary_record_falls_short; red before the fix.
- [x] The audit line names the spelling that satisfied the bar — forced: CLI gate logic, no UI (ticket says so). Proofs: PR #577 commit 9bc5cfb; tests/test_ship.py::test_review_quorum_finds_a_record_keyed_gh_when_the_body_says_refs_hash (3 iterations under GH-565, body Refs #565 -> AUTHORITY CONFIRMED without REVIEW_TASK_CODE; audit task_code == GH-565), ::test_review_quorum_finds_a_record_keyed_hash_when_the_branch_says_gh, ::test_review_quorum_authorizes_under_the_twin_when_the_primary_record_falls_short; red before the fix.

title: Native subagent identity across harnesses: complete Codex/OMP coverage without global exemptions
body:
## What
Complete one trusted, per-invocation subagent identity contract across Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and OMP. Both sanctioned detached launchers and native harness-spawned children must be recognized; main agents remain subject to the same guards.

## Why (motivation)
Alex rejected harness-wide exemptions and unusable instructions pointing a non-Claude harness to Claude-only tools. PR #620 delivered useful launcher support, but its own acceptance notes say native Codex/OMP child records were not implemented and Codex live proof was blocked by quota. Those criteria were force-checked anyway. The issue is already reopened but still carried status:done; this grooming corrects the checklist and label, not the history of the delivered work.

## User impact
Real native children can follow the delegation policy without being blocked as orchestrators, while a main agent cannot obtain an exemption by supplying an agent_id argument or changing a process-global variable.

## Cost of inaction
Native delegation either remains unusable or requires unsafe identity workarounds, and each guard repeats a different harness-specific heuristic.

## Parent / specification / dependencies
Parent: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/718
Specification: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/docs/ecosystem-grooming-2026-09-10/docs/specs/2026-09-10-guard-contracts.md#trusted-identity
OMP native implementation: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/712
Codex native implementation: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/673
Related incidents: #676, #686, #703. rig provisioning dependency: https://github.com/alex-mextner/rig-cli/issues/337

## Delivered baseline
- [x] PR #620 removed harness-wide EXEMPT_HARNESSES and added per-harness delegation guidance.
- [x] Detached Codex/OMP launcher skills and launcher-sourced identity were delivered, with forged tool-argument stripping in the bridge paths.
- Evidence: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/620, merge 6194439ea452ffe341683c04da5e787dd34c8ad0. The PR reports launcher/bridge tests and OMP live proof; those are not proof of the missing native paths, and this grooming did not rerun them.

## Remaining acceptance criteria
- [ ] Native Codex spawn_agent and OMP task-child fixtures come from confirmed harness events/records, with documented versions and trusted provenance; missing upstream metadata remains an explicit blocker.
- [ ] Native child and grandchild calls receive their own session/parent identity; two siblings sharing a PID cannot inherit or overwrite one another's trust context.
- [ ] Main-agent calls remain gated under every supported harness; tool arguments, inferred path depth and a caller-controlled identity string cannot grant child status.
- [ ] Launcher and native paths normalize through one shared contract consumed by every subagent-aware guard, with correct per-harness remediation text.
- [ ] Negative tests cover forged arguments, process/session reuse, missing metadata and concurrent siblings; real child fixtures pass without global exemption.
- [ ] Authorized live Codex and OMP checks separately verify native and launcher paths at named revisions. Quota-unavailable proof stays unchecked with its blocker, never force-checked as success.

## Closure / priority
P1. Complete #712 and #673 against the same contract, not successive label/path special cases. Do not invent PI/RIG metadata for native children or disable protections to make a test pass.

## Reopening: live regression confirmed tonight, post-#681-sync — root cause pinned to omp's own pre-bash hook invocation, not fixable from agent-tools

Alex asked directly tonight: "Два воркера, которых я запускал ранее, почему-то были ошибочно классифицированы системой как 'я сам' (orchestrator), хотя формально были subagent-ами. разве ты ее еще не починил?" This is still happening, confirmed by live, first-party reproduction from inside a genuine `task`-tool-dispatched subagent (this very investigation), running on top of the checked-out agent-tools `main` at commit `8418729` — i.e. **after** #620, #637, #658, #676, and #681 all landed.

### What I did
1. Ran as a real omp Task-tool subagent (not simulated). My own `bash` tool calls were blocked/warned with the exact `orchestrator-stays-thin` "this session is the orchestrator" message, repeatedly, live, tonight.
2. `env` inside my own bash-tool child process: **zero** `PI_*`/`RIG_*` vars of any kind (`PI_SESSION_FILE`, `RIG_AGENT_ID`, `RIG_DETACHED_AGENT`, `PI_TOOL_BRIDGE_SESSION` all absent). Meanwhile the **eval** (Python) kernel for the exact same subagent correctly sees `PI_SESSION_FILE` pointing at my own nested transcript (`.../<top-level-session-id>/FixOrInvestigateOmpSubagentEnvGap.jsonl`) — so the identity *does* exist somewhere in omp, it just isn't reaching the bash-tool pre-bash hook invocation.
3. **Direct instrumentation of `orchestrator_stays_thin.py`'s own `main()`** (temporary diagnostic patch, applied via the eval kernel since the Edit tool was *also* blocked by the same bug, reverted after capture — no diff left in the repo) captured the **raw stdin JSON event** the hook actually receives for real pre-bash calls, across my own subagent and several concurrent sibling subagents (different cwds/worktrees, all genuine `task`-tool children):
   ```
   {"hook_api": "agents-hooks/v1", "event_id": "...", "tool": "bash", "point": "pre-bash",
    "harness": "omp", "command": "...", "cwd": "...", "args": {"command": "..."}}
   ```
   No `agent_id`, `agentId`, `sessionId`, or `sessionFile` field anywhere in `event` or `event["args"]` — for *any* sample, across *multiple different real subagents*. And the hook process's own `os.environ` at that exact moment: `PI_SESSION_FILE`, `RIG_AGENT_ID`, `RIG_DETACHED_AGENT`, `PI_TOOL_BRIDGE_SESSION` — all `null`.
4. Checked whether `lib/omp_hook_bridge/extension.ts`'s `runBridge()` (which *does* read `ctx.getSessionFile()`/`ctx.getAgentId()` per #658, and *would* forward it as `PI_SESSION_FILE` into the dispatcher env) is even the code path firing for pre-bash: added a temporary unconditional debug-log line inside `runBridge()` (reverted after, no diff left) and triggered multiple genuine blocks — the log line never appeared. `~/.omp/agent/extensions/zz-agent-tools-hook-bridge.ts` *is* correctly symlinked to `lib/omp_hook_bridge/extension.ts` (verified byte-for-byte), so either (a) the long-lived omp process for this pane (single PID, alive for days, confirmed via `lsof`) loaded the extension module once at its own startup and never re-imports it live (the `?mtime` cache-buster is a *load-time*, not a per-call, mechanism per `omp://extension-loading.md`), so I could not fully rule this path in or out without restarting a live production omp process serving ~50 concurrent sibling sessions — which I did not do; or (b) this bridge simply isn't the thing constructing the JSON that reaches `orchestrator_stays_thin.py` for pre-bash today. Either way, (5) below shows it doesn't matter which.
5. **Process ancestry is structurally impossible as a fallback for omp** (ruling out the tg-ctl `findAgentInAncestry`-style approach this ticket's investigation was asked to evaluate): `lsof -p <the omp pane's single PID>` shows that ONE long-lived omp process holds open file handles to the top-level session's own `.jsonl` **and** to every one of 50+ dispatched Task-subagent `.jsonl` files simultaneously (mine included). Every bash-tool child spawned for *any* of those sessions — orchestrator or subagent — shares the exact same PPID (that one omp process). There is no OS-process boundary between "the orchestrator" and "a Task-dispatched subagent" to walk with `ps`/`lsof` the way tg-ctl's `findAgentInAncestry` distinguishes *harness binaries* (claude vs codex vs omp) from each other — subagents aren't separate processes at all.

### Why this can't be fixed in agent-tools
- `_is_subagent()` / `_is_omp_nested_session()` in `orchestrator_stays_thin.py` are correct and match the #681 fix exactly — they have nothing to check because **the data they need is never delivered to the process**, confirmed by directly capturing the actual stdin payload and `os.environ` the hook sees, live, for the exact commands that got blocked.
- No env-based fallback exists: every candidate var (`PI_SESSION_FILE`, `RIG_AGENT_ID`, `RIG_DETACHED_AGENT`, `PI_TOOL_BRIDGE_SESSION`) is empty at the point of enforcement.
- No process-ancestry fallback exists: confirmed structurally impossible via `lsof` (single shared PID for the whole session tree — orchestrator and every subagent).
- A tool-call-scoped `env` override on the bash call itself does not help either (per this ticket's original notes) — the pre-bash hook classification runs *before* that override is visible to the classification step.

### What omp needs to fix
Whatever omp-internal code constructs the JSON payload + process environment for a `pre-bash` (bash `tool_call`) hook invocation must thread the same per-subagent identity that `ctx.getSessionFile()`/`ctx.getAgentId()` already expose elsewhere (proven reachable: the eval/Python kernel for the same subagent gets a correct `PI_SESSION_FILE`) into:
- the `agent_id`/`agentId`/`sessionId`/`sessionFile` field of the JSON event handed to the hook script's stdin, **or**
- the `PI_SESSION_FILE`/`RIG_AGENT_ID` env var of the hook subprocess it spawns,

specifically for the pre-bash enforcement path (not just whatever path `lib/omp_hook_bridge/extension.ts`'s `tool_call`/`tool_result` listener covers, which — per point 4 above — may not even be what's live for pre-bash in the currently-running process/version). This is the same root cause #573's own acceptance criterion #2 flagged as "PARTIALLY MET" back when it was written ("omp (tool_call/tool_result payload has no such field, confirmed against extension.ts)") — #658/#676/#681 built the *consumer* side of a fix (agent-tools now knows how to use `ctx.getSessionFile()` if it's populated), but the *producer* side (omp actually populating/propagating it to whatever fires for pre-bash, live, today) is still broken. Evidence above is a fresh, direct reproduction as of tonight, not a rehash of the original report.

### Plain-language summary for Alex
Alex's question tonight, verbatim: **"Два воркера, которых я запускал ранее, почему-то были ошибочно классифицированы системой как 'я сам' (orchestrator), хотя формально были subagent-ами. разве ты ее еще не починил?"**

Answer: **Still broken, and not fixable from the agent-tools side.** #681 correctly fixed the harness-label-matching bug it targeted, but that's a different, narrower bug than the one you're hitting. I reproduced your exact symptom live tonight, from inside a real dispatched subagent, and traced it all the way down: the hook script that decides "orchestrator vs subagent" receives *zero* identifying information about which subagent (if any) made the call — not in its input JSON, not in its process environment — for real `task`-tool-dispatched subagents' bash commands. I also confirmed there is no safe workaround agent-tools can add on its own (no env var carries the signal; process-ancestry can't work either, because every subagent and the orchestrator all run inside the *same single omp process* — there's no OS-level boundary to detect). The gap is in omp's own bash-tool/pre-bash hook-invocation code, which just doesn't pass subagent identity through to that specific enforcement point, even though the identity data demonstrably exists elsewhere in omp (the eval/Python tool sees it correctly for the same subagent). This needs an omp-side (oh-my-pi) fix, not an agent-tools one.

title: Read-only greps are refused as "build/test work" by the skills gate
body:
## What
The skills-read-gate hook refuses ordinary read-only commands as if they were a build or a test run. Any ripgrep whose quoted search pattern contains a pipe followed by a runner-ish word — for example `rg -n "storybook|playwright|vitest" package.json` — is read as a shell pipeline that starts the command `vitest`. So is `ps -axo pid,ppid,command | rg "ultra-setup|go build"`, and so is a `sed -n` file read that happens to sit next to such a grep. The agent is then told it must invoke the delegate-work-to-subagents and visual-proof-cycle skills before it may proceed.

## Why (motivation)
The command-start anchor _CMD_START treats a bare | as a shell separator, and BUILD_OR_TEST is matched against the RAW command string rather than against parsed argv. A | inside single quotes is therefore indistinguishable from a real pipe. This is exactly the false-positive class agent-tools#60 already fixed in the sibling hook no-long-inline-process by shell-tokenizing the command and deciding from argv[0] of each real segment; skills-read-gate never received that port.

## User impact
Measured on four real codex sessions in ~/work/private over 2026-09-05/06: 31 refusals of purely read-only commands, spanning 28 hours. Every one of the 26 distinct refused commands was verified against the live matcher and matched on a quoted pattern. Because Codex has no marker-writing path for this gate, those sessions could never clear it — the agent had to keep re-planning around a wall it could not remove.

## Cost of inaction
Every agent on a harness without a skills marker writer keeps hitting an unremovable block on ordinary code reading. The gate also loses credibility on Claude Code, where agents learn to treat its message as noise.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] A command whose only match is inside a quoted argument — `rg -n "a|vitest" package.json`, `ps -axo command | rg "go build"` — is NOT classified as a work action. — proof: ![proof](/Users/ultra/xp/agent-tools/.worktrees/skills-gate-argv/.ship-proof/578-acceptance.txt)
- [x] A genuine inline build or test run — `npm test`, `vitest run`, `bun test`, `pytest`, `git commit` — is still classified as a work action and still gated. — proof: ![proof](/Users/ultra/xp/agent-tools/.worktrees/skills-gate-argv/.ship-proof/578-acceptance.txt)
- [x] A regression test covers both directions, using the real commands recorded in the codex session logs. — proof: ![proof](/Users/ultra/xp/agent-tools/.worktrees/skills-gate-argv/.ship-proof/578-acceptance.txt)

## Screenshots
(none)

- PR: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/587
- Merge commit: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/commit/ad5dffb9c65304ca6c83471f0c291afd9a102beb

title: The memory gate blocks --help probes and file reads as "test-suite runners"
body:
## What
When machine memory pressure is at warn, heavy-op-memory-gate refuses commands that allocate nothing. Recorded refusals: a `smoo playwright --help` flag-discovery probe, a `dev start server`, and a plain source read of a couple of files with sed and cat. The message tells the agent it looks like a test-suite runner.

## Why (motivation)
The gate classifies by raw substring rather than by the parsed command, so a --help probe and a file read that merely mentions a test path are indistinguishable from actually running the suite. This is the same matching weakness as agent-tools#578 in the skills gate.

## User impact
Alex asks an agent to look at a repository and the agent is refused permission to read the files. Seven times over two days the agent could not check a tool flag or open a source file, so the work it was asked for stalled while nothing was actually consuming memory.

## Cost of inaction
A safety gate that fires on harmless commands gets routed around, and stops protecting against the real heavy operations that once nearly exhausted the machine memory.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A command whose argument list contains --help or --version is never classified as a heavy operation.
- [ ] A read-only command such as sed, cat, head or rg is never classified as a heavy operation, whatever paths it names.
- [ ] A genuine suite run is still blocked at warn pressure, covered by a regression test.
