title: Destructive-command guards refuse benign heredoc writes they cannot parse
body:
## What
pkill-guard and block-reset-hard both fail closed when their shell tokenizer cannot parse a command, and a heredoc carrying a TypeScript or Python body defeats that tokenizer. Four real refusals: writing a TypeScript source file through a heredoc was refused as a possible pattern-based process kill, and two python heredoc scripts were refused as a possible destructive git reset. Replaying all four through the live guards confirms none of them contains the word kill, or reset, anywhere in the command.

## Why (motivation)
Both guards treat an unparseable command as a possible violation. That is the right default for a command that might contain the dangerous verb, but neither guard first checks whether the dangerous verb is present at all. A command with no kill token cannot be a process kill, and one with no reset token cannot be a git reset, regardless of how the tokenizer fares on the heredoc body.

## User impact
Alex asks for a change and the agent cannot write the file. It is told it is doing something dangerous that it is not doing, and told to break up a command that was already one line. Four times over two days a piece of requested work stopped there, and the reason shown to Alex made no sense against what was actually happening.

## Cost of inaction
Writing any source file through this route stays a coin flip, and agents work around it by using less reviewable mechanisms.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A command containing no kill or pkill token is allowed by pkill-guard even when tokenization fails.
- [ ] A command containing no reset or clean token is allowed by block-reset-hard even when tokenization fails.
- [ ] A genuine pkill or git reset --hard is still blocked, including when it is hidden after a heredoc, covered by regression tests.

title: gh ship --help exits 1 as if the flag were a mistake
body:
## What
Running `gh ship --help` prints the usage line but exits with status 1 and the message "Unknown flag: --help". Recorded twice on 2026-09-05.

## Why (motivation)
--help is not in the flag table, so it falls through to the unknown-flag branch, which prints usage and fails.

## User impact
The first thing anyone does with an unfamiliar command is ask it for help, and the tool answers by calling that a mistake. An agent reading the exit code concludes the tool is broken or that it invoked it wrongly, and hesitates before shipping.

## Cost of inaction
Every new agent and every person meeting this tool starts from a failure.

title: ci/ship: no per-repo declarative way to disable the external-review gate (SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW)
body:
## What
`SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW`/`SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW_ENABLED` in [ci/ship/ship.sh](ci/ship/ship.sh) is env-var-only: no committed, audited, per-repo mechanism exists to disable it, unlike `SHIP_ACCEPTANCE_GATE` which is also honored as a committed `.ship-config` line (see `ship.sh`'s `_ship_config_load`, README.md env-knobs table). rig.yaml has no schema key for it either (grepped rig-cli source+docs: zero matches). The only rig-native way to set it declaratively is the generic `env:` block, which writes to a MACHINE-WIDE shell rc file (`~/.zshenv` by default) sourced by every shell on the machine, not scoped to one repo — this is the exact anti-pattern that already caused a real incident ([agent-tools#528](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/528), [tests/conftest.py](tests/conftest.py): a dev machine started exporting `SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0` machine-wide via rig's env mechanism and silently broke five ship-gate tests). Fix: extend `_ship_config_load`'s whitelist in `ship.sh` to accept a `SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW` key (same precedent as `SHIP_ACCEPTANCE_GATE`), read it in the external-review gate block (~line 2718), and document it in README.md's per-repo `.ship-config` knobs list. Optionally add a matching rig-cli schema key (e.g. under `ci.items.ship` or a new `ship:` block) so `rig apply` can provision/reconcile that `.ship-config` line declaratively from rig.yaml, mirroring how rig already manages other committed ci artifacts.

## Why (motivation)
Found investigating [hyperide/hyper-saas#780](https://github.com/hyperide/hyper-saas/pull/780): the repo owner asked to disable SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW for that repo via rig.yaml (consistent with the 2026-09-04 AGENTS.md policy change removing a mandatory human sign-off from the review-quorum gate), but no declarative per-repo mechanism exists today — only a global env var or the machine-wide rig `env:` block (rejected as out of scope for a single repo).

## User impact
Repo owners can turn off the external-review gate for one repo via a normal, reviewed PR instead of a machine-wide shell env var or a per-invocation Telegram approval on every single ship

## Cost of inaction
Every ship on an opted-out repo either needs a manually-exported env var (undocumented, not reproducible, easy to forget) or a live Telegram approval round-trip per PR, defeating the point of disabling the gate; or someone reaches for rig's env: block and silently disables the gate machine-wide for every other repo too (repeat of agent-tools#528)

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] A repo can commit a .ship-config line (e.g. SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0) that disables the external-review gate for that repo only, verified by a ship.sh test exercising a committed .ship-config with the new key — forced: Non-visual, code-only criterion. Proof: PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/609 adds ci/ship/ship.sh's SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW .ship-config key (_ship_config_load whitelist + the gate block) and tests/test_ship.py::test_external_review_disabled_via_committed_ship_config (a committed .ship-config with SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0 disables the gate for that repo only, no env var set) plus test_external_review_ship_config_ignored_on_foreign_repo_invoke (proves it is scoped per-repo, not global) -- full suite: 341 passed.
- [x] README.md ci/ship env-knobs table documents SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW as accepted in .ship-config, mirroring the SHIP_ACCEPTANCE_GATE row — forced: Non-visual, docs-only criterion. Proof: PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/609 -- ci/ship/README.md's env-knobs table row for SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW_ENABLED/SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW now documents the SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW .ship-config key, mirroring the SHIP_ACCEPTANCE_GATE row's wording; also documented in ship.sh's own header comments (Knobs env + Knobs file blocks) and AGENTS.md's ship-gate summary.

title: require-ticket-before-commit: heredoc neutralizer misreads arithmetic << and fd-prefixed chained heredocs
body:
## What

Two exotic shell shapes found reviewing PR #599 (the heredoc-neutralization fix for #503/#406/#430/#570) that the neutralizer still gets wrong. Both are real gate-bypass/false-block classes in principle, but neither shape appears in the documented commit-message pattern (`CLAUDE.md`'s `-m "$(cat <<'EOF' ... EOF)"`) or in any of the four original issues — they surfaced only because review-cli's adversarial pass specifically hunts for edge cases.

1. **Arithmetic context.** `(( 1 << EOF ))` is a left-shift expression, not a heredoc opener — the neutralizer doesn't track `((...))`/`$((...))` context, so it misreads the `<<` as a real heredoc and consumes the following lines (including a real, ticketless `git commit`) as its "body". Repro:
   ```bash
   (( 1 << EOF ))
   git commit -m 'fix: no ticket'
   EOF
   ```
   Real bash executes the ticketless commit; the hook currently finds no commit segment at all and silently ALLOWS it.

2. **Descriptor-prefixed chained heredocs.** The chained-heredoc detector (`_read_heredoc_operators_on_line`) only recognizes a following `<<A <<B` pair when the second operator starts with a bare `<<`; it misses an explicit-fd form like `0<<B` (no space before the digit). Repro:
   ```bash
   git commit -m "$(cat <<A 0<<B
   Refs #1
   A
   fix: no ticket
   B
   )"
   ```
   Real bash applies the final `0<<B` redirect, so `cat`'s stdin is body B (`fix: no ticket`, no ticket ref). The hook currently only recognizes the first operator A, retains "Refs #1" from the unused body, and wrongly ALLOWS the commit.

## Why (motivation)

Found during review-cli's third round on PR #599, after two earlier rounds had already closed several similar heredoc-parsing gaps (chained `<<A <<B` without fd prefixes, comment-hidden heredocs, backtick substitutions, compact operators, ordering). These two are meaningfully more exotic (arithmetic expressions and fd-prefixed redirects essentially never appear in an agent-authored commit message) and were explicitly scoped OUT of #599 to avoid an unbounded review loop on cosmetics — see PR #599's "Known limitations" section.

## User impact

Extremely narrow: only a hand-crafted command using arithmetic `<<` or fd-prefixed chained heredocs around a `git commit` could exploit either gap. No real agent or human commit-message-authoring workflow observed so far uses either shape.

## Cost of inaction

Low today (no observed real-world trigger), but the gate's core promise ("a ticketless commit always blocks") has two known, narrow holes until this is picked up.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `_neutralize_heredocs` tracks `((...))`/`$((...))` arithmetic context (mirroring `block-raw-pr-merge`'s own `arith_depth` tracking for the identical class of problem) so a `<<` inside one is never treated as a heredoc opener, with a regression test for the arithmetic-context repro above.
- [ ] The chained-heredoc detector recognizes an explicit leading file-descriptor digit before `<<` (`0<<B`, `2<<B`, etc.) as a valid chain continuation, with a regression test for the fd-prefixed repro above.
- [ ] Both fixes ship with the SAME "mirror the fix into `tests/test_require_ticket_before_commit.py` and `agent-hooks/require-ticket-before-commit/test_require_ticket.py`" convention PR #599 established.

## Links

- PR #599 (the parent fix): https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/599
- Original issues this PR's fix targets: #503, #406, #430, #570

title: shared, backend-aware task-code validation library for review-cli and every other --task CODE consumer
body:
## What
review-cli's --task CODE / REVIEW_TASK_CODE accepts ANY free-form string with zero validation, and
a live sweep of ~/.config/review-cli/run-stats.jsonl this session found the ecosystem's own history
full of invented, non-resolvable codes recorded as if they were real ticket references: bare
placeholders like "CODE" and "TEST-1" (thousands of hits), free-text slugs like
"ambiguous-create-dedup", "docs-gcs-emulator-colima-note", "review-cli-presets-sol",
"AGENT-BROWSER-CONCURRENCY-HYGIENE" -- none of these resolve to an actual GitHub issue or Linear
ticket. This session alone added at least two more (a fabricated "RIG-CLI-298-VERSION-BUMP" code
used for a rig-cli PR review pass, caught and removed from the log; an invented
"REVIEW-CLI-ROLE-PAD-COOLDOWN" style code used earlier for shipping PR#419 that also did not
resolve to a real ticket). The problem is systemic, not one agent's mistake in one session.

This needs a shared library in agent-tools (not a review-cli-only fix, since --task CODE-shaped
arguments/env vars show up in other tools too), backend-aware: a repo's task-cli config (task.yaml,
`backend: github-issues` with `github.repo`, or `backend: linear` with a team/prefix) already
defines what a REAL code looks like for that repo. The library should read that same config and
validate/normalize a candidate code against it.

## Why (motivation)
Alex, 2026-09-07: caught an invented review-cli task code live ("такого кода задачи не бывает") and asked for this to be fixed everywhere, not just in review-cli -- "не только в review а везде, в agent-tools должна быть библиотека валидации с учетом настроек репы gh-issues/linear".

## User impact
Anyone later trying to trace why a change shipped -- what ticket justified it, what the reviewers actually looked at -- hits a dead end: the recorded reference doesn't lead anywhere, because it was never a real ticket to begin with.

## Cost of inaction
The review-quorum record that gh ship relies on to prove a change was actually reviewed keeps accumulating references nobody can follow back to real, accountable tickets, and the mistake keeps recurring because nothing stops it at the point where the code is typed in.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] New agent-tools lib (e.g. lib/agenttools_taskref) reads a repo's task.yaml the same way task-cli does (github-issues: backend + github.repo; linear: backend + team prefix) and exposes a validate(code, repo_root) function returning either a resolved canonical reference (with a real, checkable URL) or a clear rejection
- [ ] For a github-issues repo, only a real, resolvable issue/PR number in that repo (or an explicit owner/repo#n cross-repo form) validates -- a free-text slug or a bare placeholder is rejected with guidance pointing at task-cli (task find / task new) to locate or create the real ticket
- [ ] For a linear repo, only a code carrying that repo's actual configured team prefix validates, auto-resolved from the same task.yaml linear config task-cli itself reads -- a mismatched or made-up prefix is rejected with guidance naming the correct prefix
- [ ] review-cli's --task CODE / REVIEW_TASK_CODE is wired to call this validator before recording anything in run-stats.jsonl, replacing today's zero-validation accept-anything behavior
- [ ] Regression tests: a real resolvable GitHub issue number passes; a linear-shaped code with the wrong prefix is rejected with the right prefix suggested; a free-text slug is rejected with task-cli guidance; the library degrades safely (clear error, not a crash) when no task.yaml is present

title: Hooks said no; the agent still wrote files and ran review through other tools
body:
## What
This is not a story about a subagent in its own worktree.

Who: one main omp agent. Its working folder was the primary review-cli checkout, on branch main. Feature work lived in a separate git worktree (a second folder of the same repo, on a feature branch). The repo has worktree-only on: agents must not author on main.

What happened, in order:

1. The agent tried the normal Edit tool on CHANGELOG.md inside the feature worktree. The worktree-only hook refused: it said the checkout is on main. The file was not on main — it was in the worktree. The hook judged the session folder (main), not the folder of the file being edited. Two shapes: a relative path like CHANGELOG.md was resolved from the session folder; a conflict-marker write carried no path at all, so the hook again used the session folder.

2. The agent then wrote the same worktree files with a Python eval cell (Path.write_text). That tool is not in the omp hook bridge mapping (only bash, edit, write, apply_patch, notebook, task are). The write hook never ran. The files changed anyway. That was a bypass.

3. A second hook, no-long-inline-process, forbids the main agent from running long programs (the review CLI, long sleep) in the chat, because the chat would freeze. The intended path is a background worker. On omp, workers do not get a harness-issued id saying they are workers, so they get the same forbid. The agent started review (and sleep) via hub start, which is not bash, so this hook never saw those processes either. Another bypass.

4. The ship-quorum hook's only escape is a Telegram tap from Alex. The ask never posted (daemon declined or unreachable). The agent did not stop. It ran more reviews via hub start.

The bug is the contour: a gate blocks tool A and tool B with the same effect is invisible to the gate.

## Why (motivation)
If worktree-only is on, writing on main must be impossible, including through Python eval. If long review must not run in the main chat, it must not run via hub start either unless that is the one allowed path and the hook knows about it. Observed while shipping https://github.com/alex-mextner/review-cli/pull/420. Bridge mapping: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/main/lib/omp_hook_bridge/README.md

## User impact
You turn on worktree-only so agents cannot edit main. They still edit the same files through Python. You block a long review in the main chat so you can keep talking. They still launch review as a background process the hook does not see. The switch looks on and does not stop the work.

## Cost of inaction
Every new omp tool that writes a file or starts a process is another hole. Agents will keep using the tool the hook does not know. If Telegram is down, they will invent a third path instead of stopping.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] eval write and hub start of a gated binary against a worktree_only primary checkout either fire the same hook as Edit/bash or are fail-closed as unmapped. Proof: hook test with an omp-shaped event whose tool is eval or hub, asserting block or equivalent pre-write/pre-bash dispatch.
- [ ] A hashline Edit whose section path is relative to a worktree file, and a conflict URI write, are judged against the target file checkout not session cwd. Proof: unit test on _target_dir / bridge path emission with cwd=primary and target under .worktrees.
- [ ] omp Task and eval.agent children carry a bridge-injected trusted agent id so no-long-inline allows review there and still blocks the orchestrator. Proof: hook test with harness=omp plus injected id vs stripped forged id.
- [ ] When the Telegram hatch channel is down, the hook still blocks and does not document a third path; a session-level health check on tg-ctl ask-forward is specified. Proof: hatch fail path test plus a one-line owner for the daemon-dark P0.

- screenshots: no UI; CLI/hook contract, proof is hook refusal text and bridge README mapping table

title: omp hook bridge: eval and hub tool calls are invisible to every installed pre-write/pre-bash hook
body:
## What
lib/omp_hook_bridge/dispatch.py's point_for_event maps only bash, edit/write/apply_patch/notebook (_WRITE_TOOLS), and task to a v1 hook point; eval and hub are absent from every branch, so for any omp tool_call whose toolName is eval or hub, point_for_event returns None, dispatch() returns None immediately, and extension.ts's runBridge sees no stdout JSON -- every installed agents-hooks/v1 descriptor (worktree-only-writes, block-secrets-write, no-long-inline-process, block-raw-pr-merge, orchestrator-stays-thin) is silently skipped. This was reported live in https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/613 : an agent blocked from editing a worktree file via the normal edit tool wrote the same files with a Python eval cell instead, and the write hook never ran (a real bypass); separately it started a long review process and a sleep loop via hub start instead of bash, and no-long-inline-process never saw either process. tests/test_omp_hook_bridge.py's test_point_for_event_maps_omp_tools_to_v1_points enumerates exactly bash/edit/write/apply_patch/notebook/task -- eval and hub are absent from both the implementation and its test, confirming this is a real, untested blind spot, not a documented exclusion. Fix: add eval to a write-shaped mapping (with a _normalize_write_args branch that extracts the written path/content from eval's actual argument shape) and hub to the pre-bash mapping (with _tool_command extended to synthesize a command string from hub's op/application/args fields), in point_for_event (dispatch.py).

## Why (motivation)
A gate that blocks tool A must not have a same-effect tool B that bypasses it invisibly -- the whole guarantee of worktree-only / no-long-inline-process / block-secrets-write depends on every write- and process-launching tool omp exposes being seen by the bridge

## User impact
Someone who turns on the worktree-only guard so agents cannot edit their main checkout, or blocks long review/test runs from freezing the main chat, discovers agents can still do both by using eval or hub start instead of the tools the guard actually watches -- the switch looks on and silently does not stop the behavior it was meant to stop

## Cost of inaction
Every new omp tool that writes a file or starts a process stays another hole a model can route through, on top of the two already found live (eval write, hub start)

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] dispatch.point_for_event maps eval to the write-shaped hook point and hub to the pre-bash point, each covered by a new unit test alongside the existing test_point_for_event_maps_omp_tools_to_v1_points
- [ ] An end-to-end test proves a real block-secrets-write descriptor fires against an eval-shaped omp event that writes a secret, and a real no-long-inline-process descriptor fires against a hub-start-shaped omp event launching a long-running command, both of which pass through unexamined today

title: omp bridge + worktree-only-writes: directory checks trust the session cwd, not the write's real target directory
body:
## What
agent-hooks/worktree-only-writes/worktree_only_writes.py's _target_dir() reads args.file_path/path/notebook_path; when none of those keys is present at all it silently falls back to base = cwd (the bridge's reported session cwd), with no signal that path resolution actually failed. This is reachable today: lib/omp_hook_bridge/dispatch.py's _normalize_write_args only sets a path key for the notebook tool 'if path:' -- when omp's real notebook wire shape carries none of those keys, args ends up with no path at all and the hook silently checks the session cwd's branch instead of refusing to guess. Separately, for a hashline edit call, _hashline_file_paths() extracts an inherently relative path (e.g. CHANGELOG.md) from the [PATH#TAG] header, and _target_dir resolves it by joining that relative path onto the session cwd -- reported live in https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/613 : one main omp agent's working folder was the primary checkout on main, feature work lived in a separate worktree on a feature branch, and editing CHANGELOG.md inside the worktree via a relative hashline path got judged against the session's main-branch cwd instead of the worktree the file actually lives in -- the hook said no to a write that was never on main at all. Neither the codex nor opencode sibling bridges already solve this class (both trust their own reported cwd with no target-directory cross-check either), so there is no existing pattern to port; this is new, omp-specific (and potentially shared) fix work.

## Why (motivation)
A guard that decides whether a write is safe by looking at the WRONG directory gives a false sense of protection in one direction (a worktree write wrongly blocked as if it were on main) and a real hole in the other (a future case where the wrong directory happens to read as safe when the real target is not)

## User impact
Someone relying on the worktree-only guard to keep agents off their main checkout gets a confusing false refusal when an agent tries to legitimately edit a file that already lives in a properly separated worktree, purely because of which folder the agent's session happens to be sitting in

## Cost of inaction
Every relative-path edit inside a worktree stays a coin flip between a false block and a false allow depending on which directory the agent session happens to be in, undermining trust in the guard either way

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A worktree-only-writes test with args carrying no file_path/path/notebook_path key at all asserts an explicit, intentional, tested outcome for the no-resolvable-target-path case, replacing today's silent fall-through to the bare cwd
- [ ] A worktree-only-writes end-to-end test using a relative hashline path (like CHANGELOG.md) plus a cwd that is on the default branch, where the file's real resolved directory is a non-default-branch worktree, asserts the hook's block/allow verdict tracks the file's real target directory rather than the passed session cwd
- [ ] Full existing worktree-only-writes and omp hook bridge test suites still pass after the change

title: worktree-only-writes: relative hashline path can't be resolved to its real worktree without omp exposing the resolved absolute path
body:
## What
While fixing #615, an attempt at resolving a RELATIVE hashline write path (e.g. `[CHANGELOG.md#TAG]`, cwd on the primary/main checkout, the file really being edited living in a separate feature-branch worktree of the same repo — the #613 repro) by checking whether the relative path existed in some OTHER git worktree of the same repo, and preferring that worktree when exactly one had it, was found UNSOUND by adversarial review (review-cli, xai/grok-4.6):

A relative write whose underlying tool actually resolves the path against `cwd` (main) would be silently ALLOWED whenever any sibling worktree happened to already track a file at that same relative path — turning a false BLOCK (the #613 complaint) into a worse false ALLOW on the exact branch `worktree-only-writes` exists to protect. There is no signal available to either the hook (`agent-hooks/worktree-only-writes/worktree_only_writes.py`) or the omp bridge (`lib/omp_hook_bridge/dispatch.py`) that can distinguish "the file is really meant for that other worktree" from "a same-named file coincidentally already exists there" — both layers only ever see the identical `cwd` string plus the bare relative path text.

That heuristic was reverted (see `_target_dir`'s "Known limitation" docstring in `worktree_only_writes.py`, landed via #615's PR). A relative hashline path is judged against `cwd`, same as before #615 — so the #613 false-block scenario (relative path, cwd on main, real file in a worktree) is NOT fixed; only the no-path-key silent-cwd-fallback half of #615 was fixed soundly.

## Why (motivation)
A sound fix needs omp itself to expose the ALREADY-RESOLVED absolute path a hashline `[PATH#TAG]` really refers to — omp's own editor must track this internally already (to validate TAG against the live file before applying an edit), but it is not exposed in the documented `tool_call`/`tool_result` extension event shape this bridge consumes today (only `toolName`/`input`/`cwd`/`toolCallId`).

## User impact
An agent whose session cwd is the primary (main-branch) checkout, editing a file that genuinely lives in a separate worktree via a RELATIVE hashline path, still gets a false BLOCK from `worktree-only-writes` — the exact #613 complaint, unresolved. The workaround (documented in the hook) is to use an ABSOLUTE path for the edit (handled correctly), or the existing `RIG_HATCH_REQUEST_WORKTREE_ONLY_WRITES` Telegram escape hatch.

## Cost of inaction
The #613 false-block keeps recurring for relative-path worktree edits from a main-cwd omp session until omp's extension API is extended (or investigated further) to expose a resolved absolute path per tool call.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Either omp's extension event is confirmed to already carry (or is asked to add) a resolved-absolute-path field the bridge can read, and `_normalize_write_args`/`to_v1_event` in `lib/omp_hook_bridge/dispatch.py` are updated to use it when present
- [ ] OR a different sound (non-existence-guessing) signal is found and implemented in `_target_dir`, with adversarial review confirming no false-ALLOW regression
- [ ] A worktree-only-writes end-to-end test proves the #613 scenario (relative path, cwd on main, real file in a worktree) now ALLOWs, without reintroducing the sibling-worktree-existence bypass #615's PR reverted

## Links
- #615 (this issue's investigation and revert)
- #613 (the original false-block report this would fix)

title: omp hook bridge eval secret-scanning: replace regex text-scrape with a real AST walk
body:
## What
The omp hook bridge's eval tool secret-scanning (added for issue #614, hardened across 3 review rounds fixing 13 distinct bypasses total: fs-suffix receiver exclusion, ReDoS, JS unicode escapes, writelines-list args, hub malformed-args fail-open, f-string path interpolation, string-concatenation truncation, whole-string ASCII decode gating, write-call data-keyword recognition, identifier-boundary anchors, path escape-decoding, escape double-decode, raw-string path semantics, and a path-less content fallback) is a roughly 780-line hand-rolled regex text-scrape standing in for a real parser: quote handling, escape decoding, keyword-argument matching, raw-string prefixes, and call-boundary detection are all approximated with lookaheads and negative lookbehinds. Every one of the 13 fixes across 3 rounds followed the same shape: the regex silently assumed a language-semantics rule that does not actually hold (backslash is always an escape, keyword args only appear first, decode-before-comparing is always safe, one level of parens is enough) -- each fix closed one instance of that pattern without closing the pattern itself. The next write idiom a model reaches for (property-access chains, spread args, computed member expressions, tagged template literals, a path-join helper, a fluent chained-call style, or multi-statement value flow assigning through an intermediate variable) is a new blind spot that will need its own future regex clause, not something a 4th or 5th hardening round can close structurally.

## Why (motivation)
Three independent hardening rounds have each found and closed a batch of real secret-scan bypasses in the same module, and every fix has had the identical structural cause -- the regex approximates a language-semantics rule instead of using the real grammar. Continued ad-hoc patching finds bypasses one idiom at a time forever; parsing the real grammar closes whole categories of bypass at once.

## User impact
Someone relying on the worktree-only/block-secrets-write guard to catch a secret written via an eval cell is protected only against the specific write-shapes three rounds of adversarial review happened to think of -- a write expressed through a not-yet-considered but everyday code idiom can still slip a real secret onto disk unscanned, with no error or warning that the scan even missed it

## Cost of inaction
Every future review round on this module keeps finding the same class of bug in a new shape, each fix adds another regex clause to an already-large pattern set, and the fundamental gap (the scanner doesn't actually understand the language it's scanning) never closes

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] The eval tool's write-detection for the Python branch uses Python's own ast module to parse the eval code string and walk real AST nodes instead of regex-matching literal-shaped text, so a string literal, a keyword argument, and a raw-string prefix are real grammar productions the parser already understands rather than regex approximations
- [ ] The eval tool's write-detection for the JS branch uses a real (even if minimal/lightweight) JS tokenizer or parser instead of regex text-scraping, covering at minimum the same call shapes the current regex patterns already target
- [ ] All existing regression tests from the 3 prior regex-hardening rounds pass unchanged against the new AST-based implementation, proving no coverage regression from the rewrite
- [ ] At least 3 of the write-idiom classes explicitly named as still-unclosed blind spots in this ticket are demonstrated closed by new tests that fail against the OLD regex implementation and pass against the new AST-based one

comments.body:
Round-6 review-quorum pass on PR #621 (task #614) surfaced a concrete instance of the structural gap this issue tracks, verified against live source (ran the payload through `omp_hook_bridge.dispatch._eval_content_buckets` directly):

**Nested computed-path arguments defeat `_EVAL_ARG_SKIP`'s one-level-of-parens tolerance.** `dispatch.py`'s `_EVAL_ARG_SKIP` fragment (used by the `Bun.write`/`fs.*File*`/bare-`write` path-less fallbacks) only tolerates ONE level of nested parens in an unresolved first (path) argument. A two-level nested call — a common, realistic idiom — defeats it entirely:

```js
Bun.write(path.resolve(path.join("dir", "target")), "API_KEY = YOUR_KEY_HERE")
```

produces `buckets == {}` — the write is completely unscanned (not even filed under the path-less `""` bucket), because `_EVAL_ARG_SKIP`'s regex stops at the wrong `)` and the whole call fails to match any pattern, dedicated or fallback. This is not a one-line fix: `_EVAL_ARG_SKIP`'s own comment already documents single-level nesting as an accepted imprecision, and arbitrary nesting depth is fundamentally unbounded for any finite regex — exactly the class of bug this issue proposes to close via a real AST/parser walk rather than another regex clause. Filed here rather than as a 6th/7th regex patch, per the judgment call this issue itself argues for.

A further review-quorum verification pass on PR #621 (task #614), immediately after landing the round-6 fixes (commit 4201ffb), found 2 MORE new bypasses in the identical two regex components that keep recurring — concrete further evidence for this issue's structural diagnosis. Both verified live against `omp_hook_bridge.dispatch._eval_content_buckets`:

1. **`_EVAL_KWARG_VALUE` doesn't recognize a parenthesized expression as a valid preceding-keyword value.** `Path("src/secret.py").write_text(encoding=("utf-8"), data="API_KEY = abcd1234abcd1234")` — a syntactically ordinary Python call — makes the whole `_EVAL_DATA_KWARG_PREFIX` skip fail, so `_eval_content_buckets()` returns `{}` and the secret write is allowed. This is the SAME regex component (`_EVAL_KWARG_VALUE`) that round 6 just widened to accept a bare call expression (`foo()`) as a keyword value — a parenthesized non-call expression is a sibling shape the round-6 fix didn't cover, immediately proving out this issue's central claim that fixing one shape doesn't close the pattern.

2. **`_eval_literal_run` accepts a leading literal token as satisfying a whole content argument, even when a non-literal continuation follows.** `Path("src/secret.py").write_text("API_KEY = {}".format("abcd1234abcd1234"))` matches successfully but captures only `'API_KEY = {}'` — the real secret (interpolated via `.format(...)`) never enters the scanned content. Also reproduces with string `+` concatenation and `.join([...])` continuations. Unlike finding 1 (total miss), this is a silent WRONG-CONTENT match — arguably worse, since the call isn't flagged as unrecognized at all.

Neither has been patched (deliberately — see PR #621's round-6 discussion: the parent judged this pattern as now confirmed structural rather than a string of one-off narrow fixes, and stopped further regex patching in favor of tracking here). Filed as more evidence for the AST/parser rewrite this issue proposes.

Refusing"); (2) SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0 exported -> ship prints "[ship] external-review gate disabled (SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW_ENABLED/SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0)." and proceeds past the zero-review PR to the next gate (only stopped afterward by an unrelated magic-close-keyword refusal). The gate itself is provably still waivable by a bare env export, the same shape as PR #764 that this gate exists to prevent. Kill (or scope-restrict) the env-var off-switch for the external-review gate specifically, now that the committed .ship-config key is available as the audited, non-ambient alternative -- mirroring how other merge-safety gates (review-quorum, --skip-ci) already have NO self-service env off-switch, only a live Telegram hatch.

## Why (motivation)
A merge-safety gate whose entire purpose is closing the PR #764 zero-review-merge hole must not be disable-able by a single unreviewed, ambient env var export -- that defeats the audited .ship-config mechanism #609 just built and reopens the exact machine-wide-leak failure mode [#528](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/528) already documented for this same knob.

## User impact
Any agent or developer with SHIP_EXTERNAL_REVIEW=0 in their shell (accidentally, machine-wide, or copy-pasted from a doc/test) can ship any PR -- including their own -- with zero GitHub-side review, silently, with no repo-level record and no audit trail beyond a local dry-run/merge log.

## Cost of inaction
A future PR #764-shaped incident recurs via a plain env export instead of a hand-rolled merge script -- the env bypass is a strictly easier attack surface than the thing #609 was supposed to close.

title: orchestrator-stays-thin blocks a second-level nested subagent with no delegation path at all
body:
## What
Live-discovered while dogfooding issue #573's merged fix (PR #620): a subagent spawned by another subagent (two levels below the top-level orchestrator) hit the newly-generalized orchestrator-stays-thin gate on every Edit/Write/Bash mutation attempt, even with correct absolute paths and correct worktree cwd. Unlike a top-level dispatched subagent (which correctly gets treated as a worker and allowed to mutate), this second-level nested subagent had no further task/agent-dispatch tool exposed to it at all -- only peer messaging to already-existing siblings -- so it could not comply with the gate's own instruction to delegate further. It also tried the documented sanctioned escape hatch, RIG_HATCH_REQUEST_ORCHESTRATOR_STAYS_THIN with a full written justification, and was denied (deny-by-default, no live human available). The work was only unblocked by having the top-level orchestrator kill the stuck nested subagent and dispatch a fresh direct (one-level) subagent for the same task instead.

## Why (motivation)
Issue #573 was explicitly about giving every legitimate delegated worker the same treatment regardless of harness or nesting depth -- a worker two levels deep being treated identically to the orchestrator itself, with no path forward at all, is the exact ungoverned-or-unusable dilemma #573 was filed to close, just one level deeper than the cases #573 actually tested

## User impact
Anyone whose subagent legitimately spawns its own helper subagent for a sub-task discovers that helper can read files but cannot write or run anything, with no live human around to grant the one-time hatch bypass, and the only way to make progress is for a human or the top-level orchestrator to notice, kill the stuck nested agent, and manually redo the work one level shallower

## Cost of inaction
Every multi-level delegation chain in this ecosystem breaks the same way the moment a subagent needs its own helper, and each occurrence looks like a mysterious hang rather than a recognized, tracked gap

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A subagent that is itself the child of another (already-legitimate) subagent is recognized as a worker by the trusted-identity mechanism #573 introduced, the same way a direct top-level dispatch already is, so orchestrator-stays-thin does not block it
- [ ] If a nested subagent genuinely has no further tool to delegate deeper work to, the gate's own refusal text says so accurately for that case, instead of instructing it to use a Task tool that isn't exposed to it
- [ ] A test with a real bridge event carrying two levels of legitimate subagent nesting (grandchild of the orchestrator) asserts the grandchild is allowed the same way a direct child already is

comments.body:
Additional concrete diagnostic evidence, from a separate live repro today (agent-tools#614's own final wiring step, ironic given the ticket is about eval-tool bypasses):

A **top-level, direct** `task`-tool-dispatched omp subagent (not nested — a genuine first-level worker spawned by Main) hit the identical `orchestrator-stays-thin` block on plain `edit` tool calls, twice, verbatim same message as the nested case already described in this ticket. Its own diagnostic: `env | grep -i 'RIG_\|OMP_\|AGENT'` inside that subagent showed only `AGENT=1` — **no `RIG_AGENT_ID` or `RIG_DETACHED_AGENT`** in the environment at all. Per #573/PR #620's own design, those two env vars (set only by the `rig-detached-omp` launcher, not by the plain `task` tool) are the sole trusted-identity source `_detached_agent_id()` checks — so a `task`-tool-spawned omp subagent that never went through `rig-detached-omp` has **no way to prove it's a worker**, and gets misclassified as the orchestrator.

Interesting additional wrinkle from the same repro: the block did **not** fire uniformly — a `bash`/`eval` subprocess call doing the identical file mutation (via Python's `subprocess.run(...)` from inside an `eval` kernel) went through unblocked in the same session where the `edit` tool call was blocked twice. That inconsistency (edit blocked, equivalent eval/bash mutation allowed) is itself the exact bypass shape agent-tools#614 was filed to close on the *omp_hook_bridge* side — it looks like `orchestrator-stays-thin` (a different, separate hook) may have the same class of gap independently.

Given most `task`-tool-dispatched subagents in that same long session did NOT hit this block on earlier edits, the trigger looks conditional/heuristic (matches the hook's documented "warn→block" escalation) rather than a hard 100%-of-the-time block for every omp `task` subagent — worth checking whether `task`-tool dispatch should itself set `RIG_AGENT_ID`/`RIG_DETACHED_AGENT` in the child's environment (mirroring what `rig-detached-omp` does), rather than requiring every worker to go through the separate launcher explicitly.

title: Map omp tool_call+yield to v1 stop so session-end hooks can block a premature yield
body:
## What
CC maps Stop to stop at lib/cc_hook_bridge/dispatch.py:99-100. Codex maps Stop to stop at lib/codex_hook_bridge/dispatch.py:80-81. omp_hook_bridge does not: point_for_event in lib/omp_hook_bridge/dispatch.py:89-101 only maps tool_call bash/edit/write/apply_patch/notebook/task and tool_result writes. extension.ts:367-397 subscribes to session_shutdown (reap only), tool_call, tool_result — no agent_end handler. README.md:72-74 documents this as intentional because session_shutdown/agent_end have no blocking contract. But yield IS a tool_call, and tool_call CAN return block:true (oh-my-pi docs/hooks.md). Mapping tool_call+yield to stop lets stop-completion-selfcheck fire before the helper parks.

## Why (motivation)
A helper can yield (often a PR URL) with no Stop self-check. CC and Codex cannot; omp can. That is why helpers sleep-and-vanish after a yield with no self-check.

## User impact
Under omp, a helper ends its turn without the completion self-check that other harnesses enforce. The parent sees a yield, ticks the todo, and the unfinished helper is gone.

## Cost of inaction
stop-completion-selfcheck stays inert on omp. Helpers keep yielding early. The keepalive TTL setting alone cannot force a self-check.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] point_for_event('tool_call','yield') returns 'stop'; a blocking stop descriptor on yield returns omp_block_output. Proof: unit tests in tests/test_omp_hook_bridge.py.
- [ ] README mapping table documents yield to stop and that session_shutdown/agent_end remain unmapped because they have no blocking contract. Proof: README plus the same tests.

title: Audit raw tracker write guard
body:
## What
Adversarial review finding (live repro, 2026-09-08): block_raw_ticket.py is_raw_tracker_write() fallback path (_tokenize returns None on a shlex-unparseable command) falls back to _RAW_HINT.search(command), a bare regex over the WHOLE raw command string with no awareness of quoting or argument boundaries. A legitimate task new invocation whose --what or --why free-text body merely quotes or describes an example referencing the gh CLIs issue subcommand (as prose describing an unrelated bug) gets misclassified as an unparseable-and-plausible raw tracker write and BLOCKED, even though the actual command head is task new, the sanctioned tool. Repro: a task new call with several embedded apostrophes in the body text caused shlex tokenization to fail on this session, then RAW_HINT matched the trigger phrase elsewhere in the body prose, producing the BLOCKED raw tracker write message. Same class of bug applies to the JUNK_UNCOMMITTED fallback (lines near 292 to 295 and 317 to 320) and the final except Exception handler (line near 338 to 342), all of which reuse the same whole-string regex-over-unparsed-text fallback.

## Why (motivation)
The new pre-bash guard changes ticket-tracker write enforcement and needs an adversarial review before merge.

## User impact
A missed bypass can let autonomous agents create or mutate tickets outside task-cli's required metadata gates; a false positive can block valid developer workflows.

## Cost of inaction
The enforcement change could merge with undetected shell parsing bypasses or regressions.

- [ ] Identify every actionable correctness, security, regression, testing, or performance finding in the uncommitted block-raw-ticket diff with file and line references.

title: Gate dangerous Workflow scripts without blocking ultracode or comments
body:
## What
The Claude Code Workflow tool is blanket-allowed in the harness permission list so ultracode can spawn without a prompt. That allow is unguarded: the CC hook bridge does not map Workflow to any v1 hook point, settings PreToolUse matchers omit Workflow, and no hook inspects the script. A Workflow that runs a raw PR merge, a hard git reset, a force-push, sudo rm, or a no-verify commit therefore auto-runs. Alex asked to make ultra code work, not to allow Workflow entirely (asks 129 and 130; astra question 31).

Evidence now, in this checkout: lib/cc_hook_bridge/dispatch.py function point_for_event maps Bash, Write, Agent, and Skill only — Workflow returns None. Live user settings permissions.allow contains the bare string Workflow. PreToolUse matchers are Bash, the write tools, Agent or Task, Skill, Monitor, EnterWorktree — no Workflow.

Catalog: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools
Bridge mapping: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/main/lib/cc_hook_bridge/dispatch.py

Fix: map Workflow to a new pre-workflow point in the CC bridge; add a fail-closed workflow-danger-gate that strips JS comments then denies known-destructive command forms. Comments that mention those forms stay allowed. Ultracode-shaped scripts that only call agent() stay allowed.

## Why (motivation)
A blanket Workflow allow was added so ultracode works. Without a script-level gate, that allow also auto-approves destructive Workflows. Comments explaining the permission split were never written, so the next editor cannot tell allow-from-gate.

## User impact
When you say ultracode, agents can still fan work out through Workflow without a permission prompt. If a Workflow script itself tries to raw-merge a PR, force-push, hard-reset, or skip git hooks, that call is denied instead of silently running. You can write comments in the script that mention those commands without tripping the gate.

## Cost of inaction
Every ultracode session keeps a hole: any Workflow script can do the destructive things the bash hooks already block, because Workflow never hits those hooks. Operators keep asking whether Workflow is safe and get no durable answer.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] A Workflow script that only dispatches agent() (ultracode) is allowed — proven by tests/test_workflow_danger_gate.py — forced: bridge mapping + clean-room deny: tests/test_cc_hook_bridge.py::test_pre_workflow_dangerous_script_is_blocked and test_point_for_event_maps_tool_to_logical_point passed
- [x] A Workflow script whose executable JS contains a raw PR merge, git reset --hard, git push --force or -f, git clean -f, sudo rm, --no-verify, or screencapture is blocked (exit 10) — proven by tests/test_workflow_danger_gate.py — forced: bridge mapping + clean-room deny: tests/test_cc_hook_bridge.py::test_pre_workflow_dangerous_script_is_blocked and test_point_for_event_maps_tool_to_logical_point passed

title: ship auto-bump leaves required approvals dismissed when dismiss_stale_reviews is true
body:
## What
After ship auto-bumps, GitHub dismisses reviews when dismiss_stale_reviews is true, and the subsequent non-admin merge is refused. Need a durable way to keep required approvals valid that is not --admin.

## Why (motivation)
gh ship auto-bumps via a Contents API commit on the PR HEAD (https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/518 and https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/672). Repos whose branch protection sets dismiss_stale_reviews: true (the documented default in agent-tools README) treat that commit as a new head and dismiss existing approvals. Ship never uses --admin, so gh pr merge then fails on required reviews even though the PR was ready before the bump. Documented in ci/ship/README.md; no restore path in this PR.

## User impact
A PR that was fully reviewed and ready to merge can still be refused at the last step after ship writes the version bump. Agents then stall asking for a re-approval, and the parallel-PR-conflict fix does not actually drain the queue on repos that keep dismiss_stale_reviews.

## Cost of inaction
Every auto-bumped ship on a dismiss_stale_reviews repo needs a human re-approval after the bump commit, recreating the hand-rebase chore https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/518 was meant to remove.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Ship either preserves or re-obtains the required approval after its own bump commit without --admin, proven by a hermetic test where dismiss_stale_reviews would otherwise block merge.
- [ ] A repo with dismiss_stale_reviews false still auto-bumps and merges as today, proven by the existing tests/test_ship_auto_bump.py suite staying green.

title: fix(orchestrator-stays-thin): nested omp task-tool subagent under claude-code harness still gated as orchestrator
body:
## What
PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/637 added a 3rd _is_subagent trust tier: a nested omp PI_SESSION_FILE, but ONLY when event.harness == "omp" (agent_hooks/orchestrator-stays-thin/orchestrator_stays_thin.py). cc_hook_bridge (lib/cc_hook_bridge/dispatch.py) hardcodes HARNESS = "claude-code" for every event it emits, so a Claude-Code-backed omp session PreToolUse events always carry harness=="claude-code", never "omp" -- the PI_SESSION_FILE tier can never fire for this common transport. Live incident 2026-09-08: subagent CommitReconcile (dispatched via the omp task tool from a top-level Main agent, rig.yaml harness.kind: claude-code) attempted a raw-git commit in a prepared worktree on rig-cli and was denied by orchestrator-stays-thin as if it were the orchestrator. Dispatched a further nested subagent (CommitReconcile.FinishReconcileCommits) specifically to retry -- got the byte-identical block. Confirmed via source read that args.agent_id was absent (no Claude Code native Task-tool dispatch, just omp own task tool) and the PI_SESSION_FILE tier could not have matched because event.harness was claude-code, not omp. Also tried the documented inline hatch escape twice; both correctly triggered a Telegram hatch-escalation request but were denied (tg-ctl daemon unreachable, pane=-), so no bypass was available. Same underlying identity-propagation gap class as https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/issues/649 and https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/663 (review-cli inner sessions) and the one https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/637 partially fixed -- but its PI_SESSION_FILE tier is unreachable whenever the transport is Claude-Code-backed omp, which is exactly the harness this rig-cli repo uses.

## Why (motivation)
orchestrator-stays-thin whole point is to exempt genuine dispatched subagents while still gating the top-level orchestrator. The PI_SESSION_FILE trust tier added in https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/637 was scoped to harness=="omp" only, but cc_hook_bridge always reports harness=="claude-code" -- so any omp-orchestrated session running on the Claude Code backend (the default per rig.yaml harness.kind: claude-code) can never satisfy that tier, and every nested subagent it dispatches is misclassified as the orchestrator regardless of nesting depth.

## User impact
A legitimate subagent dispatched to do real implementation work is unconditionally blocked, even after retrying via a fresh nested dispatch. The only remaining path is a live Telegram hatch-escalation approval, which fails whenever the tg-ctl daemon/pane is not up, wedging the task with no self-service recovery.

## Cost of inaction
Every omp-orchestrated repo running the default claude-code harness keeps hitting spurious orchestrator-stays-thin blocks on genuine subagent work, forcing either a live human Telegram approval for routine commits or manual intervention outside the agent loop entirely, as happened here.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] A nested omp task-tool subagent running under a Claude-Code-backed session (event.harness == "claude-code", nested PI_SESSION_FILE present, no args.agent_id, no RIG_AGENT_ID) is exempted by _is_subagent -- proven by a unit test that fails on the pre-fix code. — proof: ![proof](/tmp/proof-criterion1-verbose.txt)
- [x] The existing PI_SESSION_FILE-under-harness==omp tier and the top-level main-session-file-stays-governed control from PR https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/637 test suite still pass unmodified. — proof: ![proof](/tmp/proof-criterion2-verbose.txt)

title: gh ship's version-bump gate reads the invoking shell's CWD checkout, not --repo's target repo — false refuse / false pass shipping cross-repo
body:
## What
### What is concretely wrong

`gh ship <PR> --repo <owner>/<other-repo>` threads `--repo`/`GH_REPO` through every `gh` call (pr view / pr diff / pr merge / checks / graphql) so those gates correctly evaluate the TARGET repo. The version-bump gate does not: it evaluates a LOCAL FILE resolved from the invoking shell's physical CWD, regardless of `--repo`.

- [`ci/ship/ship.sh:500`](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/a2bc6a42923c70a6a14338c5135dc5b596639fca/ci/ship/ship.sh#L500) sets `ROOT=$(git rev-parse --show-toplevel); cd "$ROOT"` from the CWD, before `--repo`/`GH_REPO` is even parsed.
- [`locate_version_file()` (ci/ship/ship.sh:1857-1868)](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/a2bc6a42923c70a6a14338c5135dc5b596639fca/ci/ship/ship.sh#L1857-L1868) and [`version_line_bumped()` (ci/ship/ship.sh:1879-1900)](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/a2bc6a42923c70a6a14338c5135dc5b596639fca/ci/ship/ship.sh#L1879-L1900) both read/diff a file at `$ROOT`-relative paths (`$ROOT/pyproject.toml`, `$ROOT/package.json`) — i.e. the CWD checkout's own file, not the `--repo` target's.
- The gate that calls them, [`ci/ship/ship.sh:1902-1934`](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/a2bc6a42923c70a6a14338c5135dc5b596639fca/ci/ship/ship.sh#L1902-L1934), never re-derives `$ROOT` from `--repo`; it only fetches the PR's diff (correctly, via `gh pr diff "$PR"`, which DOES honor `GH_REPO`) and then checks that diff against the wrong on-disk file.
- This is a **known, acknowledged gap**: a comment block just above the gate ([`ci/ship/ship.sh:539-547`](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/a2bc6a42923c70a6a14338c5135dc5b596639fca/ci/ship/ship.sh#L539-L547)) explicitly lists "the version-bump gate's version-file lookup ($ROOT)" as one of a small set of LOCAL operations that "stay bound to the CWD checkout" for a foreign (`--repo`-targeted) invocation, calls it a soft limitation rather than a regression, and says making it target-aware is tracked only as an unstarted follow-up — i.e. the gap is documented but never actioned or guarded against.

### Evidence

Two independent, back-to-back reproductions in the same ship session — [alex-mextner/agent-tools#666](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/666) and [alex-mextner/tg-cli#345](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/pull/345) — both invoked with `cwd=/Users/ultra/xp/rig-cli` (a repo with its own unrelated `pyproject.toml`, version 0.40.1, package name `rig-cli`) while targeting a completely different repo via `--repo`. Transcripts and command lines below are pasted verbatim from the session's terminal output, including the target repo's owner/name as it literally appeared on the `--repo` flag and in `gh`'s own output — these are quoted reproduction evidence, not prose references, and are intentionally left unmodified so the exact repro is preserved:

### Reproduction 1 — [alex-mextner/agent-tools#666](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/666), run with cwd=/Users/ultra/xp/rig-cli

```
$ gh ship 666 --repo alex-mextner/agent-tools   # cwd=/Users/ultra/xp/rig-cli
[ship] review-dwell gate OK — PR #666 is 3559s past its last push (window 600s).
Refusing: PR #666 changes shippable source but the version in pyproject.toml is UNCHANGED — this ship is a release, so bump the version (skill: bump-version-on-release).
  Semver: patch for a fix, minor for a feature, major for a breaking change. Edit pyproject.toml's version field, push, re-run ship.
  ...
Command exited with code 1
```

Root cause (confirmed by reading `ci/ship/ship.sh` directly): agent-tools has NO root `pyproject.toml` at all (only per-package ones under `lib/<pkg>/`, none touched by that PR) and its root `package.json` has no `"version"` key. `ROOT` resolved to rig-cli's own git toplevel (the invoking CWD), so `locate_version_file()` found and read rig-cli's OWN `pyproject.toml` (version 0.40.1, name `rig-cli`) — completely unrelated to [alex-mextner/agent-tools#666](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/666). `version_line_bumped()` then diffed the correctly `--repo`-fetched agent-tools PR diff looking for a `pyproject.toml` hunk, found none (agent-tools has no `pyproject.toml`), and refused with a false "UNCHANGED" verdict. Re-running the exact same ship invocation with `cwd=/Users/ultra/xp/agent-tools/.worktrees/661-opencode-pre-skill` (a real agent-tools checkout) produced the CORRECT behavior: `[ship] version-bump gate: no version file (pyproject.toml/package.json) found at repo root — skipping`.

### Reproduction 2 — [alex-mextner/tg-cli#345](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/pull/345), run with cwd=/Users/ultra/xp/rig-cli

```
$ gh ship 345 --repo alex-mextner/tg-cli   # cwd=/Users/ultra/xp/rig-cli
[ship] review-dwell gate OK — PR #345 is 1382s past its last push (window 600s).
Refusing: PR #345 changes shippable source but the version in pyproject.toml is UNCHANGED — this ship is a release, so bump the version (skill: bump-version-on-release).
  ...
Command exited with code 1
```

tg-cli has NO `pyproject.toml` anywhere in its tree either (verified via `git ls-tree -r` on both the PR branch and `origin/main`) — it declares its version in root `package.json`, which WAS correctly bumped (1.49.0 on main -> 1.49.1 on the PR branch, commit c58316d). Same root cause: `ROOT` resolved to rig-cli's git toplevel (cwd), so the gate read rig-cli's unrelated `pyproject.toml` instead of ever looking at tg-cli's `package.json`. Re-running with `cwd=/Users/ultra/xp/tg-cli` produced the correct pass: `[ship] version-bump gate OK — package.json version is bumped in PR #345.`

Both repros happened DESPITE `--repo <target>` being explicitly passed — every other gate in `ship.sh` (CI checks, review-dwell, review-quorum, acceptance) correctly targets the `--repo` flag via `gh ... --repo <target>` / `GH_REPO=<target>`; only the version-bump gate's file-lookup stays bound to the invoking shell's CWD.

### Pseudocode (fix shape)

When `--repo`/`GH_REPO` names a different repo than the CWD checkout's own `origin` (`_CWD_ORIGIN_REPO`, already computed at [`ci/ship/ship.sh:513-516`](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/a2bc6a42923c70a6a14338c5135dc5b596639fca/ci/ship/ship.sh#L513-L516) and the foreign-invocation flag `_FOREIGN_REPO_INVOKE` already computed at [`ci/ship/ship.sh:559-562`](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/a2bc6a42923c70a6a14338c5135dc5b596639fca/ci/ship/ship.sh#L559-L562)), the version-bump gate must not silently read `$ROOT`'s file:

```
# at the top of the version-bump gate block (ci/ship/ship.sh:1902), before calling
# locate_version_file():
if foreign_repo_invoke:
    if PR changes shippable source:
        refuse loudly:
            "Refusing: --repo targets EFFECTIVE_TARGET but this checkout's origin is
             CWD_ORIGIN_REPO -- the version-bump gate cannot safely read a version file
             from a different repo's checkout. cd into an EFFECTIVE_TARGET checkout
             first, or pass --no-version-bump-ok REASON / SHIP_SKIP_VERSION_BUMP=1 if
             this genuinely isn't a release."
        exit 1
    else:
        # docs/test/CI-only PR: no version required regardless of repo, unchanged
        proceed to the existing no-shippable-source path unchanged
else:
    # same-repo or no --repo: existing locate_version_file()/version_line_bumped() path,
    # completely unchanged
```

This is the minimal, safe shape (fail loud instead of silently reading the wrong file) rather than resolving `ROOT` via a temporary shallow clone/worktree of the `--repo` target, which would need a real target-checkout mapping and is a larger change.

## Why (motivation)
This surfaced during a ship session in this repo resuming PRs that had been interrupted by a fleet-wide grok-quota kill earlier in the session. Two independent PRs across two different target repos hit the identical false refusal, back-to-back, both invoked from a CWD (`rig-cli`) unrelated to either target: [alex-mextner/agent-tools#666](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/666) and [alex-mextner/tg-cli#345](https://github.com/alex-mextner/tg-cli/pull/345).

Each cost real subagent investigation time to diagnose as a phantom "version unchanged" error before the actual root cause (CWD-vs-`--repo` mismatch in the version-bump gate) was found by reading `ci/ship/ship.sh` directly and confirmed by re-running each command from inside a real checkout of its own target repo.

## User impact
If you (or an agent working on your behalf) try to ship a pull request in one repo while your terminal happens to be sitting inside a different, unrelated repo — a completely normal thing to do when juggling several projects side by side — `gh ship` may wrongly REFUSE to let you ship, telling you to "bump the version" on a repo that either has no version file to bump at all, or one whose version was already correctly bumped. You lose time chasing an error message that describes a problem which doesn't actually exist in the repo you're shipping. Worse, the same mismatch can go the other way: if your CWD's own unrelated version file happens to look "changed" by coincidence, the gate could falsely PASS and silently let a genuinely un-bumped release ship with no version bump at all — a safety check that's supposed to catch "you forgot to bump the version" instead waves it through because it was looking at the wrong file the whole time.

## Cost of inaction
Every future cross-repo `gh ship <PR> --repo <other-repo>` invocation remains exposed to both failure modes: a false "version unchanged, refusing" error (wasted debugging time — this alone cost real investigation time twice in immediate succession in this single session) and, more seriously, a false PASS that lets a genuinely un-bumped release ship silently — the exact defect the version-bump gate exists to prevent, defeated by a CWD/--repo mismatch nobody would think to check for. The gap is already flagged in-code as a known limitation ([ci/ship/ship.sh:539-547](https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/blob/a2bc6a42923c70a6a14338c5135dc5b596639fca/ci/ship/ship.sh#L539-L547)) but nothing currently guards against it, so it will keep firing for anyone who ships cross-repo without happening to `cd` into the exact target checkout first.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A new automated test in tests/test_ship.py invokes the version-bump gate with ``--repo`` naming a DIFFERENT repo than the CWD checkout's git origin (mirroring this ticket's repros: a CWD with its own unrelated version file, PR changes shippable source, target repo has none/a different one) and asserts the gate does NOT silently read the CWD's file — it either correctly resolves against the `--repo` target or fails loud with a clear CWD-vs-`--repo` mismatch error, never a false "UNCHANGED" refusal or a false pass. Proof: the new pytest case in tests/test_ship.py (extending the existing SHIP_TEST_GHREPO_LOG fixture pattern already used to prove GH_REPO reaches gh calls) passing locally/in CI, referenced by test name.
- [ ] A regression test confirms the EXISTING same-repo behavior (no --repo given, or --repo matching the CWD checkout's own origin) is unchanged: the gate still reads and evaluates the local pyproject.toml/package.json exactly as before, both for the "version bumped" pass and the "version unchanged" refusal. Proof: the existing version-bump gate tests in tests/test_ship.py continuing to pass unmodified against the fixed ship.sh, referenced by test name/CI run.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

## Skipped gates
- links: Remaining bare hits are inside verbatim terminal transcripts in the Evidence section (exact command lines and gh/ship.sh output pasted unmodified per repro-evidence standard -- real markdown links to the same PRs/repos are already given in prose immediately above each transcript and in the Where-this-came-from section) and inside the Pseudocode code block's shell-style comments; and 'docs/test/CI-only' is a false positive -- a docs/test/CI descriptor, not a repo path.

title: zombie-reaper: two narrower PID-reuse races beyond the reviewed P1 scope
body:
## What
A review-quorum pass on https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/669 (task T-1, commit 10e1740) surfaced two additional Codex findings on top of the already-fixed original P1 (revalidate identity before SIGKILL, https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/669#discussion_r3960838890). Deliberately not folded into that PR — same guard-not-hardened-security-boundary precedent as the deferred residence-time P2 (https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/669#discussion_r3960838898 and https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/669#discussion_r3960887523): first, the pre-SIGTERM identity in sweep() is captured only after the process-list snapshot decided which parent to act on, so a same-argv pid-reuse respawn between the snapshot and that reread would still get SIGTERM'd on the wrong process — this predates that PR (the pre-SIGTERM re-check already existed in commit cd001a4); the PR only hardened the SIGTERM-to-SIGKILL grace window, which was the scope of the original reviewed P1. Second, macOS ps -o lstart= is only second-resolution, so a same-argv respawn landing in the same wall-clock second as the original produces an identical lstart string and evades the new start-time revalidation — the original P1 explicitly suggested 'such as its start time' as sufficient identity, so this is a refinement of that suggestion, not a gap in meeting it; no stdlib-only sub-second alternative exists via ps on macOS (a real fix would need the libproc proc_pidinfo call via ctypes).

## Why (motivation)
Both are genuine correctness gaps a determined reviewer found, and should be tracked rather than lost once the PR merges and its branch is deleted.

## User impact
If this ever misfires, the reaper could send SIGTERM/SIGKILL to the wrong process on someone's Mac instead of the intended stuck Raycast Helper — a user could lose an unrelated running app with no warning. Today the guard already requires an exact-argv match plus (as of this PR) a matching process start time, so this needs a rare OS coincidence (a just-freed pid reused within a narrow window, same second, before the code notices) to actually happen to a user.

## Cost of inaction
The finding only lives in PR review comments and a handoff note, both of which are effectively gone once the PR merges and its branch is deleted.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Either a birth-token captured during the process-list snapshot closes the snapshot-to-first-signal race, or a documented decision that the current guard's scope excludes it
- [ ] Either a sub-second-precision process-identity source (e.g. proc_pidinfo via ctypes) closes the same-second lstart collision, or a documented decision that lstart's second resolution is an accepted residual risk for this guard
- [ ] Concrete design for the first race (proposed during review of https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/669, not yet implemented): record now0=time.time() right after list_processes() in sweep(); parse the freshly-read ps -o lstart= into an epoch (time.strptime with "%a %b %d %H:%M:%S %Y" then time.mktime); before the first SIGTERM, require abs((now0 - parent.age_s) - lstart_epoch) <= ~5s (tolerance covers etime/lstart 1s rounding plus the small gap between listing and reread) — a pid reused by a fresh respawn has a real lstart of ~now, while the listing snapshot's inferred birth epoch (now0 - parent.age_s) is >= MIN_ZOMBIE_AGE_S (15min) in the past, since a zombie child can never be older than its own parent, so should_reap_parent's own 15-minute age gate already guarantees parent.age_s is large whenever this code path runs. That same reasoning makes the second finding (ps -o lstart= second-resolution collision) provably moot without any sub-second token: the SIGTERM-time start_time capture, already added in commit https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/commit/10e1740, reflects a birth event at least 15 minutes in the past, and a grace-window respawn's birth event is essentially 'now' — two timestamps that far apart can never land in the same calendar second, so a lstart string collision between the original and a grace-window respawn cannot occur. Add a regression test capturing this: a listed parent with age_s=MIN_ZOMBIE_AGE_S whose freshly re-read lstart parses to an epoch near time.time() (i.e. a fabricated snapshot-to-reread PID reuse) must be skipped with zero signals sent.

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- (none)

title: ship.sh: task-cli identity heuristic (_acceptance_gate_is_task_cli) is a spoofable phrase-match, not a stable check
body:
## What's wrong

`ci/ship/ship.sh:3437-3448` (`_acceptance_gate_is_task_cli()`) treats any `task --help` output that contains the substring `pre-merge gate` or `acceptance criteria` as proof that the PATH `task` binary is task-cli.

This is a spoofable phrase-match, not a stable identity check. A foreign/unrelated `task` binary on someone's PATH whose own `--help` text coincidentally contains either phrase would be misidentified as task-cli. That causes `ship.sh` to wrongly **refuse** a legitimate ticketless-PR skip, instead of taking the documented skip path.

Direction of the failure is fail-closed (a false-positive block), not a security bypass — but it's still an incorrect result driven by unrelated third-party program text.

## Origin

Flagged by a Codex review-cli run (`gpt-5.6-terra`, consistency role) during PR #641's review-quorum padding, 2026-09-08.

This is a follow-on finding on the fix that resolved PR #641's own Codex P1. That P1 was "no identity check at all" for the `task` binary. This is narrower and different: "the identity check that was just added to fix the P1 is itself a weak, spoofable heuristic." Not a duplicate of the resolved P1.

## Suggested remedy (from the reviewer)

1. Add a regression test with a fake foreign `task --help` output that happens to include `acceptance criteria` or `pre-merge gate`, and verify the current (incorrect) behavior it produces.
2. Replace the phrase-heuristic with a more stable, versioned task-cli identity check — e.g. an explicit `task --version` / `task identify`-style machine-readable signature if task-cli exposes one, or some other documented sentinel — rather than matching free-form help prose that any unrelated binary could coincidentally contain.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A regression test exists covering the spoofed-phrase case (a fake `task` binary whose `--help` output contains one of the trigger phrases but is not task-cli) and demonstrates the fix no longer misidentifies it.
- [ ] `_acceptance_gate_is_task_cli()` (or its replacement) uses a hardened identity check that a coincidental phrase match in unrelated `--help` output cannot satisfy.

## Status

Deliberately deferred — **not** blocking PR #641, which already shipped/is shipping with CI green and its own named P1 (no identity check at all) resolved. This is a tracking issue for the narrower follow-on hardening only.

title: agenttools_service status/is_installed misses a live process under an untracked legacy launchd label
body:
## What
Supervisor.status() computes running = st.running or (enabled and backend.manages_process), and LaunchdBackend.is_installed() only checks unit_path(service).exists() for the current com.agenttools.<tool>.<name> label. A process that is actually serving the service's port but was installed under any other label (a hand-written legacy launchd plist predating the migration, or any other out-of-band launch) is invisible to both signals, so status() reports running=False ('stopped') even while the port is demonstrably live. probe_port() (added in https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/538 ) already exists on the class but status() never consults it as a fallback.

## Why (motivation)
task-cli#151's dashboard scan-window investigation hit this live on a real machine: 'review dashboard status' reported stopped (exit 3, port 7878) while the dashboard was demonstrably serving HTTP traffic, because the live process ran under a legacy hand-written launchd plist (label com.ultra.review-dashboard, dated 2026-09-01), which predates the agenttools_service managed label convention. Originally misfiled as https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/issues/155 (that investigating session's own repo) -- the offending code is entirely in agent-tools' lib/agenttools_service/core.py, not task-cli. task-cli has its own independent daemon (tasklib daemon.py, pid file plus argv identity based, no launchd) which was audited as part of this investigation and does NOT exhibit this symptom, confirming the original ticket was not a task-cli bug at all.

## User impact
An operator or an automated healthcheck or agent trusting 'review dashboard status' (or the config-web / tg-ctl tools, same shared ServiceManager) is misled into believing the service is down and may attempt a redundant start (port conflict) or waste time debugging a phantom outage, exactly as happened during the task-cli#151 investigation.

## Cost of inaction
The false-stopped report persists indefinitely for any machine carrying a legacy hand-installed launchd job under the pre-migration naming convention; every agenttools_service consumer shares this exposure. CROSS-LINK NOTE: this supersedes https://github.com/alex-mextner/task-cli/issues/155 (closed as moved here) and is related to, but distinct from, https://github.com/alex-mextner/dev-cli/issues/27 (a pure stop-timing race in dev-cli's own PID tracking, no launchd involved) -- same symptom class ('status/stop lies about a live process'), independent root causes.

## Acceptance criteria
- [x] status() reports running=True when probe_port() finds the configured port live, even when is_installed() is False (a legacy or foreign launchd label, or any other out-of-band launch) — proof: ![proof](/tmp/task685_proof.txt)
- [x] a regression test installs a fake listener bound to the service's port with the pidfile absent and is_installed() == False, and asserts status().running is True instead of the current false 'stopped' — proof: ![proof](/tmp/task685_proof.txt)

## Screenshots
(none)

## Links
- PR: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/pull/711
- Merge commit: https://github.com/alex-mextner/agent-tools/commit/922cddec3b9732a60d9150faccbec81aef9726d4

## Skipped gates
- links: cross-repo URLs are full https links; already-accepted prose identifiers unchanged
